GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

PHILIP NORBOURNE MYERS
GRA N D MASTER

PHIL N. MYERS
Grand Ma ster
October 3, 1958 - October 2. 1959

Philip N. Myers, Grand Master of Masons in California for the
term ending October 2, 1959, has endeared himself to the craft
throughout California and Hawaii by his kind and fraternal approach
to all problems and by his unremitting zeal and devotion in the discharge of his duties, not only as Grand Master but also in his previous
years of service to Masonry.
He is a humble and a gentle man, but his humbleness should not
deceive those who might seek to move him from a position which he is
convinced is right. He is also a member of that group of which our
country is justly proud, "a self made man."
He was born in Hemet. California, on January 12, 1897, the son of
Philip Norbourne Myers, Sr. and Alma Gray Newman Myers. H is
father was associated with land development projects in Kern and
Riverside counties. Both his parents are now deceased. H e has one
living brother, Harvey H . Myers, a member of Orange Grove Lodge. at
Orange. California.
In 1909 the family moved to Los Angeles. Our Grand Master attended grade school at 24th Street and Western Avenue, where the
principal was the sister of Past Grand Master James A. Foshay, and
in 1912 entered Los Angeles High School. In those days Southern
California was not enjoying its present high level of prosperity, and
financial conditions forced him to leave school and seek gainful employment. H owever, he continued to pursue an education in night school
and correspondence courses, specializing in accounting and management with a diligence that is manifested by his success in later life.
Prior to the entry of the United States into World War I, he was
employed for a time by the Southern Pacific C ompany in a nd around
Los Angeles in several capacities. Following this, he entered the Army,
and the end of the war found him in the O fficers Training School at
Camp Pike in Arkansas.
After employment in an accounting a nd ma nagement capacity with
several firms , including the Los Angeles Motor Transit Company and
the Fresno branch of Mack Trucks, he entered the service of The
Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway in 1923 and remained with
it for six years, rising from accountant to system traveling accounta nt
and then to senior traveling accountant. Most of this service was in
California but for a short period he was in Chicago.
The 1929 depression found him with the credit department of International Harvester Company at Los Angeles, from which position he
was called, on June 16. 1930, to become Auditor for the McCloud River
Railroad Company in northern California .
The McCloud River Ra ilroad Company is a short line railroad, its
chief business being the servicing of the lumber industry in that heavily

2

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

wooded and mountaino us section of the State. Our Grand Master was
with this railroad continuou sly from 1930 until April. 1952, serving
successively as Auditor, Assistant Superinte ndent. General Manager,
Treasurer , Vice-Pres ident and President.
His ability and efficiency in the manageme nt of the McCloud River
Railroad attracted wide spread attention and resulted in his being called,
on April l, 1952, to serve as President of Trona Railway Company ,
which position he still holds.
The Trona Railway has headquart ers at Los Angeles and operations
at Trona, in the desert area of Kern and San Bernardin o Counties. It,
also, is a short line railroad, a common carrier wholly owned by American Potash and Chemical Corporati on, and carries chemical products
from Trona and Westend (both on Searles Dry Lake) to a connection
with the interconti nental railroad system. Since assuming this position,
our Grand Master has been a resident of Los Angeles, in the Brentwoo d
area.
From 1943 to 1958 he served as a director of the American Short
Line Railroad Association, composed of some 275 industrial and short
ine common carrier railroads. From 1954 to 1958 he was ~ts VicePresident for the Pacific Region. He declined re-election prior to his
installatio n as Grand Master, but has now been again elected to its
Board of Directors.
Married to Anne Fletcher Thorp on January 15, 1927, he and his
wife brought to the union children of previous marriages : Phyllis Myers
Morgan, now living in McCioud where her husband, Allyn K. Morgan,
is a member of McC!oud Lodge; Mary Ellen Thorp Workman , who
resides in Monrovia with her children and husband, George T. Workman, a member of Monrovia Lodge; and Robert Grant Thorp, also a
member of Mc Cloud Lodge, but now living in Sacramen to with his
wife and child.
Our Grand Master was raised in McCloud Lodge on January 23,
1945, served as Senior Deacon and Senior Warden, and was its Master
in 1947.
He was Grand Standard Bearer of the Grand Lodge in 1948, appointed to the Pay of Members Committe e in 1949 and a member of
the Finance Committe e from 1950 to 1955. He was elected Junior Grand
Warden in 1955, Senior Grand Warden in 1956. Deputy Grand
Master in 1957 and Grand Master in 1958.
He is a member of Cyrus Chapter No. 15, Royal Arch Masons.
Yreka; Los Angeles Command ery No. 9. K. T., Los Angeles; the Los
Angeles Bodies of the Scottish Rite; St. Gabriel Conclave No. 11, Red
Cross of Constanti ne; AI Malaikah Shrine; and the McCloud Chapter
of the Order of the Eastern Star. He is also a member of the Jonathan
Club in Los Angeles and of the Los Angeles Athletic Club.

DR. EDWARD D. KoHLSTEDT, Grand Chaplain

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Members of Grand Lodge:
Permit me, first of all, to voice my appreciation of the privilege of
serving as your Grand Chaplain during the past Masonic year. Developments that led to this appointment seem to have been providential.
Saturday evening. March 15, 1958, I served as substitute Chaplain
at the Installation Ceremony of our newly organized El Camino Research Lodge in Redwood City. The then Deputy Grand Master Phil
N. Myers, whom I met for the first time, conducted that ceremony as a
substitute for Grand Master Leo E. Anderson, who was unable to
be present.
The next morning, after taking Deputy Grand Master Phil N. Myers
to the San Francisco International Airport, I had a telephone call from
Worshipful Master Thelo A. Perrott of Josiah W. Roller Lodge No.
761, who inquired: "Brother Ed, would you be interested in an appointment as Grand Chaplain of the Grand Lodge of Freemasons in
California?"
Speechless with surprise for a few moments, I finally replied: "Being
a Mason, who wouldn't be interested in such a challenging service opportunity. However, it is very unlikely that a man of my age will be
entrusted with that responsibility."
My reaction was prompted by a couplet at the close of a letter from
an eighty-two-year-old lady, a long time friend, who shared this bit of
octogenarian philosophy:
"I am fully aware that my youth has been spent.
My get-and-go has got up and went.
But I really don't mind when I think, with a grin,
Of all the grand places my get-up has been."
Due to the .r ecommendations of Past Grand Master L. Harold
Anderson, Past Master of Palo Alto Lodge No. 346, and many Masonic
brethren, I was thrilled by this message from Deputy Grand Master
Phil N. Myers on August 25, 1958: "This will confirm that I have
included you in my list of appointive officers for 1958-59 as Grand
Chaplain."
It has been a year of life-enriching activities and associations with
as fine a group of Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors, Past Masters and
Masters as any one could choose for personal fellowship and cooperative service. To our Most Worshipful Grand Master, his administrative and appolntive officers, I am immeasurably indebted for their
brotherly consideration, personal courtesies and wholehearted friend-

ship. Despite calendar limitations that are about to alter our official

"God has not promised skies always blue.

A strenuous schedule has made the going a bit rough, at times. A
few bumps and bruises had to be reckoned with, en route, but none
of us became involved in a dilemma like that portrayed by Columnist
Jerome Beatty in the March I, 1958 issue of Saturday Review. He
didn't say whether it was after a Cornerstone or Dedication Ceremony,
but vouches for this letter from a Barbados, Island of Antilles bricklayer to the firm for which he works:
"Respected Sir: When I got to the building, I found the hurricane
had knoc_ked some bri~ks off the top. I rigged up a beam at the top
of the bu1ldmg and hoisted up a couple barrels of bricks. After I fixed
the building, there was a lot of bricks left. I hoisted up an empty
barrel and secured the line at the bottom. Then I went up and filled
the empty barrel with the extra bricks, and went to the bottom to
cast off the line.
"Unfortunately, the barrel of bricks was heavier than I a nd, before
knew what was happening, the barrel started down and jerked me
off the ground. I decided to hang on and, half way up, met the barrel
coming down and got a severe blow on the shoulder. I continued
to the top, banging my head against the beam and getting my fingers
jammed in the pulley.
. " When the barrel hit the ground its bottom burst, spilling out the

must have lost my presence of mind, because I let go of the line, so
the barrel came down again, giving me another heavy blow on the
head and putting me in the hospital. I respectfully request sick leave."
. Your appointive officers endorse the validity of calendar limitations
m an organization like Freemasonry. but none of them is asking "sick
leave."

S ocial and spiritual stability is a desirable state of mind and heart.
It is within the realm of practical possibilities. Among our Old Testa~ent pr~phets. no name has greater significance than Isaiah. Despite
his pressmg personal and political problems, Isaiah's faith, observation
and experience taught him the secret of social and spiritual stability.
Such an achiev_ement ena?,led a mere man to talk to Almighty God in
these confidential terms: Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace whose
mind is staid on Thee : because he trusteth in Thee." He had learned
that:

"But God has promised strength for the day.

Modern social and spiritual statesmen, who have earned the right
to be heard and heeded, remind us that
"We are living. we are dwelling
In a grand and awful time;
In an age on ages telling:
To be living is sublime."

The signs of our times are pregnant with possibilities of weal
or woe for mankind. For the first time 1n human history, an aerial trail
has been blazed from the earth to the moon, American and Russian
satellites orbit our planet, even the sun, and transmit scientific information from regions beyond man's telescopic vision. Space ships.
interplanetary travel at incredible speeds, dreams that are bound to
become realities, are now familiar topics of conversation and conjecture.
It took the ship that brought my father from Northern Germany to
the United States of America six weeks to cross the Atlantic Ocean.
Lockheed Aire.r aft's June 17, 1959 news release informs us that, by
1965, man will be able to shrink this ensmalling world to the size of a
breakfast table. Using our existing airports, 2200-mile-an-hour jet
transports will pick up passengers, after a late breakfast in London,
at 11 a.m., British time; bring them to New York City by 9 :30 a .m ..
Eastern time; and land them in Los Angeles for another breakfast at
7: 45 a.m., Pacific time.
Another total eclipse of the sun, visible throughout this area in
case of a clear day, has been scheduled for October 26, 2151. You
may not be interested in that event; for, by that time the youngest
person here should be engaged io celestial activities. But all of us
ought to be interested in the fact that such a prediction is not a guess,
but a guarantee; that its fulfillment is an absolute certainty. Why?
God's vast physical universe of suns, moons, stars and solar systems, the very thought of which staggers one's imagination, is governed
by such exact. changeless laws that astronomers and scientists are able

12

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

to compute and predict the advent of this and other heavenly phenome na
many years in advance, even to the moment of their actual occurren ce.
Scientific achievements can do much toward the enrichme nt or impoverish ment of life; the help or hurt of humanity ; the lengthen ing or
shortenin g of man's earthly span; the blessing or cursing of succeedi ng
generatio ns. Yet, despite its amazing powers and possibilities, science
has limitatio ns: it Jacks the facilities to evaluate factors in the realm of
religion and life. Science alone isn't equipped to ensure a realizatio n of
man's basic need: social and spiritual stability. Scientific areas of activity
and research are admitted ly mathema tical. not moral; material, not
spiritual ; matters of the head, rather than of the heart.
But there is no conflict between true science and real religion. The
antagoni sms that sometimes clutter their relations are created by pseudoscientist s and opiniona ted theologia ns, who take themselves too seriously. Both could render a more construc tive service to mankind by stressing
basic beliefs in realities that matter most, instead of majoring in unwarranted assumpti ons and theologic al technicalities. In recent years. organized religion has made substant ial strides toward cooperat ion and
unity, but we still have a long way to go in that direction .
The late Dr. Wilfred Grenfell , famous medical missiona ry to the
poverty stricken fishing communities of Labrado r and Newfoun dland,
once advertise d for an artificial limb to substitut e a leg lost by one of
his amputee s. The Methodi st widow of a Baptist husband , who had been
similarly afflicted, saw the advertise ment and sent her deceased husband's artificial limb to Doctor Grenfell . who reported as follows:
' Tm an Episcopa lian. I advertise in a Congreg ational periodical for
an artificial limb. A Methodi st woman sends me a Baptist leg, which I
fit to the body of a Catholic fisherman. who now has a truly interdeno minational understa nding." A sequel to this factual story speaks for itself.
Address ing an interdeno mination al gatherin g in a large Detroit
church on "Cooper ation and Organiza tional Unity," I used the Grenfell
experien ce as an illustrati on. An ardent Baptist sister in the audience
wrote me a note on a collection envelope and placed it on the plate, in
lieu of an offering. At the close of the service, the usher handed me· her
note, and this is what she said: "But you'll have to admit, Sir, that the
Baptists were the only ones who had a leg to stand on."
Freemas onry is a fraternal brotherh ood. not a religious organiza tion. Our craft and the church, whateve r its name or formal expressio n
of faith, are neither competit ors of nor substitut es for each other.
Masonic teaching s are intersper sed with biblical tenets, their moral
implications and spiritual significance. but we are content to stress these
two basic concepts : the fact of God, Supreme Architec t of the Universe; and the authority of the Holy Bible as our guide for faith and
practice in the laborato ry of life.

The challenge of our times prompts us to pray with Josiah G.
Holland:
"God give us men! A time like this demands
Strong minds. great hearts. true faith. steady hands :
Men whom the lust of office does not kill;
Men whom the spoils of office cannot buy;
Men who possess opinions and a will;
Men who have honor; who will not lie;
Men who can stand before the demagog ue
And damn his ftattering s without winking:
Tall men, sun-crow ned. who live above the fog
In public duty and private thinking ."
Our current internati onal situation . with its unholy rivalries and
terrible tensions. is the most disturbin g social and spiritual problem
humanity has ever known. Whe.n we are realistic about the alarming
status of our twentieth century world, with so many areas afflicted by
doubt, dismay and despair; when we face the fact that, in certain
countries . "Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of Happine ss" is as meaning less an objective to their dictatori al overlord s as it was in the bloody
arena of ancient Rome's Coliseum . it is immeasu rably heartening to
remembe r that
God's Spiritual Universe is governed by as exact and changeless
laws as those that govern God's Physical Universe . Moral and spiritual
values are real and permane nt. Scriptur al assuranc es underHir d a
functiona l faith in eternal verities. God's limitless love and matchles s
mercy are unalterab le. Biblical steps toward the ach ieve ment of social
and spiritual stability are as clearly defined as they ever were: an
inquiring . receptive mind: a penitent, purposef ul heart; and a realistic.
functiona l faith. The Bible says: "Withou t faith it is impossible to
please God : He that cometh to God must believe that God is, and that
He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek Him." (Hebrew s I I: 6)
The superstructure of social and spiritual stability is undergir ded by
three basic concepts that merit construc tive consider ation and action:
First-F aith in the fact of God. Architec t of the Universe , Author
of all Good. Giver of all Mercy. Creator. Enricher and Preserve r of
Life. The Psalmist tells us : "The fool hath said in his heart. there is
no God;" also. he reminds us that "The heavens declare the glory of
God. and the firmament showeth His handiwo rk." (Psalms 53: I and
19 : J ) We believe with N. K. Richards on that

"There is a God! The towering mountains cry:
Jehovah's name is blazoned on the sky;
The dancing streamlet and the golden grain,
The lightening gleam, the thunder and the rain,
The dewdrop on the lily's breast,
The tender leaf. by every breeze caressed,
The shell. whose pearly bosom ocean laves,
The seaweed, bowing to a troop of waves;
The glow of Venus, and the glare of Mars,
The tranquil beauty of the lesser stars;
The eagle, soaring in majestic flight.
The morning, bursting from the clouds of night;
The child's fond prattle and the mother's prayer.
Angelic voices. floating on the air;
Mind, heart and soul. the ever restless breath,
And all the myriad mysteries of death.
There is a God! The dying believer's hand.
Pale with disease, points to a better land,
And ere his body mingles with the sod,
He. sweetly smiling. faintly murmurs: 'God.'"
In the First Degree of Blue Lodge Masonry. you were taught
never to mention the name of the Deity, except "with that awe and
reverence which are due from the creature to his Creator."
Second-Faith in the authenticity and authority of the Holy Bible
is a crucial concept, treasured by our Masonic Fraternity as a fundamental factor in the philosophy of life. In the language of that same
Blue Lodge First Degree Charge. you were taught to regard the Holy
Bible as ''the volume of the Sacred Law; as the Great Light of your
profession; to consider it as the unerring standard of truth and justice;
and to regulate your actions by the divine precepts it contains."
Authored over a period of approximately 1500 years by nearly
forty different writers, schooled and unschooled. some of whom were
dead when others wrote, while still others of them had not yet been
born, the unity of basic biblical teachings warrants the prevalent conviction that those authors must have been inspired by the Master Mind
of the Universe; for, as John Dryden so well said:
"Whence but from heaven could men unskilled in arts,
In several ages born, in several parts,
Weave such agreeing truths; or how, or why
Should all conspire to cheat us with a lie?
Unasked their pains, ungrateful their advice,
Starving their gain, and martyrdom their price."

In 1560, the invention of printing was featured by the production
of a Holy Bible, the first book printed from movable type. Since that
historic date, our Holy Bible has maintained its place of preeminence as
the best seller among the millions of books produced by the printing
press. It is still published in more languages and dialects, read and
studied by more people of all ages, throughout the world. than any
other book. Percy Dearmer penned this factual appraisal:
"Book of Books. our people's strength,
Statesman's, teacher's, hero's treasure,
Bringing freedom, spreading truth,
Shedding light that none can measure:
Wisdom comes to those that know thee;
All the best we have, we owe thee."
Third-A realistic appreciation of the idealism taught and practiced
by the Carpenter of Nazareth. Among our great humanitarian, social
and spiritual leaders of the past, whose memory we revere, he perfected a body of idealistic teaching that has never been surpassed or
equaled. Besides . he demonstrated the validity of his idealism in the
laboratory of life. His historic ministry to mankind personalized
selfless service.
When the emissaries of John the Baptist, one of Freemasonry's
Patron Saints, sought to learn his identity and the purpose of his mission,
Jesus didn't confuse them with theological technicalities, but stressed
matters of immediate moment. saying: "Go your way and tell John what
things ye have seen and heard : how the blind see, the lame wal k, the
lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear. and to the poor the gospel of good
news is being preached." (Luke 7: 22).
Erudite definitions of religion confuse the average man. He is bothered by Dr. Henry Slosson's statement that "Religion is the perpetual
realization of God, the spiritualization of daily life." However, he has
no difficulty in understanding what Saint James meant, when he wrote :
"Pure religion and undefiled before God, the Father, is this: To visit the
fatherless and the widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.'' (Jam es 1 :27).
Dr. Albert Schweitzer , Nobel Prize-winning humanitarian, philosopher and physician, the story of whose dedicated activities in behalf of
equatorial Africa's underprivileged communities has recently been publicized, is this twentieth century's most convincing illustration of the
worthwhileness of such selfless service, stressed in the ritual of our
Masonic Hall Dedication Ceremony: "Enable us to prove to mankind
by our actions that our lives are sincerely dedicated to Thee, and to the
relief and wellbeing of our fellow creatures."
A reasonably contented, measurably productive life is the rightful

16

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

goal of every normal man. Goethe's nine prerequisites for the achievement ~! social and spiritual stability merit prayerful pondering on our
part: Health enough to make work a pleasure; wealth enough to support your needs; strength enough to battle with difficulties and overcome
them; grace enough to confess your sins and forsake them; patience
enough to toil until some good is accomplished; charity enough to see
some good in your neighbor; love enough to move you to be useful, and
helpful to others; faith enough to make real the things of God; and
hope enough to remove all anxieties concerning the future."

Benediction: "Now unto Him that is able to keep you from falling,
and to. pr~sent you faultless before the presence of His Glory with
exceedmg )Oy, to the only wise God, our Saviour, be glory and majesty,
dominion and power. both now and ever." (Jude 24-25).
DR. EDWARD D. KoHLSTEDT, Grand Chaplain.

The Grand Master announced the appointment of Past Grand
Masters Arthur M. Warren and Edgar V. Stewart, Jr. to serve on the

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
PHI L N. MYERS, Grand Master
Brethren:
The past year has been one of great activity on the part of the
Grand Master and the Grand Lodge officers. A very heavy schedule
has been followed by all of us in conducting ceremonies and attending
receptions at many points in the jurisdiction. A full lis ting of the various
functions is contained in the statistical appendix to this report. which
will appear in the printed copies and in the Proceedings.
Grand Lodge w as opened in special communication on thirty-one
different occasions : F or constitution ceremonies for eleven new lodges,
dedication ceremonies for eleven new Masonic Temples, and for cornerstone ceremonies for four public schools, three public buildings, and
three Masonic buildings. In addition to the school cornerstone ceremonies, dedication ceremonies were conducted for six public schools,
and ground breaking ceremonies for the new hospital facility at the
Masonic Home, Decoto, and for new Temples at Hemet and at Folsom.
Six new lodges were placed under dispensation nnd institution ceremonies conducted. Numerous receptions. breakfasts, dinners, and other
functions were attended throughout the jurisdiction from Lihue on the
Island of Kauai on the West to Susanville and Beckwourth on the E ast
border of California; from Tulelake and Ukiah on the North to El
Centro and Chula Vista on the South. It is estimated that through
attendance at the various Grand Lodge openings. ceremonies, receptions and other fu nc tions, the Grand Master was able to meet with
officers and members of well over 500 constituent lodges in C.:ilifornia
and Hawaii.
Several matters of unflnished business were referred to me a t the
1958 communication :

MAYA LODGE U.D.
T!LA PASS LoDGE U.D.

Of the several lodges placed under dispensation and instituted during
the year, two deserve special mention: Maya Lodge U .D. and Tila Pass
Lodge U.D .. both l~cated at Los Angeles. Membership in these lodges is
almost wholly made up of brethren of Mexican ancestry or Filipino
ancestry though. of course, the two lodges work in the English language.
The inauguration of these two lodges in the Los Angeles area should do
much to discourage clandestine membership among those of Spanishspeaking descent living in that area. and it was a great pleasure for me
to be able to place both of them under dispensation and to conduct
the institution ceremonies.

19

It came to my attention that it has been the practice for many years
for several of the larger lodges in the Los Angeles Metropolitan Area to
hold open installation ceremonies for their officers in private rooms in
hotels, clubs or other similar buildings in which public bars may be
operating. Since the ruling in 1956 which is now ~nnot~ted in the
California Masonic Code as Section 199-f. as modified m 1957 by
Section 199-g. the practice of holding such installations. which are
Masonic functions, in such buildings, is in technical conflict at least
with the ruling referred to. On investigation I found that in each case
there was no bar operating on the same floor as that in which the installation ceremony was conducted: hence in order to clarify the rulings, I
have included as Grand Master's Decision No. 8 a ruling to the effect
that such open installation ceremonies may continue to be held in .a
building in which a public bar is also operating provided that such bar ts
not on the same floor as that in which the installation is held.
Another question was also raised in connection with open installations, and that was whether a lodge. chartered for example, to meet in
the City of Los Angeles, might hold open installation cue.monies in a
hotel in the City of Beverly Hills or the City of Santa Monica. Also to
clarify the rulings. I have included as Grand Master's Decision No .. 9 a
ruling to the effect that an open installation of officers may be held m a
city or community other than the one in which a lodge is chartered to
meet provided the distance from the lodge hall is not excessive.

RECEPTION FOR THE GRAND MASTER OF NEBRASKA

YoRK RITE SovEREIGN COLLEGE

During a reception which was held for me by the officers of lnspectoral District No. 622 at Long Beach. May 14, it was my pleasure to
receive the Most Worshipful John E. Beaver. Grand Master of Masons
in Nebraska, and the Very Worshipful Carl R. Greisen, Grand Secretary of Nebraska. These Grand officers made a special trip to Long
Beach to confer a fifty-year button on Brother Arthur L. Palmer, a
distinguished resident of Long Beach, and a member of one of the
lodges in the Nebraska Jurisdiction. It was a pleasure to cooperate with
the Grand Master of Nebraska in the presentation ceremony.

I was asked to define the status of the York Rite Sovereign College.
so far as the States of California and Hawaii were concerned. Based
on information furnished me, I held that the organization was not in
existence in this jurisdiction on September 27, 1957, nor was it sponsored by or under the control of the California York Rite Bodies; hence
it had no official standing within our jurisdiction under Sections 332.1
and 332.1-a, C.M.C.
Just prior to this communication, however. the one who has been
promoting the establishment of the York Rite Sovereign College in
California has asked for reconsideration of my ruling and has presented
additional information bearing on the two points referred to above. It is .
therefore, my recommendation that the entire matter be held in abeyance and referred to the incoming Grand Master for final determination after reviewing all of the evidence.

PRINTED MATTER ISSUED BY COMMIITEES

There were several instances this year in which Grand Lodge committees or joint committees of the lodges issued printed instructions or
letters which included statements which were inadvertently, no doubt.
at variance with our law and policy. Orderly procedure would require
that all such printed matter be checked for correctness of statement
before it is issued; hence I have requested all committees preparing
printed letters, pamphlets or other communications to submit the copy
to the Grand Secretary's office and order such printed matter only
through the Grand Secretary's office.

RESEARCH PROGRAM

Reports of the Grand Lodge Committee on Research and the several
Research Lodges indicate great progress in the Research program
inaugurated several years ago. One new Research Lodge was chartered,
it being El Camino Research Lodge. located at Mountain View but

process of being formed at Fresno. All of those who have been instrumental in forwarding the important work of Masonic Education and

this most profitable enterprise.
HAWAIIAN TRIP

During the month of July the Grand Master made the customary
visit to the lodges in the Hawaiian Islands and was received everywhere
with the utmost in hospitality and good will. I attended many social
functions and met with the officers and members of all of the lodges
in the State of Hawaii. As the guest of Admiral Herbert G. Hopwood.
Commander in Chief of the Pacific Area Command, I was accorded the
privilege of laying a wreath on the partially submerged hulk of the
USS Arizona in Pearl Harbor, and was shown through the Pearl Harbor
Naval Base as a guest of Rear Admiral Robert L. Campbell, Commander
Service Force. United States Pacific Fleet.
The policy approved at the last communication of sending an Assistant Grand Lecturer to the Hawaiian Islands at regular intervals is
already producing excellent results in improvement of the ritualistic
work and in strengthening our ties with the Island Lodges.

GRAND MASTER S D ECISIONS

Compared with the large number of decisions which were rendered
a t the last communication and in prior years, your Grand Master has
been called upon this year to make relatively few. Apparently greater
familiarity with effective rulings as now carried in our excellent California Masonic Code, has resulted in fewer questions to refer to the Grand
Master. The decisions which I have made during the year are summarized in question and answer form below for your consideration:
DECISIONS

1. Question: Does C.M.C. 403-1 ( d). providing that a lodge may
invest its funds in "securities as are legal investments for California
savings banks," authorize loans such as those secured by deed of
trust on real property?
Answer: No. Real estate loans are not classified as investments

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

21

under the terminology of the California Banking Act. In banking
practice there is a marked distinction between investments and
loans. Different sections of the California Banking Act control.
The loan phase of the banking business is separate from the investment phase. Loans, for example, require appraisals, supervisions,
collections and foreclosures. The funds secured by trust deeds
are frozen. Although yielding sometimes higher rates of interest,
they cannot quickly be converted into cash at the face amount. On
a sale, a loss through discount is often the case. T he operations
required are a different type of activity than was contemplated for
lodges in the investment of lodge funds.
2. Question: Is a portion of the cost of a cornerstone for a new public
school building to be laid under Grand Lodge auspices and
Masonic ceremonies a proper lodge expense?
Answer: Yes. Section 137, C.M.C. makes cornerstone ceremonies
for a public school a program of the Grand Lodge and our constituent lodges. Since a cornerstone is essential for such ceremonies,
it may be furnished tmder Section 410, C.M.C.
3. Question: May lodge funds be used to purchase a television set for
a member who is a guest at Decoto?
Answer: Yes. This is a proper lodge expenditure for charitable
purposes under Section 409, C.M.C.
4. Question: Must minutes of special meetings be read in full at the
following stated meeting, or may they be approved "as though
read?"
Answer: They must be read in full. E very member present at a
stated meeting is entitled to know what has taken place since the
last stated meeting, and this can only be accomplished by reading
the minutes in full.
5. Question: Must a Master Mason belonging to a lodge in this
jurisdiction wait a full year before he can become a plural member
of another lodge in this jurisdiction?
Answer: No. Section 432 ( 3). C.M.C., would permit such plural
membership without the requirement for waiting a full year.
6. Question: May a building association rent to another organization
the dining hall of a temple for a lunch or dinner after which bingo
or whist is played for prizes?
Answer: No. The building association may not rent to another
organization space in a temple to do what is illegal to be done by
a Masonic organization. ( C.M.C. 199-f; 685-c, d, £, g.)
7. Question: May a Masonic Building Association which leases
ground floor space in its Temple to a department store permit such
store to maintain a package liquor department. when such department is incidental to the operation of the department store and is
not advertised as a liquor store?
Answer: No. The sale of alcoholic liquors in Masonic Temple

22

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

property under any conditions is prohibited by prior rulings now
annotated as Section 199-b, C.M.C.
8. Question: May a lodge hold an open installation of officers in a
hotel. non-Masonic private club or other similar building, in which
one or more public bars are in operation?
Answer: It may, provided such a public bar is not on the same
floor as the room in which the open installation ceremony is held,
and further provided that the provisions of Sections 403 and 324,
C.M.C., are complied with.
9. Question: May a lodge hold open installation ceremonies in a
building located in a municipality or community other than the one
in which the lodge is authorized by its charter to meet?
Answer: Yes. Provided that provisions of Section 324-a, C.M.C..
are complied with, and that the distance from the lodge hall to the
place of open installation is not excessive.
I 0. Question: May a lodge or temple corporation pay a monthly pension to a Past Master who has served it for many years as
Secretary?
Answer: No. Such an expenditure would not be permissible under
Sections 409, 410 and 411, C.M.C.
11. Question: May Masonic funeral services be held for a brother who
has previously specified in his will that his body be turned over to
a medical research organization and, therefore, the body is not to
be present at the ceremony?
Answer: No. By previously directing disposition of his body, the
brother has, by implication at least, indicated a desire not to have
a Masonic funeral. The circumstances in this instance are different
from those referred to in Section 605-g, C.M.C.
In closing the year, may I express to the brethren of the Grand
Lodge my sincere thanks and appreciation for the honor of serving as
Grand Master, for the many courtesies ex tended to me and to the other
Grand Lodge officers throughout the entire jurisdiction, and for the
enthusiastic cooperation on the part of all.
I particularly thank the Deputy Grand Master. the Senior and Junior
Grand Wardens, for their support and cooperation, and all of the
officers and committee members who have so faithfully attended the
various functions and who have contributed so greatly to the success of
the year's work. To the Inspectors and Masters and Wardens of the
various districts, my thanks also for the kindnesses shown to me and to
the Grand Lodge officers in arranging transportation and hotel accommodations. and for the careful planning which went into every one of
the functions.

EXHIBIT
PROCLAMATION
FORTIETH ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

Public Schools Week in California will be observed April 27 to
May 2, inclusive.
The theme for this year's observance will be "Keep faith with our
country- Know and support the public schools."
Since the inception of Public Schools Week forty years ago, Masons
of California have diligently promoted observance of the week and hav~
increasingly taken advantage of the opportunity for visiting. encouraging

Again, we wil observe Masonic Homes Endowment Month during
May, 1959.
Here is our opportunity to share with those less fortunate than we,
in making sure that our two great charitable institutions, the Masonic
Home for the older folks at Decoto, and the Home for children at
Covina, are adequately financed, and that for the future they will
continue to provide the loving care which they now afford to those
who need it.
Contributing to such a cause does not deprive us of anythingindeed we are immeasurably benefited ourselves by thus giving expression to our Masonic ideals. We welcome the opportunity to participate,
with unselfish and heartfelt gratitude for the many blessings we enjojy
through our Masonic association.
This proclamation is to be read at stated meetings held during the
months of April and May, 1959.

PROCLAMATION

RESOLUTIONS

The Constitution of the United States is the greatest document for
the government of a people ever evolved by the mind of man. As the
years pass by this remarkable instrument demonstrates again an.cl again
its flexibility in meeting the demands of a growing nation without losing
its power to maintain and support democratic self government.
We, as citizens of this great nation and especially as Masons, are
proud of the work of our forefathers and of those among them who were
members of our Craft, who had the foresight and wisdom to forge this
great instrument of human liberty, born as it was out of sorrow, suffering, hardship and self-sacrifice. As citizens and as Masons we take
time each year to pause and meditate on these things. to give joyful
thanks for the blessings we enjoy, and for the bountiful opportunities
that are ours as free men in a free land.
Therefore, I hereby proclaim that each lodge in this jurisdiction,
independently or in conjunction with other lodges or by Masonic Districts, shall set apart one day during the month of September or October,
1959, but preferably in September, of which the 17th day is the one
hundred seventy-second anniversary of the signing of the Constitution
of the United States, to memorialize the occasiQll in the giving of a
suitable program which will be open to the general public. Further,
that when several lodges join in the same program, no lodge among
them shall hold a meeting or schedule an event, for any other purpose
on the appointed day, except its stated meeting.
It is especially recommended that the lodges endeavor to make the
observance a community event, in which the entire community takes
part and to which the general public will be invited.
This proclamation to be read at the first meeting following its receipt
and at the September stated meeting.
Dated: July 31, 1959.

referred by the Grand Master to the committees as noted:

RESOLUTION ON FINE ARTS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
We, the undersigned. respectfully submit the following Resolution
for your approval and adoption:
WHEREAS, Beauty is one of our basic fundamentals; and
WHEREAS, this Grand Lodge owns many valua ble pieces of art;
and
WHEREAS. many forms of art are used by this Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS. our artistic possessions are visible examples of our
good taste and judgment; and
WHEREAS. many poorly painted portraits have been made of our
Grand Masters: and
WHEREAS, many members of our Fraternity are recognized artists:
and
WHEREAS. art in many graphic forms is used by this Grand
Lodge;
BE IT RESOLVED that a Grand Lodge Standing Committee on
F ine Arts be established to :
1. Approve the artistic quality of all designs, drawings, scrolls, etc.,
used by Grand Lodge.
2. Assist the constituent Lodges with any problems concerning art .
3. Commission an appropriate Portrait Artist each year to paint the
portrait of the Grand Master.
4. To have the Grand Master's portrait properly framed and displayed.
5. Arrange for the proper display of art objects owned by the Grand
Lodge.
6. Assist the Grand Master in any problems concerning art.
Respectfully submitted,

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK SCHOLARSHIP AW ARDS
(A-2)
Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Grand
Worshipful
Most
To the
WHEREAS. for many years the Grand Lodge of California has.
through its sponsorship of Public Schools Week, promoted and encouraged the development of our Public Schools system, and
WHEREAS, the Public Schools Committee is on record as favoring
the award of scholarships in connection with the observance of Public
Schools Week, and
WHEREAS . no machinery presently exists whereby constituent
lodges may adequately administer and effectively control such a system
of awards, and
WHEREAS, it is believed that the most effective administration of
such awards may be accomplished at the local level, thereby promoting
greater interest in the program and identifying the awards more closely
with the Masonic fraternity, therefore
BE IT RESOLVED. that constituent lodges or groups of lodges
be authorized to develop scholarship award programs in their own localities and to expend thereon such sums as may be required in their discretion and consistent with sound financing.

QUALIFICA TIONS OF OFFICERS' COACH
(C-1)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. Section 161 (4th) of the California Masonic Code
requires that the Inspector appoint in each lodge within his district an
Officers' Coach who shall be a qualified Past Master of the lodge, to
assist in teaching the ritual to the officers. and
WHEREAS. it has been interpreted that "a qualified Past Master
of the Lodge" be one who has served a term as Master of that particular
Lodge. and
WHEREAS. a lodge under dispensation, or a newly constituted
lodge, does not have "a qualified Past Master of the lodge" until the
successor of the charter Master has been iinstalled, and
WHEREAS. Section 161 (4th) imposes a duty inconsistent with
the meaning of our law, and
WHEREAS. in certain areas of this jurisdiction the one most
qualified to serve as Officers' Coach may not be "a Past Master of the
Lodge."
NOW, THEREFORE . BE IT RESOLVED: That Section 141
( ith) be amended by striking the words "of the Lodge" and substituting
therefore "of a Lodge of this Jurisdiction" and further striking out the
word "his" and substituting therefore the word "the."

as expeditiou sly as possible;

petition Grand Lodge to institute a revolving fund available for loans
to lodges for capital improvem ents for Temple purposes; and further,

Code, to wit:
Section 288 : Revolving Fund for Loans to Lodges for Building
Purposes.
Grand Lodge shall collect, in addition to the assessmen ts and per
capita levies set forth in Section 283 of this Code, the sum of $............
per year from each member of a lodge in this jurisdictio n, to be transmitted by the Secretary to the Grand Treasurer on the first day of
January in each year.
The Grand Treasurer shall, with these funds, institute the Grand
Lodge Revolving Loan Fund. which shall be disbursed to constituen t
lodges in the form of loans to be used for temple constructi on and
improvement, but not for furnishing s.
The Grand Lodge Committe e on Lodge Financing shall adopt rules
and regulation s, subject to Grand Lodge approval, setting forth the
other terms and conditions upon which such loans shall be made, including interest charges, audits, reports. inspection s, terms of loans, manner
of repaymen t, and such other matters as may be needed to conserve
the fund. This committee shall administer this fund.

resolution adopted in Grand Lodge, for such other purposes as may
be deemed meet.

DUES COLLECTION EXPENSE
(E-5)
To the Mo st Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Some members of the lodges in this jurisdiction, as a matter of habit.
or practice. frequently allow their dues to become delinquent, and pay
them only after repeated telephone calls, and notices sent by registered
mail. When they finally tender their dues, either before suspension, or
within the two years after, the lodge has to bear the cost of the expenses
of notifying them into paying the arrearage. It would be equitable, and
salutary. if the habitually delinquent dues payer were required to add
these costs to the price of bringing his delinquencies to date. Therefore,
the following Grand Lodge action is urged, to-wit:
That Section 581. Masonic Code. be amended to read as follows :
"Any member thus suspended shall be restored who, within two
years . shall pay the arrearages due at the time of his suspension,
together with such further dues as would, had he retained his membership. have accrued against him to the date of such payment, or who
shall have had such arrearages and dues remitted by his Lodge, and. in
the case of payment of arrearage is required, together with such other
costs expended by the lodge. as certified by the Secretary, in the nature
of telephone calls, certified or registered letters, telegrams, travel, or
other expenses reasonably expended in order to apprise him of his
delinquen cy and the consequences thereof."

RESOLVED. that the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M .,
of the State of California , adopt the following policy regarding t~e
playing of BINGO and that a nnotation ( d) of Section 685 of the
California M asonic Code be amended accordingly:
BINGO ga mes may be conducted by lodges or so-called collateral
Masonic organizations subject to the following restrictions:
1. Attendance must be limited to members of the lodge or organization and their families and guests.
2. No charge can be made, directly or indirectly, for attendance
or participation in the ga me.
3. Prizes awarded must be of nominal value, such as boxes of
candy, or items of similar value.
4. There can be no lottery. drawing or raffle for prizes conducted
incident to such game.
5. The event cannot be advertised or publicized other than in the
regularly published bulletins to members of the lodge or organization .
Any lodge or Mitsonic org anization, or any member thereof. conducting or pa rticipating in a BINGO game in which the foregoing
restrictions are not complied with shall be regarded as violating
Masonic law and policy .
Respectfully submitted,

BINGO RESTRICTIONS
(E- 7)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. o A . M. of California:
WHEREAS. for many years prior to 1955 the game of BINGO
(as hereinafter described) was one of the most popular social events in
many California Lodges and so-called collateral Masonic organizations.
and
WHEREAS, when the game of BINGO is planned by the Lodge
or organization solely as a social activity for the entertainment of its
members and their families, no charge is ma de for admission or to play
the game, the public is not invited a nd the event is not publicized outside the lodge or organization and the prizes are limited to those of
nominal value; the game has no public connotation of gambling because
the public is in no w a y involved and the members and their families
are fully aware of the non-commercial nature of the event, and
WHEREAS. the playing of BIN GO in California Lodges and socalled collateral Masonic organizations ha s been terminated by the
ruling in 1955 by the Most Worshipful Grand Master that the game
of BINGO is against Masonic law and policy. and
WHEREAS, many members of California Lodges and collateral
organizations do not agree that the ruling of the Most Worshipful
Grand Master in 1955 is correct and said members desire that this
Grand Lodge adopt a more reasonable policy regard ing the playing
of BINGO in said lodges and organizations, it is

good standing may. at your request, appear as your counsel and assist
in your defense, or may represent you if you cannot be present. Such
counsel need not be an a ttorney at law."
ALBERT F. Ross, Past Master, Lodge No. 254

(F-4)

To the Most W orshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
RESOLVED, that Section 707 of the Masonic Code be amended
to read as follows:
Service of Summons. If the accused be within the jurisdiction of the
lodge or within the county in which the lodge is located, the summons
and copy of the charges shall be issued and served upon the accused at
least ten days prior to the day appointed for the trial. and shall be
served personally by the Tiler or some other member of the lodge
authorized by the Master for that purpose, or s hall be left at his ordinary
residence or place of business, or may be forwarded to his addres s by the
Secretary, by mail. If he be without the said jurisdiction, but within
the state. and his residence be known, they shall be issued and served
upon the accused at least thirty days prior to the day appointed for
the trial. and shall be forwarded to his address by the Secretary, by
mail. If he be without the state and his residence be known, they shall
be issued and served upon the accused at least sixty days prior to the
day appointed for the trial, by the Secretary forwarding the same to his
address by mail. If his address be unknown the Master shall order the
trial to proceed at once upon the testimony. ex parte. In the event the
trial shall be held ex parte the record shall contain a full statement of
the facts showing due diligence in the effort to locate the accused.
Service by mail as herein permitted shall be complete from and
after depositing the documents in the mail in a sealed envelope with
sufficient postage thereon. upon due proof thereof by certificate of the
Secretary.
ALBERT F. Ross. Past Master, Lodge No. 254
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Grievances.

RESTORATION FOLLOWING EXPULSION
( F ~6)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
RESOLVED, that Section 767 of the Masonic Code be amended by
adding at the end thereof the following:
If the lodge which expelled petitioner was not the lodge of which he
was then a member, similar notice shall be given to the lodge of which

PROCE!!.DINGS OP THE

petitioner was a member at the time of his expulsion, if the same was a
lodge within the jurisdictio n of this Grand Lodge.
The notice must be read at the next stated meeting of the lodge after
its receipt and the Master must state to the members present that a vote
may be taken then or at the following stated meeting on the question of
approval or disapprov al of the restoration . If a motion is made and
seconded either to approve or disapprov e the restoration a secret vote
by ballot shall be taken and the result entered in the minutes. and the
secretary shall promptly notify the Grand Secretary of the result of
said ballot.
The Master shall also announce that any member may express his
endorsal of or objection to the restoration by communication to the
Grand Secretary or that any member may orally state his approval or
disapprov al to the Master. Prior to the opening of the next annual
communic ation of Grand Lodge the Master shall inform the Grand
Secretary in writing the number of endorsers and of objectors.
ALBERT F. Ross, Past Master, Lodge No. 254
Referred to Committe es on Jurisprude nce and on Grievatlce s.

REPO RT OF GRAN D TREA SURE R
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
It is a pleasure for me to present this. my fifth annual report. as your
Grand Treasur er. This report is for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1959.
During the year your Grand Treasur er has had numero us telepho ne
and other confere nces with our auditors , Skinner & Hammo nd. Their
coopera tion and assistan ce has been invalua ble to me. for which I express my grateful thanks. I strongly urge that each member of this Grand
Lodge study the reports carefull y. reading the auditor s' certificate, exhibits. schedul es, balance sheets and income stateme nt, in conjunc tion
with the compar ative summar y of Receipt s and Disburs ements which
is
a part of your Grand Treasur er's report.
In order to facilitat e ymtr study of the audit reports. they are combined with and made a part of this report. By so doing, we reduce the
number of individu ally printed reports, thus resultin g in some moneta ry
savings to Grand Lodge.
Each year our Commi ttee on Finance . present ly under the able
chairma nship of P. G. M . Frank Harwel l. Jr .. present s to this Grand
Lodge a budget of estimat ed income and expense . In order to facilitat
e
paymen ts under Grand Lodge authorit y, starting two years ago they
have also submitt ed a supplem ental budget coverin g that period from
dose of fiscal year July 1 to the end of the next Annual Commu nication
.
The results of this procedu re are most satisfac tory.
In closing this report I wish to express my appreci ation as Grand
Treasur er, and the appreci ation of the Grand Lodge, for reasono bly
strict adheren ce by Commi ttee Chairm en and Grand Lodge officers to
the adopted budget a s present ed each year by our hard working Finance
Commi ttee. Those few addition al appropr iations request ed and which
will be present ed for approva l at this Session , were of a minor nature
and, on analysis. seemed justified and reasona ble.
Again, my sincere thanks to the office staff for the very splendid
coopera tion during the year under review.
Respect fully Submitt ed,
EDWARD , H. SIEMS,
Grand Treasurer

per capita tax. It is respectfully requested that this be approved.

MEMBERSHIP
The review of our members hip experien ce as publishe d in my last
report for the past several years, and particula rly last year, has caused
much concern in some circles. This is especially true as it relates to the
net gain which has decrease d annually from 6,025 in 1951 to 2,474
in 1959.
A number of people have expresse d anxiety that Masonic membership is not keeping pace with the growth in state populatio n, but I
believe there are a number of factors to which attention should be
directed which are reasons why I do not express the same grave concern.
We are told that about 400,000 new inhabitan ts come into Californ ia
annually . These range in age from babies in arms to old people in
wheelcha irs. A very large percenta ge are older people who have come
to Californ ia to retire or have come here to later qualify for the high
state old age assistanc e. These people are not candidat es for Freemasonry .
All of the women and girls must be eliminated, and there are other
large percenta ges whose own religious advisors prohibit them from
applying for the Degrees of Masonry even though Masonry itself has
no such prohibiti on. All men under 21 years of age must be eliminate d
for any given year. Non-Cau casians likewise do not make applicati on to
our Lodges.
There is also that large percenta ge who do not apply for financial
reasons, since our initiation fees are high and our average dues are the
highest of any Grand Lodge in the country.
It should be kept in mind that of the losses incurred 1,270 were by
suspensi on for non-pay ment of dues and 4,219 were lost by death.

53

This latter figure increases year by year as the membership age rises.
There are two other factors which must be kept in mind-na mely,
that a great many men among the newcomers are already Masons from
other states and that we are not a members hip seeking organiza tion.
Taken all in all I think that raising 7,04.7 men in the last fiscal year was
a satisfact ory number. The more importan t achievem ent is that new
Lodges are being formed all the time in various sections of the state,
there having been nine in the year just closed.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER

ports again show that most of our lodges are in good working condition
and that most of them are actively at work. Some matters have been
disclosed by the reports which require attention, and the Inspectors
will endeavor to see that these matters are corrected.
It is interesting to note that there has been one of the smallest
turnover of Inspectors this year of any year of my service on the Ri tual
Committee. except for last year. In that 10 years. over 180 new Inspectors have been appointed. Only fi fteen Inspectors are still serving who
were in the Corps when I was appointed an Inspector in January, 1941 .
Last Spring, I sent Assistant Grand Lect urer Arthur J. Kahn to
Hawaii, where during a ten-day stay he conducted nine schools for
Inspectors and officers of the various lodges. H is report, and those of
the Inspectors, indicate that we are making real progress in ra ising the
standard of ritual in the Islands.
Two years ago, I expressed concern over the degrees conferred at
so-called Past Masters' night, and I reminded the Masters that they
were responsible for the conferring of all degrees in strict accordance
with the ritual, and that Past Masters were not to be regarded as exceptions. From reports received by members of the Ritual Committee.
it appears that this timely warning has gone unheeded, and that the
Masters are failing to require proficiency from their own Past Masters.
We have heretofore provided controls over degree teams, to assu re the
Masters of their proficiency and adherence to the ritual. These controls
have ha d very salutary effects. We now consider it necessary to suggest
to the Inspectors that they require the Master to hold one or more
rehearsals by the Past Masters with the Officers' Coach of the lodge
prior to conferring any degree on a Past Master's night. If that is unavailing, we would suggest more stringent rules to require conformity
to the r itual on the part of Past Master degree teams.
Section 161 - 10th of the Masonic Code provides that it shall be
the duty of the Inspector "to examine the books and record s of each
lodge to determine if its manner of transacting its business. making its
returns, and paying its Grand Lodge dues conform to our laws, and
shall report to the Grand Master the result thereof at the same time as he
makes his report."
The sufficiency of the Lodge's returns and payment of Grand Lodge
dues is a matter which has been supervised by the Grand Secretary for
many years. and no Inspector to my knowledge has made any such
report to the Grand Master in the last 20 years. I recommend that the
provision should be amended to read as follows: ''To examine the books
and reports of each lodge to determine if its manner of transacting its
business conforms to our laws , and shall report to the Grand Master
any violations of law."
As I have reported in previous years, the Committee has no suggestions whatever for any changes in the esoteric work.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is my seventh annual report, covering the activities of the
Grand Lecturer and those of the Committee on Ritual.
The usual Spring Conferences of Inspectors were held as follows:
Divisions I and 2, at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 19-21, 1959, conducted jointly by Worshipful Clare B. Campbell and Worshipful Ralph
M. Foote. Assistant Grand Lecturers.
Division 3, at Guerneville, May 15-17, 1959. conducted by Worshipful Arthur J. Kahn, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division 4, at Yosemite, June 5-7, 1959, conducted by Worshipful
Raymond G. Taylor, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division 5, at Ventura, April 17-19, 1959, conducted by Woshipful Donald G. Campbell, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division 6, at Garden Grove, March 20-22, 1959. conducted by
Worshipful W. Ben Sorrells, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
At each of these conferences the work was fully and well done by
Inspectors of the respective Division.
Despite his crowded schedule, the Grand Master was able to be
present for a short time at four of the Conferences. At three of the
Conferences. the Grand Secretary addressed the Inspectors on suggested instruction for Masters and Wardens in Masonic parliamentary
law as related to the conduct of stated meetings. We believe this subject
should be pursued by the Inspectors in their District Associations.
At most of the Conferences meetings of the Ritual Committee were
held to consider matters pertaining to the ritual. A special meeting of the
Committee was also held at San Francisco on November 29th and 30th,
1958, with all members of the Committee present, at which meeting the
entire work of the three degrees was reviewed and performed by the
Assistant Grand Lecturers.
All of las t Saturday was devoted to conducting the annual School
of Instruction for the 172 Inspectors of the jurisdiction. This school,
I believe, demonstrated the high quality of our ritual.
It is with much personal regret that I learn from Assistant Grand
Lecturer Ralph M. Foote that he feels unable to continue as hea d of
Division Two. This kindly brother has served this Grand Lodge
faithfully and efficiently as Inspector and Assistant Grand Lecturer for
more than 37 years, seven of them a s Assistant Grand Lecturer. He has
endeared himself to a ll who have worked with him, and no one can
appreciate more than I do the devotion of Brother Foote to the. ritual.
We hope that he continues to serve Masonry in some capacity.
The annual reports from the Inspectors, required by section 161
of the California Masonic Code, have been received by me. These re-

thanks for the opportunity of serving you.
Respectfully submitted,
ELBERT

w. DAVIS,

Grand Lecturer

of the Board.

and on motion duly made. seconded and carried he was elected a member
of the Board.

Master of Edgar V. Stewart, Jr., vice Myron E. Smith, retired. and on
motion duly made, seconded and carried he was elected a member of the
Board.

elected Trustee Emeritus.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE
FINANCE

You are urged to make a careful study of the financial reports
prepared by our auditors.
In spite of greater endowment income and a small annual increase
from per capita collections due to the rise in overall membership, operating deficits continue to occur.
A survey of the last six fiscal periods discloses four operating deficits
after making allowance for gain on sale of securities. See following
examples:

The gain on securities has made it possible to operate without dipping
into the Unappropriated Reserve which is providing most of the funds
for the erection of the new hospital. Without this reserve we would
require an additional per capita for construction purposes.
The Decoto population is at a peak and is continually rising. The
climbing cost of administering to our charges is due primarily to the
impact of higher wages and shorter hours in line with the national
experience of employers. In addition, your trustees have added the
following services, all of which are paid for out of Homes Funds.
1. Retirement plan for employees.
2. Complete medical coverage for residents.
3. Absorption of funeral expense to the extent of $200.00.
4. Extended outside relief program.
5. Absorption of Endowment Fund campaign expense.
6. Absorption of expense of annual Decoto visit during Grand
Lodge week.
7. Allocation of $20.000.00 annually toward services rendered by
Grand Lodge staff.
As you are aware. we are now in the process of erecting a new
hospital facility to replace our existing infirmary. The present area is
not adequate for our Home population and the building itself has been
declared unsatisfactory by State authorities.
The funds for this improvement are in hand. However, it means that
we must sell almost $1.500,000.00 of securities over the next twelve
months. We will lose approximately $60,000.00 in annual revenue from
this source alone. Further. when the hospital is opened next year we
will have to add to our professional staff to meet State requirements.
The area vacated will be converted to additional space for residents
which will automatically increase our Home population. This will also
effect our general payroll.

79

Effective last July I, 1959, our entire Decoto staff was placed upon a
five-day week and corresponding increases in wages were made to meet
salary standards in the East Bay area. This adjustment will increase
our annual expense by $40,000.00 over the last fiscal period.
There has been a gradual decline in the number of new applicants
for Masonic degrees which in turn reduces this source of income. As
you know, the sum of $25.00 is paid into our General Fund by each
applicant for the degrees, as well as each affiliate from outside Jurisdictions.
The rise in expenses and the decrease in revenue means only one
thing. If we are to meet our responsibility and at the same time take care
of the influx of new Home applications, we must have additional funds.
The only source is an increased per capita tax. This has been carefully
considered and after mature deliberation, the Trustees deem it necessary
to request a per capita tax of $1.00 for the support of the Homes to be
levied as of July I , 1960.
This is an increase of 50 cents and is the first time in six years that
we have requested additional monies. When our construction program
is completed and our new facilities are staffed we will have an opportunity to again review our situation.
The Brethren may be assured that the Trustees will not request
more funds than necessary to operate this great Charity which has been
entrusted to their care.
DECOTO

Hospital Facility.
Two hundred and sixty seven acres of land were purchased near
Decoto in the early nineties for the purpose of establishing a Masonic
Home for aged Masons and their wives or widows. The cornerstone for
the first permanent building was laid in 1898. Through the years, as the
demand for space increased and finances were available, additions were
made to the orJginal building and other units added . At the present time,
there are three hundred sixty guests, 77 of whom are hospital patients,
living in these buildings constructed at various periods in the past sixty
years. Despite the age of some of the buildings. an excellent maintenance
program and good care has preserved their livability and use. However,
during the ensuing years, design of institutional homes and hospitals,
construction methods and details, building codes, and required safety
measures have changed greatly. The requirements for safety are now
under the control of the State Department of Social Welfare. the State
Fire Marshal. and the local building inspection department. Periodic
surveys are made by the state and local authorities. particularly when
applications are n:ade for the renewals of the license to operate.
In 1958. the State Department of Health made such a survey and
reported that it would be mandatory upon the Board of Trustees to

80

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

bring the existing hospital up to the minimum requirements of the latest
codes for safety. After a review of the report by the Board and the
Architects, it was concluded. that due to obsolescense, over crowded
conditions, multiplicity of changes necessary, and other requirements
seemingly impossible of accomplishing, the best answer was to select
a site adjacent to the existing kitchen, nurses' home, and main buildings.
and build a new modern hospital facility complying with all codes. The
space which would be vacated when the new hospital was completed
would then be remodeled for bedrooms for which codes and requirements
are not so stringent.
A year ago, the Board of Trustees presented a report on contemplated new construction at the Masonic Home at Decoto. In that report,
a proposed new 131 bed, four story. modern hospital was described in
detail. Today, the new hospital facility is under construction, with concrete work completed to and including the third floor.
The Board of Trustees began a series of conferences with the
Architects in April. 1958, to study the problems at the Home and in
particular the hospital. Five months later, in September, preliminary
drawings were completed and approved by the Board. Final drawings
and bidding documents were completed and approved by the Board and
all governmental agencies in March, 1959. After bids were received from
six selected contracting firms, a contract was signed with the successful
bidder in April and ten days later work was started on a contract for
work to be completed on April 20, 1960. At present, this work would be
on schedule, except for a few days delay due to the teamster's strike
and failure to deliver reinforcing steel.

Additional Fire Safety Requirements
In May of this year, the State Fire Marshal reported certain other
deficiencies which it will be mandatory to correct before the renewal of
the license will be granted. His report stated that the open stairway in
the Administration Building from the first floor to the fourth floor was
a hazard in the event of a fire on the first floor due to smoke and hot
gases rising in the open stair well. The first floor of this unit, has a high
incident of combustible material, particularly in the office, library. and
the parlor. The recommendation given was to enclose the stair with one
hour fire resistive walls, and install class B. metal doors at all floors from
the first to the fourth. From the standpoint of plan, this is almost impossible. The Fire Marshal's alternative was to provide a complete
sprinkler system covering the entire first floor of the Administration
Building and to paint wood wainscots with fire retardant paint. This
alternative, while not without difficulties, appears the simpler and more
economical of the two. The lobby, library, and parlor ceilings are the
exposed and painted concrete structural framing of the floor above. The
sprinkler piping would therefore be in the open. but can be concealed
for appearance's sake in those rooms with new suspended acoustical

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

81

ceiungs. This work is now under study. Before proceeding with t~is
work, the Fire Marshal will be consulted to verify his approval of all
details to meet his minimum requirements.

Requirements of the Department of Social Welfare
Another mandatory requirement by the State Department of Social
Welfare was to install a complete communication system from a central
station in the first floor office to each room in the existing buildings. In
an emergency, each room in the building can then call the office and the
office can communicate with the room. A large board in the office will
register the calls from any room. This signal system is now being
planned, measured drawings have been made of existing rooms, and
bids will be received soon.
Another requirement was to provide an auxiliary lighting system for
stairs and corridors in all buildings in case of emergency. This involves
considerable new wiring. The diesel plant for the hospital would supply
the power.
General
The present hospital contract includes some additional work in the
old buildings. A required new fire alarm system for all of the old units
is in the contract and will be installed. A new stainless steel hood over
kitchen ranges with new fan, filters, and stacks will be installed in the
main kitchen.
The exterior masonry bearing wall of the south terrace between the
administration and the north wing has settled for a length of approximately forty feet and must be under-pinned. Drawings for this work
have been prepared and bids will be received from the contractor now
at work on the hospital.
Additional necessary work not now provided for is to repair certain
areas of the kitchen floor finish which is in bad condition.
Earlier this year, the entire boiler plant was remodeled and two new
boilers were installed to replace the original boilers. The installation
of water softeners has been accomplished and much clearing of hot water
piping has been done and is now in progress.
When all items mentioned are completed, the entire plant will be in
a satisfactory operating condition for some time to come.

Brethren: It is a pleasure and a privilege to submit my fourth annual
report as Superintend ent of the Masonic Home at Decoto for the year
ending June 30, 1959.
At the beginning of the fiscal year, there was a total of 353 members
in the Home, consisting of 139 men and 214 women. During the year
35 men, average age of 80.83 years, and 30 women, average age of

age of 81.58 years, and 20 women, average age of 83.45 years who
passed away. A total of 2 men and 3 women were withdrawn. Our
population on June 30, 1959 was 359, consisting of 138 men and 221
women, including 10 married couples.

VISITATIONS

The visitations of Masonic Lodges and other organizations continues
under the visitation program established in previous years. Reservations for a maximum of four hundred visitors are made every Visitation
Sunday, which is the third Sunday of every month. Reservations are
filled not further than a year in advance. The visitation program has
been well received by the hundreds of Lodges making use of this medium
to tell to its membership the true meaning of Masonic Benevolence. It
is worthy of note that the policy of visitations on the third Sunday of
each month is of immeasurable value in guaranteeing and affording the
children the benefits of relaxation and diversion of routine programs.

Ladies and Gentlemen: We are gathered here this afternoon fo r
the purpose of breaking ground for the construction of a new addition to
this, our great Masonic Home, - the addition of a new hospital.
In accordance with the teachings of our Institution, we should.
before entering upon any great or important undertaking . invoke the
aid and blessing of God. We shall, therefore. reverently unite in prayer
with our Grand Chaplain. ( *"")
Grand Chaplain: Almighty and Eternal God. Who laid the foundations of the earth! We beseech Thee to look with favor on this undertaking. the performance of the first physical act of consecrating the
ground for the erection of this building. Cause Thy face to shine upon
us that what we now do may please Thee. Let Thy work appear unto
Thy servants a nd Thy glory unto their children. Establish Thou the
work of our hands; yea, the work of our hands establish Thou it! May
the Great Architect of the Universe accept our labors for His own
glorious purpose, now a nd evermore. Amen. ( ... )
Grand Master: Brethren a nd friends. M asonry in California has
fairly justified its claim to the principles of Brotherly Love and Relief,
and its record in this respect is worthy of the best traditions of our ancient institution.
This great Masonic Home located at Decato was first conceived by
our Masonic forbears in 1890, a nd the land on which it stands was
purchased by the Grand Lodge of California for the Trustees of the
Home in 1893. The corner stone was la id with Masonic ceremonies by
the Grand Master and his officers on October 14, 1896. less than 63
years ago. Yet during that period the properties of our Homes have
accumulated by donations fro m our brethren and t he fri ends of the Craft
