Most Worshipful , Ladies, Brethren and Friends:
It is indeed a great privilege for all of us to assemble again on thE
grounds of this beautiful Home.
It is a privilege because all of us feel that once more on this afternoon. we ~ave ag~in wi~nessed, and are participatin g in a ceremony
ma~km~ with physical evidence the discharge of perhaps our most sacred
obligation. The same ground which our Most Worthy Grand Master
has ~urned_ over sym_bolizing the commencement of building a modern
hospital with the ultimate in modern comfort and convenience to care
for our own, has witnessed similar ceremonies on this very location since
1892 when the Grand Lodge acquired this tract of originally 267 acres.
Grand Master Preston in 1896 laid the original cornerstone for the flrst
of this group of buildings. Since that time 63 years ago many changes
have taken place, and all we need do today is look around us to see
that fro~ that time on California Masonry has with foresight and confidence builded well, and with a desire to comfort our brethren and their
':idow~. Today we can claim a record for this great home that establishes 1t as a model of world-wide repute. And when we who have
been P~.ivileged to visit the Children's Home at Covina think of "our
Homes we can not help but swell with pride and satisfaction at the
work of California Masonry.
This building that we start today will, upon its completion, ever be
a monument to the devotion of the Master Masons of our Jurisdiction
to t~e great Homes which through their generosity have been of such
service to the cause of freemasonry in California.
These two great homes represent in a material way why our great
fraternity has prospered these many years. Where else can we find
sue~ evidence of dedication to a principle, such evidence of sincere
desire to properly discharge an obligation, such evidence of benevolence
~ithout a vestige of ostentation? It is indeed a tribute to our institution and every brother of every Lodge in California can be proud of the
part h~ has played in making possible this necessary addition to this
splendid Home. For here at Decato we indeed have a home; it is a
home for all of us even though we are not and will not perhaps ever be
act~ally _in residence here. It has been and will ever be the Home of all
Calt~orma Masons. Its growth, not only in residents, which is not
the important thing, but rather its growth in facilities and in true
home ~tmo~~here and service is proof also of the sincerity and true
Masomc spmt that pervades our great jurisdiction.
I have mentioned the members of our constituent lodges who, of

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

93

course, are the great builders of Masonry in California, but like any
other constituency these true brethren of Masonry must have leadership.
The best evidence that that leadership has been forward looking and
devoted is the great work they have accomplished, but again I feel we
must admit that it is the membership which must be complimented, for
in California they have chosen well over the years. This leadership,
from our very beginnings. has had as its primary concern the relief of
distress. It is said that true charity, be it Masonic or otherwise, is not
true charity unless the giver really deprives himself of something in the
giving . Many of our Lodges over the years, and there have been lean
ones, have not found it easy to pay their Home taxes, yet year after
year in Grand Lodge the constituent Lodges have regularly maintained
the Home funds and have kept inviolate the building funds so that we
today may see another stride toward fulfillment of our ambition to ever
improve the lot of those who look toward us for comfort and solace in
the declining years of their lives.
True, we break ground today so that others in years to come may
have the benefit of a modern hospital facility. but in doing so we undertake not only for ourselves but for future generations the oblig ation of
continuing on in this great work. Our present contribution is this building, but it will also stand as a challenge to those who will follow us.
They must, if we build well. continue to build after we are gone. The
institution of the Masonic Homes is a great institution because it has
never been allowed to rest on its laurels. To stand still would mean
decay, and that would mean defeat not only for all of us, but for those
true and devoted Masons who since the beginning of Masonry in
California have always walked uprightly and forward . If we have been
fortunate in our. time to have modestly carried on and to have had the
privilege which we enjoy today, then we must so build this building
that future generations will say it was well built, not only physically,
but that it was well built in purpose, and that it may be a shining
example to those who follow, to encourage devotion to our institutions,
for as our roots go down and nurture deep in the soil so will our spirit
grow into full fruition and become a guidin g mark on the road to future
progress.
I am sure that this has been the story of the past; we hope that we
have not faltered on the road but have progressed another step forward .
This building will be evidence of our own progress. and we pray that
because of our works we today leave a guiding mark to the future.
Masonry in California must continue in this splendid work. Hospitals such as this one are not merely havens of mercy to relieve suffering
if we are to continue with our eyes on the future. It is a great forward
step we have taken, and who knows but that from this modest beginning
some day in the future great and lasting contribution to the general
welfare of mankind may spring forth to alleviate the lot of old age. This
statement today may sound terribly far-fetched since only one spadeful

94

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of earth has been turned. but I think you will agree with me that when
progress is given a start, even just a small beginning, great things are
accomplished by man in a free world. It was ten years after the Grand
Lodge acquired this tract of land, in fact it was in December of 1903,
that the Wright Brothers made their first flight at Kittyhawk; if you
have any doubt that progress isn't swift take a look at a current airline
schedule. So I say again, by building well today, as our predecessors did
in days gone by, we may be opening the door to things far beyond our
present comprehension.
This thing we do today is simply in discharge of our Masonic obligations, but if we do it well and wisely it will have results beyond our
greatest expectations. May we look forward to a bright and glorious
result from our present efforts, and may we be rewarded not just with
personal satisfaction. but with the knowledge that by progressing in
our time we make it possible for progress to continue in the years to
come, and by charting a course ever onward and upward we help insure
a future not only for Masonry in California, but for mankind everywhere.
In closing. let us thank God for the privilege he has given us this
day, and let us acknowledge the responsibility placed upon us to continue in the service of mankind by discharging many good works
throughout the years to come. May we continue to administer to the
soul of man as well as to his body. as Masonry has done in the past;
may today be a new beginning and a rededication of our minds and
efforts to continuance in this necessary work.

Cornerstone Ceremony
By the last week in September progress on the building had advanced
to the point where it was possible for the cornerstone to be appropriately
placed with Masonic Ceremony. On the afternoon of September 30,
which was Wednesday of the Annual Communication. Grand Lodge
was opened at the Masonic Home and the cornerstone was laid by the
Grand Master, assisted by the Grand Lodge Officers, in accordance with
our ritual. Past Grand Master L. Harold Anderson represented the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes and his remarks are included herewith.
as are also the address given by the Grand Orator and a tabulation of
the items included in the cornerstone casket.

Board of the Masonic Homes. I have been requested by the Grand
Master to act as master of ceremonies on the occasion of laying the
cornerstone of our magnificent new hospital facility.

We have been taught that before entering upon any great or
important undertaking we first invoke the blessing of God. Therefore
I call upon the Rev. Dr. Edward D. Kohlstedt, Grand Chaplain of the
Grand Lodge of California, to give the invocation.
Ancient and eloquent are the traditions and the rites of Freemasonry.
Between the first verse of the Book of Genesis in the Old Testament
and the last verse of the Book of Revelations of the New Testament,
the alpha and omega of the great light of Masonry, is to be found the
complete record of divine guidance and human experience in laying
the foundations of our civilization.
A cornerstone of that great foundation is our trust in the Supreme
Grand Master of the Universe. Sealed within that cornerstone are the
tenets and philosophies of our ancient and venerable Order.
We are assembled here today to celebrate the rite of a ceremony
that is ancient in the practices of Freemasonry and in so doing we will
establish another landmark in the traditions of California Freemasonry
and at the same time identify and enshrine a hospital facility which
will protect and safeguard the health. welfare and contentment of our
elder brothers and sisters.
Let the events of this day remind us all that we continue our travel
along the level of time, progressing from year to year, from generation
to generation, striving for perfection. We should all recognize that
in practicing the tenets of Freemasonry. brotherly love, relief and truth,
we are exemplifying the strength and beauty of a great cornerstone of
our fraternity and that in recognizing the noble purpose for which this
hospital facility will serve, the cornerstone of the next generation must
come from the strength and wisdom of this generation for a better and
happier humanity.
The wisdom of our brethren of years before us, who conceived and
implemented our Masonic Homes program, who built the foundations
and laid the cornerstone upon which we of more recent years have
added and strengthened, to them not to us. be a ll the glory, the praises.
and the honor.
It is my distinct privilege, this day, to present to you those .~ho
serve the Masons of California a s Trustees of our two great chantJes :
the Masonic Home for Children at Covina and this great Home for
the Aged at Decato, or should I say Union City. I understand Decoto
has become a name of the past.

LODGES CONSOLIDATED
The Grand Secretary reported that all the requirements of the law
respecting consolidation of Lodges had been complied with by Arlington
Lodge No. 414 and Acacia Lodge No. 438. On motion duly made,
seconded and carried Grand Lodge approved the consolidation with the
Lodge to be known as Arlington Lodge No. 414.
Adopted unanimously.

99

Herewith is the 27th Annual Report of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board, covering the period of July l, 1958 to June 30, 1959. The
information in this report. if carefully read and thoughtfully studied.
will reveal that the brethren of this Jurisdiction are continuing to show
an ever-increasing interest in this great Humanitarian Cause. A comparison with last year's report will show that many lodges had tremendous increases in contributions which reflects an unusual amount of
effort expended in those lodges.
PERCENTAGE OF PARTICIPATION

This past year, 93,425 brethren made a cash contribution to the
Endowment Fund. This number compares with 81,686 contributors the
previous year for a net increase of 11, 739. Percentage-wise. this total
raised the " Percentage of Participation" from 34.4% the previous year
to 39.2% this year. Even with this increase, it will be noted that more
than 60% of the members of the lodges are still not making even a
small contribution annually to this most worthy Cause. We hope that
all interested brethren will join with us in a determined elfort this year
to materially increase the number of contributors and that the "Percentage of Participation" will increase to at least 50% for 1960.
CASH CONTRIBUTIONS

During the past year, the individual contributions through the lodges
totaled $502,120.43 for a net increase of $80,486.81 above the previous
year (comparative figures are shown on another page of this report).
These figures are for individual contributions through the lodges and do
not include bequests. memorials, profits or appreciation on securities, or
special gifts. This is another all-time high in Annual Contributions and
further reflects the increased interest and accelerated efforts of all who
contributed time, energy and/or money to the Endowment this year.
HoNoR RoLL LoocEs
This report lists 453 lodges on the Honor Roll for 1959, as compared
to 365 a year ago, for a net increase of 88 Honor Roll Lodges. Even
more encouraging is the fact that 60 of those lodges are on the Honor
Roll for the very first time (the others having been on the Honor Roll
in some previous year or years). Approximately 65% of the lodges are
now on the Honor Roll and it is hoped that a ll such lodges will make a
determined effort to stay on the Honor Roll for the coming year and
that the lodges which are not on the Honor Roll this year will make a
special effort to attain that distinction in 1960. The above figures prove
that "it can be done",

A year ago there were only 36 lodges in the above listing. This year
there are 79. To these 79 lodges the Honor Roll of $2.00 per member
average is simply a stepping- stone or mile-post to greater accomplishments, but not the ultimate goal. Again, our special thanks to these 79
lodges for their outstanding accomplishment.

In addition to the contributions through the lodges. as shown above,
$87,251.28 was contributed to the Endowment Fund during the past
year through Bequests, the final and lasting expression of love and
affection from those who have been called from labor in this life. A
special pamphlet is available for mailing to members to encourage this
method of contribution, by making a new Will, or by Codicil, and
including the Homes Endowment therein. During the past year more
than 40,000 such pamphlets were ordered by the lodges and sent to
members. We hope many other lodges will do so this year.
PRINTED ITEMS

During the past year, the lodges ordered more than a million printed
items of information for mailing to lodges, such as pamphlets, Stop-Think-Consolidate cards, and Grand Master's Proclamations (re Endowment Month). In addition countless thousands of letters, cards. etc.
were sent out to members by the lodges in connection with the Homes
Endowment. This year an unusually large number of lodges sent out
letters to their members regarding contributions to the Homes Endowment and this method has proven to be very effective. A special thanks
is due to those lodges which are willing to spend a few dollars of the
lodge funds in order to do a greater job for the Homes Endowment.
Many of the pamphlets furnished by this Board contain much factual
information about our two fine Homes and are intended to keep the
brethren informed about the Homes they are, or should be, supporting.
Among several new pamphlets recently prepared is one giving information about the wonderful new hospital which is now under construction at the Home for Aged at Decoto.
CHANGES IN ENDOWMENT BOARD PERSONNEL

The second three-year term of Brother John Kahler, of Santa Ana,
expired as of the close of Grand Lodge on October 3, 1958 and he
requested that he not be appointed for another term, because of pressing and increased demands on his time in his occupation. He had
served this Board for six years in the Orange-Riverside-San Bernardino
Counties area and did outstanding work. It was he who "tested" the
Stop-Think-Consolidate cards in the lodges of his area for two years
and then suggested that this Board furnish them to all lodges, instead
of just printing the form in the Information Manual as had been done
theretofore. His suggestion was adopted and the lodges have since
ordered and used nearly half a million such cards and they have proven
to be one of the most effective printed items. Though no longer a
Member, John is still assisting the Board in every way possible.
In November, 1958, Brother Rue W. Sims, of San Leandro, resigned
from this Board because of increasing demands in his occupation. He

I 02

had served the lodges in the East Bay area for some seven years. He
had been assigned to some 70 lodges extending from Martinez on the
north to near San Jose on the south. This large area and large number
of lodges required a lot of work and much of Brother Sims' time until
he finally came to the conclusion that he could not do justice to his own
occupation and at the same time give the necessary time to the Endowment work. He has been greatly missed by those lodges and by this
Board.
Brother Marion A. Long, of Fresno, passed away on January 26.
1959 after an illness of five months. He had served in the San Joaquin
ValJey for eight years. His friendly and affable nature. and his sincerity and devotedness to the Homes and the work of this Board will
be greatly missed and long remembered .
M.W. Phil N. Myers, Grand Master, appointed the following to
Membership on this Board: Brother Charles H. Grace, of Riverside.
to s ucceed Brother John Kahler; Brother Paul A. Brom, an Attorney
in Oakland, to succeed Brother Rue W. Sims; and Brother William
Schooler, of Redding. to succeed Brother Marion Long. All three of
these brethren are well qualified for their assignments and have been
doing a fine job for the Endowment since their appointmen ts.
OuR THANKS To ALL

It is impossible to adequately thank the very great number of brethren who have had a part in the Endowment work, and still more difficult
to name all of them. but we give a special thanks to: the Masters. who
have worked so hard that their lodge may have an outstanding record
during "their" year; the lodge Secretaries, who are the guiding light for
the Endowment in so many lodges and who do so much work for this
cause; the local Endowment Chairmen and their committees for their
devoted work; the Ins pectors and Assistant Grand Lecturers, who have
given so much encouragem ent to the lodge officers. whose influence and
efforts have been of such great value to this work, who have given such
excellent cooperation and assistance to the members of this Board; to
the Grand Master a nd all Grand Lodge Officers and Committeem en
who have given so freely of their encouragem ent. influence and cooperation; to Lloyd E. Wilson. Grand Secretary, Henry D. Oliphant, Assistant Grand Secretary, and all members of their staff. for the most excellent assistance and cooperation given so willingly, cheerfully and
devotedly to the members of this Board in general and to its Chairman
in particular; and last, but certainly not least. to the 93,000 members of
this great fraternity who have contributed of their financial means to
"insure the continuance of loving care" to the residents of our two fine
Homes at Decoto and Covina; again , we say thanks a million to all who
have had a part, large or small, in this great Masonic work.
We sincerely hope that all will share with the Members of this Board

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 5 A. M. of California:
The Board of Control is pleased to submit its annual report covering
the activities of our eighteen Boards of Relief and five Employment
Bureaus maintained within our Grand Lodge jurisdiction.
It is gratifying to report that the work being done by our Executive
Secretaries and Employment Managers is continuing to measure up to
the high standards of our Fraternity. These devoted Masons go far
beyond the call of duty in carrying out their work. The Board of Con~
trol appreciates their endeavors and wishes to commend them for the
unselfish manner in which they approach their task and discharge their
duties. I am sure that this Grand Lodge agrees with us in our com~
mendation of these great and devoted Masons.
BOARDS OF RELIEF

At the present time, we have in our jurisdiction eighteen Boards of
Relief. The activities of these Boards are supervised by the Board of
Control. This is accomplished by supplying each Board a set of Rules
and Regulations and also a Standard Practice Bulletin, the latter having
been prepared several years ago in order that we would have uniformity
in policy, statistical reporting, financial reporting, and the various other
factors that are included in the work of these Boards.
The Rules and Regulations cover many items such as method and
procedure for holding elections, committees required, function ef these
committees, and instructions on how the work of the officers is to be
conducted.
The Board of Control also holds at least three meetings each year
with the Boards of Relief in order that we can have personal contact
with the Executive Secretaries, Employment Managers, and Officers of
our Boards of Relief.
After carefully analyzing the reports that have been submitted by
our eighteen Boards of Relief, we submit the following statistics for the
Masonic year ending June 30, 1959.
Advanced for Relief.................................... $40,222.29
Funerals ConductecL ..............................................981
Total Calls Made................................................ 30,177
Calls on the Sick. ................................................. 9,467
Investigations Conducted .................................... 2.536
Relief Calls............................................................ 8,113
Miscellaneous Calls............................................ 10.061
As you can see from these figures, many man hours are required to carry
on this vital work. It should also be remembered that a considerable
portion of this activity takes place after normal working hours.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

117

BLOOD BANKS

Many of our Boards of Relief maintain blood banks, and those who
do not have such banks usually make some other provision wherein they
can supply blood not only to our Masonic Brethren but also. to ~embers
of their families. The activities of these blood banks are rapidly mcreas~
ing. and the following figures will give you an indication as to the extent
of their activities during the past Masonic year.
Units of blood donated........................................ 2,969
Units of blood withdrawn ....................................3,309
Actual Cost Saved our Brethren................ $81,773.00
EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

The Rules and Regulations prepared by the Board of Control make
it possible for Boards of Relief to also have Employment Bureaus. All
requests for the formation of Employmen~ Bureaus must b_e ~p~ro~ed
by the Board of Control. In our California Grand Lodge _JUt1sd1ction,
we presently maintain five Employment Bureaus. You will note that
the number of Employment Bureaus has been reduced from six to five
since our last Grand Lodge Communication. This reduction was caused
by the discontinuance of the Glendale Employment Bureau and was
brought about because unemployment in this particular area was so low
that it was not felt advisable to continue this Bureau. As you are well
aware, the expense of maintaining Employment Bureaus is considerable,
and your Board of Control is constantly obs~ng the placements m~de
in comparison to the expense involved. It might be ~ell t~ mentio~
that the Glendafe Board of Relief made the request to discontinue their
Employment Bureau, and due to the circumstances, it was immediately
approved by the Board of Control.
The following figures will give you an idea of the activity in our
Bve remaining Employment Bureaus for the past Masonic year.
Registered for Employment.. ..............................7,007
Jobs Sec:ured.......................................................... 1,423
Positions Offered by Employers ..........................4,319
All of our Employment Bureaus operate without making any charge to
either the employee or the employer for this service. There are in the
State of California many employment agencies which charge a fee for
their services. The amount of the fee that can be charged is regulated
by the State of California. If this same fee schedul~ had b~en used
by our Employment Bureaus during the ~ast ~~omc year, it w~uld
have cost our Masonic Brethren and their famihes who secured Jobs
through our Employment Bureaus the sum of $112,736.95. Stating it
another way, the members of our Fraternity and their families actually

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

saved $112,736.95 by virtue of making use of the services of our Employment Bureaus.
While the Board of Control feels that securing positions for our
people is a very worthwhile undertaking. we must not lose sight of the
cost involved in performing this service. These costs have been continually rising, and the Board of Control wishes to report to this Grand
Lodge that we are continuing our investigation in an effort to reduce
these costs.

APPROPRIATIONS

It has been the custom of our Grand Lodge to -give financial assistance to our Employment Bureaus where such is deemed necesary. The
Board of Control has made a careful analysis of the appropriations being
requested by the various Employment Bureaus and makes the following
recommendations for the ensuing Masonic year.
East Bay ......................................................$ 2,500.00

The Board of Control has ref erred the matter of appropriations to
the Chairman of the Finance Committee as required by the Ordinances,
Section 265 of the California Masonic Code.
REIMBURSEMENTS TO MASONIC BOARDS OF RELIEF

As previously mentioned in this report, our eighteen Boards of Relief
advanced more than $40,000.00 to sojourners and their families during
the past Masonic year. These cases are all very carefully analyzed by
the Executive Secretaries of our Boards of Relief. and an effort is made
to get reimbursements from the sojourner's home lodge. It is gratifying
to know that out of $40,222.29 advanced for relief during the past yeM,
only $763.61 was not repaid by the sojourner's Lodge.
REIMBURSEMENT TO THE SAN FRANCISCO BOARD OF RELIEF

The San Francisco Board of Relief has requested $753.61, which
covers three cases, one of which is a Brother from Scotland and the other
two cases are from Lodges in the State of Illinois. They are all worthy
cases, and the Board of Control has recommended that the Finance
Committee approve the reimbursement to the San Francisco Board of
Relief.

119

This case involves only $10.00 whkh was used to purchase a floral
piece for a departed sojourner. There was no time to contact the Lodge
prior to making this purchase, and, as a result, the departed brother's
Lodge elected to stand on the technicality, that because they did not
authorize the expenditure, they would not reimburse the Sacramento
Bo~rd of Relief for same.
The Board of Control has recommended that the Finance Committee
approve this reimbursement to the Sacramento Board of Relief.
Total amount requested for rambursements-$7 63.61.
The Board of Control has had excellent support from the Most
Worshipful Phil N. Myers, Grand Master, and we wish him to know
that we are most grateful for his support. We .would also like to thank
the Grand Secretary. Lloyd E. Wilson, the Assistant Grand Secretary,
Henry D. Oliphant, and his very efficient staff for their help and cooperation during the past Masonic year.
Respectfully submitted.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES, CALIFORNIA
MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE CORPORATION

names of all "Temple Builders". It will be a record in which all Masons
should be proud to have their name recorded.

This is the Fifth Annual Report issued by the Board of Trustees of
the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
The Board of Trustees met following the close of the 1958 Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge, as is required by the By~Laws for
the purpose of organization. The election of Brother Joe L. Shell,
Deputy Grand Master, Brother Alfred F. Breslauer, Senior Grand
Warden, and Brother Guy B. Mize, Junior Grand Warden, was formally r~ported to the Board, and on motion duly made, seconded and
carried, they were elected members of the Board.
This .report co_vers the first fiscal year of operation. The report of
the Certl~ed. Public Accountants, Skinner & Hammond, and the report
of the Building Manager, Brother Alvin A. Horwege, are made a part
of this report.
. T~e business of the Temple was carried on by the staff under the
dir~c~ion. of the Special Temple Committee comprising the Trustees
residing in the San Francisco Bay Area and P.G.M. L. Harold Anderson. The Temple Committee has met on call of the Chairman. It has
bee11 our objective to assist the staff in carrying out the policy as prescribed by the Board of Trustees, and to report to the Board of Trustees
our action and recommendations for its approval, particularly when
matters pertaining to finance were involved.
In addition to the three items of improvement to the facilities mentioned in the Manager's report, it has been determined by your Board
of Trustees that because of the wide range of temperatures in San Francisco, resulting in extreme expansion and contraction of the endomosai~ window panels: the screen originally contemplated to protect
~he wmdow should be installed. This has been authorized and, accordingly, should be installed, if schedules can be maintained, by the time
of our Annual Communication.
Engineers and scientists in this field assure us that this screen will
deflect in excess of 6~% of the direct heat from the sun. They also
as~ured us that the wmdow could be viewed with less eye strain on
bright sunny days. (The fog does lift occasionally.)
OPEN BOOK
~he work of setting the names in type for the Open Book is pro-

ceedmg. It.was our original hope to have it completed by this Grand
Lod~e session .. The volume of work and many questions arising in connection therewith has made this impossible. We appreciate the cooperation of the lodges in checking and rechecking the names. When
the Book is conqJleted and in place, it will be a permanent record of the

MERIT ROLL PLAQUE
As of August 31. 1959, (the date this report was released for printing) 412 lodges have made the "Merit Roll". This is an increase of 72
lodges since our last Annual Report to this Grand Lodge.
We are happy to be able to include for the first time in the Annual
Report a photograph of the "Merit Roll" plaque. This plaque was
proudly unveiled a year ago at the dedication communication. It is
located on the second floor of the Temple for all who visit the Temple
to see.
This "Merit Roll" plaque is unique in that a space is reserved for
each constituted lodge and for any newly instituted lodge. It will be
possible for lodges to reach "Merit Roll" status as long as there is a
debt on the Temple. The name plate for each constituted lodge is
available and ready to be put in place. Name plates for U.D. lodges and
U.D. lodges reaching "Merit Roll" status, subsequent to being con~
stituted, will be made available as soon after reaching Merit Roll status
as is possible.
The quota for all newly institued and constituted lodges since July
31. 1955, is based on their membership at the close of the preceding
fl.seal year. New groups wishing to be on the "Merit Roll" on their in~
stitution night may use as their quota $10.00 for each charter member.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF BUILDING MANAGER
To the Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple:
Brethren:
It is my privilege and pleasure to present to you my first annual
report as manager of the California Masonic Memorial Temple for the
year ended June 30, 1959.
.
With the assistance of Brother Harry F. Haines, superintendent
in charge of electrical and mechanical equipment, and our janitorial
staff (consisting of Brother Charles Frasier and Brother Jim Oakley).
we have endeavored to cal'lry on the maintenance of the Temple in a
manner which has been pleasing to all of you.
In addition to the above staff, we have a contract with the California
Building and Maintenance Company to handle all the janitorial work
in connection with our rental facilities. The contract price for this
cleaning is included in our lease agreements.
During the year, the garage operation (which has been leased to
Tidewater Oil Company) has been above our expectations.
Our rentals on the auditorium and exhibit space for the year covered 87 days of occupancy. (See Financial Statements-Exhibit B
attached.)
Taking into account the fact that our main source of revenue comes
from the convention business (which is planned years in advance), we
may be several years in getting our facilities into the swing of this class
of business.
We were fortunate to pick up a few very important convention
accounts, and feel that we will increase our tempo in the years ahead.
Included in the 87 days noted above, 48 days were accounted for
by National conventions which drew a large share of their attendance
from all over the United States and Canada. It is estimated that their
attendance during these 48 days totaled 106,350 people.
The balance of the rental days were accounted for by one State
convention, shows, concerts, and church services with an estimated additional total attendance of 92,000 persons.
A study of our guest register (which was started in September,
1958, and was checked to the first of July. 1959) shows that 7,000
visitors signed the register. These represent visitors from 46 states and
the District of Columbia, as well as from 30 foreign countries.
Looking into the coming fiscal year, we have on the books 82 days
of occupancy-having an approximate value of $70,000.
Three major changes and improvements have been made in the
building with the thought of making it more attractive and useful to
our rental public. First, our restroom facilities for women proved to be
inadequate, and we have added eleven new units in these facilities.
In the exhibit area, we have made available 26 telephone Boor jacks

127

for the use of exhibitors, and the telephone company has pulled in a
100-pair cable as a permanent installation to implement their use.
The telephone company has had so many inquiries for television
shows originating in the auditorium that they have just completed the
installation of a 450-pair cable-capable of handling the largest television shows. Your Building Committee had anticipated this need and
provided the conduit in the original construction of the building.
Now under contract is a hydraulic ramp at our Pine Street loading
dock, which we hope in the future will eliminate to a considerable
extent the trouble of getting cars out of the garage after a large show
in the auditorium. With the Pine Street ramp working, we will be able
to turn approximately one-half the cars out into that street. Our garage
operator anticipates with two exits in use the garage can be emptied in
about thirty minutes after the close of a full house program.
We have been relying on the San Francisco Convention and Visitors Bureau to promote our facilities, and they have been most cooperative in this respect. I feel. however, that in the future. further
effort on our part should be undertaken to advertise and promote these
spacious facilities throughout the convention and theatrical world. I
would like to submit this thought to the Board of Trustees for consideratio~

May I express my thanks (and those of the Temple staff) for the
splendid help and cooperation tendered during the past year.
Respectfully submitted,
ALVIN A. HoRWEGE,

Building Manager

GRAND LODGE OF CAIJFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
FoR F1scAL YEAR ENDING JuNE 30, 1959

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee concludes its ninth year of activity, and
herewith renders its report for the twelve months ending June 30, 1959.
Each year's report gives a certain amount of historical background and
basic information, which should be helpful to those attending Grand
Lodge for the first time.
The Prudent Man Rule in modified form was adopted by Grand
Lodge at its 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges a
Prudent Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
was formed for the purpose of administering the investable funds of
Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California and the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund. The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent Lodges. Grand Lodge makes the services of
its investment advisor available to the Lodges. Many Lodges are now
making use of this service, as evidenced by the fact that 226 Lodges
with $4,696,500 of investments are now consulting with our investment
advisor.
The Investment Committee is composed of the Grand Treasurer, the
Assistant Grand Treasurer, the Chairman of the Finance Committee,
the President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees or a Trustee
of that Board designated by him, and the Chairman of the Masonic
Homes Endowment Board or a member of that Board designated by
him. The President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees has
designated Brother Past Master Ralph H. Head as his representative,
and Brother Past Master Eugene Bashor, who was Chairman of the
Endowment Board a year ago, appointed Brother Past Master John
W. Davey as his representative. Subsequently Brother Past Master
John M. Gordon became Chairman of the Endowment Board and by
virtue of his office he will personally serve henceforth as a member of
the Committee.
By Ordinance, under Section 246 (formerly 86) with respect to
investment of Grand Lodge funds, and Section 403 (formerly 152.1)
respecting investments by Constituent Lodges, the following provisions
and subsequent amendmew.ts were promulgated:
GROUP I. At least 40% of the funds available for investment
must be in:
A) Cash and/or bank accounts.
B) Obligations of the United States.

129

C)

Obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions.
D) Such other securities as are legal investments for California
savings banks.

GROUP II. Up to 20% may be invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will be fully
listed and registered on an exchange registered with the
Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that this listing requirement shall not
include railroad equipment trust issues ( 1955).
B) Preferred stocks, which are or will be fully listed and
registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and
Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange,
except that full listing and registratfon of preferred stock
shall not be required whenever the common stock of the
corporation issuing such preferred stock is fully listed and
registered on such an exchange, provided that such preferred
stock is traded on such an exchange ( 1956).
GROUP III. Up to 40% may be invested in:
A) Common stocks, which must be fully listed and registered
on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that
this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance stocks.
B) Share~ of Investment Trusts.
C) Shares and/or certificates of insured Federal or State Savings and Loan Associations ( 1957). The amount invested
in any one Association shall not exceed the amount covered
by insurance. (THIS AMENDMENT APPLIES ONLY
TO CONSTITUENT LODGES AND DOES NOT
APPLY TO THE INVESTMENT OF GRAND
LODGE FUNDS.)

With respect to the authority to invest in Groups II and III, the
Ordinances read as follows: "No such investments, however, shall be
made which at the time of purchase will result in the total market value
of the securities referred to in this section exceeding twenty per cent
(or forty per cent) of the total market value of all the cash, bank accounts and securities held,"-the controlling point being that there
cannot be more than 20% or 40% invested in Groups II and III, respectively, at the time of purchase.

Several amendments are proposed by the Committee at this Communication of Grand Lodge. The most important suggestion relates
to the percentages which can be invested ·in the various categories
under our Modi.6ed Prudent Man Rule. This has been under discussion and study for several years.
The Committee endeavors to keep in as close touch with economic
and changing conditions as is humanly possible.
The suggested amendment would increase the percentage which can
be invested in Group III. Brother Ralph Head, who represents the
Masonic Homes Board of Trustees on our Committee, will present
details to this Grand Lodge.
Several additional amendments relating to Hawaii are proposed.
These amendments will bring our investment provisions up to date with
respect to our newest State, which is a part of our Grand Lodge.
The Investment Committee continues to pursue a conservative policy,
as shown by the amounts invested in the three categories, namely,
Groups I. 11 and Ill.
Our thanks to the Grand Secretary, the Assistant Grand Secretary,
and my thanks to the members of the Investment Committee for their
wholehearted and generous cooperation at all times. Our special thanks
also to Brother John W. Davey, who has served on this Committee for a
number of years, and is now retiring as the representative of the Endowment Board.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE .

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
MANUAL FOR THE. FoRMATION oF A MASONIC LoDGE

During the year, we have completed and published "The Manual
for the Formation of a Masonic Lodge," which includes procedures
under dispensation. The Manual is now available without charge from
the Grand Secretary's office in response to qualified requests.
We urge the full use of this Manual by those working on the formation of new Lodges, and by the Inspectors a!'.ld officers of Lodges under
dispensation. It is designed to make your work easier, and to assist you
in providing the type of information and records the Committee on
Charters requires in order to properly prepare its reports.
CHARTERS RECOMMENDED

At the 1958 Communication, all Lodges then under dispensation
were granted charters, and the current Masonic year began with no
Lodges under dispensation.
During the year, six new Lodges were instituted, and of these, five
have applied for charters.
·
We have examined the work and proceedings of the five Lodges
seeking charters and have conferred with their delegates. We found the
work and proceedings of all five petitioning Lodges to be satisfactory,
and that they were clear of all indebtedness. In some cases there were
errors or omissions of a minor nature in keeping records and presenting
same as prescribed by the Masonic Code. Your Committee was assured
that these items would be rectified. There were no errors or omissions of
a major nature.
We, therefore, recommend that charters be granted and numbers
assigned to the five petitioning Lodges as follows:
Millbrae Lodge, No. 792, at Millbrae, in the County of San Mateo.
Maya Lodge, No. 793, at Los Angeles, in the County of Los Angeles.
Mt. Wilson Lodge, No. 794, at Altadena, in the County of Los
Angeles.
·
.
American River Lodge, No. 795, at Folsom, in the County of Sacramento.
Golden Valley Lodge, No. 796, at San Bernardino, in the County of
San Bernardino.
CONTINUING UNDER DISPENSATION RECOMMENDED

Tila Pass Lodge, U. D .. at Los Angeles, in the County of Los Angeles, was instituted July 30, 1959, and desires to be continued under
dispensation. In conformity to this request, the Lodge did not Ole a

135

petition for a charter. The Committee concurs in the Lodge's request,
and recommends that it be continued under dispensation for the ensuing
Masonic y.ear.
.

.

· Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
LOCAL TEMPLE ASSOCIATION FINANCES
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Local Temple Association Finances met, on a
number of occasions during the past year, with the members in Southern
California, but, because no finances had been appropriated for this
Committee it was impossible to have a meeting of the Committee as a
whole.
We also held a meeting Wlith Herb Hargrave, Chairman of the Lodge
Finance Committee, on a number of matters, in Los Angeles.
It was the concensus of opinion of the Southern California members
that a new form be prepared, to be filled out by all local Temple Associations and to be submitted to the Lodge Finance Committee. This
form would inclutle a statement for two years, and would also include
an appraisal of the property involved.
A number of changes are recommended for this form whiich will be
of great help to the ·Lodge Finance Committee, and, in further discussions with your Chairman of the Lodge Finance Committee, we feel
that, if this form is adopted and made mandatory that the Lodges fill
in same, that the Lodges Finance Commtitee can then handle the entire
work of our Committee, as well as their own Committee.
We, therefore, recommend the adoption of the attached form, and
further recommend that our Committee be disbanded, and all papers
turned back to the Lodge Finance Committee.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN T. BOND
JOHN A. DULL

REPO RT OF COMM ITIEE ON SOJOU RNER S
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your sojourn ers' Committee can report continu ed activity on the
part of the committee and the various lodges through out the jurisdiction. It seems to the committeemen that the lodges are becoming more
aware of the importance of sojourn ers in their future, and that gradual ly
the program "Sojour ners' Night" is becoming a feature in the annual
lodge calenda r.
In the beginning of this year, the lodges were divided into Inspect or's
District s and assigned to the Committeeman living closest to them. In
some cases, unfortu nately, the Committeeman resided many miles away,
and, in such instances the Committeeman could only correspond with
the lodges, urging their cooperation and assistance.
In a state such as California, embracing both urban and agricultural
areas, and both old and new population districts, many diverge nt views
and problems as to sojourn ers are encountered. In some of our Mother
Lode country lodges, for instance, it is likely that there are no sojourn ers
around. On the other hand, in such boom areas as San Diego and Los
Angele s to the south, and Sacram ento and the San Mateo peninsula
to the north, there are countless sojourners looking for a Masonic restinq place. It is in such places that our lodges can reap a fertile harvest .
We have been informed that around the San Diego area, particularly.
work among the sojourners has made splendid progres s.
In general. and in addition to local committeemen effort, the Committee wrote to every lodge on two occasions during the past year:
flrst, at the beginning of the year urging the formation of sojourn ers'
committees in the individual lodges, and the laying of plans for a
sojourn ers' program: second, later in the spring, when at considerable
effort, and after many days of research into the past records and correspondence in the flies of the committee, we produce d a kit entitled,
"A New Look at Sojourn ers." This, with suggest ed helps, programs,
and argume nts as to the reasons for working with sojourners, went to
the Secreta ry of each lodge. The kit was designe d as an aid to the
Master and/or his chairma n of the lodge Sojourn ers' Committee, and
was not meant to be a substitu te for the ingenuity and enthusiastic thinking each lodge could bring to this problem.
Our rate of affiliations keeps a steady pace every year, with hundreds of sojourners entering the stream of Califor nia Freema sonry and

TRIBU TE TO RALP H M. FOOT E
Past Grand Master Leslie E. Wood, on behalf of the three living

Past Grand Lecturers and the Grand Lecturer, present ed a resolution
of commendation as follows:
Men of true heart labor with pride and joy in the perfection of
their craftsmanship, and with love and respect for the institution which
they serve.
Such has been the industr y of Assista nt Grand Lecturer Ralph M.
Foote, who now .flnds it necessa ry to lay aside the working tools of our
Craft and .flnd time for the personal rest, refreshm ent and repose which
he has so justly earned.

138

.. PROCEEDINGS OF THE· :

For more than forty-two years continuously, Brother Ralph has
labored in the vineyard, · industriously and effectively, for the benefit
and honor of the Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons of the
State of California, for its ideals, for its great truths, and for its purpose of building strength and good character into the lives of all men.
Ralph M. Foote was raised October i 4, 1916, in Valley ~dge No.
135, F. & A. M., at Linden, California. In 1917 he was appointed and
installed as Junior St~ard of that Lodge and by successive annual
advancements became its Master in 1921. He continued his service to
that Lodge by accepting appointments as its Ch_aplain for two terms
in the years 1922 and 1923.
..
.
On September 5, 1922, he was appointed Inspector of the 26th ~a:
sonic District, now designated as No. 228, which office he held until
1952 when he assumed the responsibilities of his present office of
Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 2, taking over supervision of sixteen
inspectorial districts with a total of 70 Lodges.
By this resolution the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California, does commend and thank
Worshipful Ralph M. Foote for his long and continued service to the
Craft. It bespeaks for him many ensuing years of health and comfort,
wherein he may bask in the warmth of the love, affection, and appreciation of his Brethren for his services to the Fraternity.
And be it directed that the Most Worshipful Grand Secretary of
this Grand Lodge cause to be prepared, suitably inscribed, and presented to Brother Foote, a metallic case card expressing the sentiments
of this resolution that he may always have with him a physical reminder
of our esteem.
Most Worshipful: In the offering of this resolution, we request
that the record show that it is presented jointly by the present Grand
Lecturer and all the now living Past Grand Lecturers under whom
Brother Foote has so ably served and who have 1had more than superficial opportunity to observe and appreciate the perfection and assiduous performance of his duties and responsibilities in his several
Masonic offices.
Respectfully submitted, ·
LESLIE E. WooD, P.G.M. and P.G.L.
CHE.STER H. WARLOW, P.G.M. and P.G.L.
ARTHUR M. WARREN, P.G.M. and P.G.L.
ELBERT W. DAVIS, Grand Lecturer

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON COMMERCI ALISM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M. of California:
. Your Committee on Commercialism again is indeed happy to advise
that reported violations of our law appear to be on the wane.
This .unquestionably is due to the definite pattern which was~ developed in years past under this committee's able and competent chairman, the late Worshipful Ralph K. Pierson, who in conjtJnction with
the Worshipful Donald G. Campbell, former Committee Secretary and
now Assistant Grand Lecturer Division 5, solidly established the foundation of the house in which we now labor and to whom all credit for the
improved situation must be given.
SHRINE

The fullest cooperation has been received from the various Shrine
Temples throughout this Grand Jurisdiction. As occasion required, the
advise of this committee has been sought to ascertain whether or not the
contemplated activity was within our law and, if found lawful, the concurrence of our Grand Master was secured and the Temple advised
accordingly. This is as it should be and such continued action should
further cement the cordial relationships which now exist.
SclOTS

Last year this committee reported a number of violations of our
law in regard to this appendant body. Because of the seriousness of
these violations, our then Grand Master, M. W. Leo E. Anderson, found
it necessary to write the Pharoah of the Supreme Pyramid and later
met with him, at.which meeting our Grand Master was assured that the
Sciots would make a special effort to see that there would be no more
violations of our law among the various Pyramids. This action apparently has been most effective as there have been no violations reported
to this committee.
ROYAL ORDER OF CARITAS
AMARANTH FOUNDATION, INC.

Your committee has nothing to report with regard to these organizations this year as all files with regard to them were forwarded to the
M. W. Henry C. Clausen, Judge Advocate, for his use in a lawsuit filed
by Amaranth Foundation, etc. vs. Grand Lodge et al for approximately
$800,000.00 which suit our Judge Advocate was successful in defending.
ZuLO GROTTO
ONTARIO

A group belonging to this appendant body originated an organization called the "PHEZENPH UN CLUB" which has been incorporated
in the State of California. The membership, not now restricted, consists

140

PROCB!IDINGS OP THB

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

of Masons, non Masons, men and women of Protestant, Catholic and
Jewish faiths. Clubrooms were secured, a liquor license obtained, and an
arrangement entered into between the "Club" and the "Grotto" for the
latter to use the Club for its meetings. Arrangements state that: "The
bar shall be closed, locked, and vacated during Grotto business, stated,
or special meetings." There was nothing to prevent the bar from being
open until just prior to or immediately following any "Grotto" meeting.
Our Grand Master pointed out to the Zone Director, Supreme Council,
Grottoes of North America, who is located in Los Angeles, that the
holding of Grotto meetings in these premises was contrary to Masonic
Law and must be discontinued. The Zone Director was asked to require
Zula Grotto to discontinue holding meetings in the quarters referred to.
Zula Grotto is now meeting in the Casa Blanca Hotel. Ontario. There is
no bar on the premises.

NATIONAL FRATERNAL NEWS

Ros1cRuc1ANs

There has been some complaint made to this committee with regard
to the alleged illegal commercial use by this organization of the words
"Mason," "Masonry" and "Masonic" emblems. This matter is now
under study by this committee.
PUBLICATIONS

The "Masonic Review Digest" has again been called to our attention. While we have had no complaints, we have been in correspondence with the Grand Lodge of Oregon in regard to this publication. We
have also had correspondence regarding it with the Grand Lodge of
British Columbia. Both jurisdictions are quite concerned about the
activities of this magazine. The owner of this pubUcation, so far as we
have been able to ascertain, is not a member of the Craft, though we have
been informed he petitioned a lodge in Eureka several years ago but was
not accepted. He maintains res·idence in Scottsdale, Arizona. The magazine stationery carries in its masthead the following: "The Northwest's
Outstanding Masonic Publication."
From the foregoing, and from an examination of the magazine
which carries no California advertising, it is apparent that soUcitation
is limited to Oregon, Washington, Idaho, and British Columbia. From
the printer's bug on the magazine, also such stationery and billheads as
we have seen and from the mailing, it is obvious that the printing is done
in California and mailed from this state, though from no particular
locality as the owner skips around the state with each printing. The
magazine cover carries the square and compass which, of course, is
illegal.
This publisher has been the subject of a number of investigations
by the U. S. Government but so far the Government has not been able
to develop anything which would warrant action on its part. Our Judge
Advocate has this matter under advisement.

141

Representatives of this magazine, published in Chicago, recently
contacted a man, not a member of the Craft, but one who is friendly to
it, by long distance telephone, representing the magazine to be an official
Masonic publication having nationwide circulation restricting its advertising to those having Masonic affiliations and only rarely accepting
outside advertising. The solicited person, because of his friendliness
agreed, based upon these representations, to take a quarter page ad at
an agreed price of $130.00. Upon investigation which negated these
representations, a telegram was sent rescinding the agreement based
upon misrepresentation. When the telegram was received in Chicago the
magazine's representatives again contacted by long distance 'phone the
solicited person and tried to change his mind. A police official in one of
our large cities is a close personal friend of the man who had been
solicited. This police officer is also a member of the Craft. He wrote the
Grand Lodge of Illinois outlining the circumstances and in reply the
Grand Master of that jurisdiction wrote:
"The National Fraternal News has the dubious distinction of
being the largest blot on the reputation of our fraternity for
the past several years. Its notoriety for misrepresenting the
extent of its circulation has been a continued source of local
aggravation and we now regret to learn that its unorthodox
activities are being practiced on a national scope."

.
There have been several other matters of less serious nature called
OTHER PUBLICATIONS

to our attention, but they have been taken care of by personal contact
by members of this committee and brought in line.
NEWSPAPER ADVERTISING

Late last year there appeared in the Wall Street Journal, Pacific
Coast Edition, an ad for a job; the headline of which was the ineffable
word given in the Master Mason Degree. The advertiser was contacted.
He was a sojourner, a member of a lodge in New York State who moved
to California one year after becoming a Master Mason and had been in
this state some eleven years. Because of this inexcusable breach, our
Grand Master set the matter for trial, but before trial could take place
the accused moved to New Jersey where he now resides. Not wishing to
proceed with the trial in absentia, on instructions of our Grand Master,
the charges were forwarded by our Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge
of New York for such action as it might care to take.

the 84 Temple Associations which reported a loss. The total cash depreciation set aside by Temple Associations in the past year amounts to
$170,698.00. These figures represent a greatly improved condition, and
we trust that future operations will improve even more.
Another bright facet of the financial condition of Temple Associations iis shown by the expenditure in the past year of over $116,000.00
for capital improvements in the form of remodeling and renovating
necessary to put existing Temples in first class modern condition.
While the financial condition. of Temple Associations is generally
improvdng, we must not lose sight of the fact that during the past year
145 Temple Associations did not report any depreciation account. This,
of course, must be rectified in order to have consistency throughout the
jurisdiction in the matter of reporting financial operations, and to ease
the pressure on the Temple Asociations because of their working too
close to their income and not allowing funds for repairs and incidental
items that are always popping up. During the coming year the Committee will concentrate on these Temple Associations and render all
assistance possible.
One of the difficulties encountered by the committee in its work has
been the manner of reporting financial condition on the present Form
200. This will be rectified by the adoption of an improved method of
reporting which embodies a comparative system and will be a lot easier
to understand by the persons directly connected with the preparation
of them.
In addition to the following resume of the Committee's activities for
the past year, hundreds and hundreds of added communications from
various Lodges and Temple Associations relative to matters under the
jurisdiction of the Committee on Lodge Financing have been acknowledged and processed.

Santa Cruz Lodge applied for consent to transfer $700.00 of its

NATOMA LoDGE No. 64
Folsom
The Masonic Hall Association of Folsom, controlled by Napa Lodge,
requested $7.000.00 from the Lodge in order to complete the enclosure

Hall Association and approve the construction plans.
HUMBOLT LoDGE No. 79
Eureka
Humboldt Lodge requested permission to transfer $4,000.00 to the
Humboldt Masonic Temple Association so that the Temple Association
could refinish and modernize the Temple to comply with terms of a
lease. Lease was for a commercial rental and rentals were adequate to
repay that amount. Lease for 15 years at a minim um rental of $12,000.00
per year plus percentage. The Committee approved the lease and the
loan.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON PUBUC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Fortieth Observance of Grand Lodge Public Schools Week
represents a crown of glorious distinction for California Grand Lodge.
for Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams, for Grand Master
Myers and his officers.
As the expansion of California Public Schools in their efforts to meet
demands of. increasing population and extended offerings required in
modem society evolves, so the !intensity of numbers and efforts of
Masonic friends for public education are required.
Californi~ is glori~us .in its many faceted aspects of growth, developm4:'11.t· expans~~n, and m its advances in culture, productiveness, and the
spmtual stability of its people. What happens, how it is done, and the
ways of happening in all fields of human advancement in California are
examples to many states and many lands.
The Californi~ Public School System has since the inception of
~rand Lo.d.ge Public Sch~ols programs never been found in second place
m reco~nitlon and standing among the great Public School Systems in
the United States of America. This refers to quality of educational program, adequacy of finance for public schools, expansion and extension
of offerings of public schools. This has great meaning in matters of
standards of teacher training and certification, facilities, services, and
m~nagement for educational advantage for the people, especially the
children and youth of our state.
During our fo~y years of. publ.ic school interest and dynamic activity
every phase of ~his great California educational program and its growth
have had our vigorous, constant, and intelligent study and support.
Let us look for a moment at the dimensions of our California Public
School System.
. For the 1959-60 school year there will be enrolled in public schools
m our State 3,866,000 pupils. 2,450,000 of these will be children in
elementary public schools. Nearly half a million will be adults in public
~chools. '1!1e largest percentage of public school population in any state
in the United States will be in colleges of the public school system of
education in California.
. I? California there are 1774 individual public school districts. Some
districts are small, one is the third largest in our nation. Each of these
districts is governed by a Board elected by the people of the district.
Here we find a fertile area for constant cultivation as we with our Masonic devotion to public education would have the electorate be intelligent in choices at ballot marking time.
I~ 19.59-60 the budgets for the public education program of- Cali~ornia will be o~e and one-half billion dollars. The main expenditure
is that for teaching services. A total of 122,400 members make up the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

157

public school professional educational staff as the 1959-60 school year
opens.
OUR PURPOSES

Clear, strong, firm, and simple Masonic purposes to be served in
relationship to public schools have been in force during the 1958-59
Masonic Public Schools Committee year. Throughout the year and
with particular emphasis during Public Schools Week 1959 purposes as
follows have been served:
1. To know the "why" of public education in and for our state
and country.
2. Having real and true knowledge about public schools.
3. Developing a dear understanding of the reasons for Masonic
interest in and advancement of public schools.
4. Being informed as to the needs of public schools in the places
where Masons live and devising ideas and plans for helping in
the services of needs of public schools.
5. Becoming leaders in the advancement and improvement of the
conditions of public schools and their support.
6. Informing the public schools that Masons are friends of public
education and that they are ready to be called to the service of
public schools.
WHAT HAPPE.NED-1 959

There was extreme Masonic alertness and ready service concerning
public schools everywhere in California. No non-political, non-sectarian, non-professional body of intelligent thinkers gives more attention
to public education, public schools, or children in public schools than do
the more than 1,000 Masonic Lodges and related Masonic bodies in our
state.
The statistics concerning visits, meetings, attendance at special
occasions, all held in behalf of advancement of public education, are so
tremendous that they are impossible to tabulate. More important than
numbers and facts concerning participation are the reports of spirit,
leadership, goodwiJI, cooperation, and results in community support for
public schools expressed through Masonic activity.
It is particularly significant now that support for Public Schools
Week is practically unanimous. Most objections to the purposes. plans,
activities, and programs are erased. In fact, private and parochial
schools, too, take part in the general emphasis on education, home-school
cooperation, and child and youth services and leadership.
It may be said positively that the same purposes for youth and
country as are served in public schools, with the encouragement of the

158

159

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

activities of our fraternity. are now approved, accepted, supported, and
advanced by nearly all youth-centered organizations. This applies
whether such organizations . are religious, social, public, civic, private,
volunteer, or paid.
Forty years of Masonic Public Schools Week effort is not due the
entire credit for the development of youth services through public schools
-yet, none of the extensions, expansions, constructive changes and new
services in public schools have failed to have prompt, early, real, and
vigorous support by California Free Masonry.
The things that have happened in behalf of public education through
speciftc, direct, and constant effort during 1958-59 are summed up as
·
follows:
1. Parents, citizens, taxpayers, older pupils, and espectially Masons came to know the "why" and "hO\V" of public education.
More than two million "visitors" came to public school meetings
during Public School Week 1959. In round numbers, 5000
meetings were held throughout California Grand Lodge jurisdiction-and think of it-Public Schools Week stimulated participation by 825,000 children and youth in programs, contests, ·
meetings, demonstrations, community events where the fine,
good, clean, cultural. wholesome, and favorable side of youth
and the school were shown to such advantage that great faith
in children, youth, and schools was vigorously restored and
established.
2. Publications, news reports, broadcasts, speeches, posters, demonstrations and public as well as school displays told the "good
story" for young Californians and for public schools. Masons
were in the background but were ever potent forces in every
effort.
3. The Adult education program of the public schools took sharper
and keener interest in the 1959 observances than ever before.
Every adult who is a part of a Masonic organization was capable
and ready to tell the significant need for constant. high quality.
free public schools in our state. They told a remarkable story.
The work of research Lodges and Grand Lodge Committees
keeping the precepts, practices, and workings of Freemasonry
interpreted and integrated into year-around fraternal meetings
is the foundation of an informed Lodge membership which
speaks in behalf of public education and public schools in
California.

Great Masons have said-"Better unfed than untaught," "Let us as
patriots push forth the pursuit of wisdom for all," "An educated people
is easiest and best governed," "Better unborn than untaught," and "Better untaught than illtaught."
We have taught ourselves during forty years that we can learn of the
need for public education in our school districts.
These forty years have written history in Masonic interest and
strength in relation to public education. What has been learned is a
four-way accomplishment. While all progress in California Public
Education during the last forty years is not credited to California
Masonic interest nor may the entire field of advancement in public
education in California even be completely known to Masonry, it is yet
true and certain that the broad advances made by public schools in
California have been better known and certainly no better studied and
supported than by Masons in the jurisdiction of California.
This four-way learning program sums up in a general fashion as
"What people have learned about public education during the last forty
years," "What educators have learned about Masonic faith in public
education in these forty years," "What school students have learned
about public · education during their participation in Public Schools
Weeks programs during the last forty years," and "What California
Masons have learned about public education in forty years of California
Grand Lodge support of the public schools of our state."
Let us take a general look at each of these learning programs and
experiences:
I. "What people have learned as public school support has been
stressed by Masonic Lodges."
People have l~rned that the schools are only as good as the people
want them to be. People have learned that in order to support the
public schools, they must understand the public schools. People have
learned that no function of governmental service in our democracy and
under the system of controls of public schools in California is as close
to the people and their desires as are the public schools of California.
People ·have learned that the California structure of public education is a simple, intimately associated, directly responsive program in
which public interest, public intelligence, and public wishes are reflected
by action of the public. Only the public can control its public schools in
California, if it will. Just as in every aspect of the direction of life,
whether public, private, individual, group life, social life, or civic life; so
with public education, the intelligent interest of the people can be expressed and can control. in fact it must control. the public schools.
People have been exposed to teachings by discussions held in Masonic Lodges. They have learned that not only can the people have the
kind of public education they want, but that the people must know
what are the characteristics of good public education and good public

LET

Us NoTE THis!

Great Masonically-thinking men throughout history have given the
"mind-set" for our interest in public schools-yes, for our responsibility
in advancing public education.

160

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

schools, and they. the people, must demand such type of public education
and public schools.
Where there are not good public schools in California, the life of
the community can perish.
During forty years of Public Schools Week. services conducted by
Freemasonry. the people have been urged to know and visit their schools.
Last year one out of every four of our people in California did visit and
share in a Public Schools Program during Public Schools Week Observances.
The people have learned why we have public schools, why they
must be strong public schools, why the schools must have friends. The
people have learned the great advantage of eternal vigilance in knowing
public schools, supporting public schools. showing fearless defense of
the structure of public education in California. Our citizens are recognizing that the American ideals of democracy. freedom, equality, justice,
and charity are presented in good public education and are also exempli.fled by the principles and practices of Freemasonry.
People in California during forty years of Public Schools Week and
through Masonic advancement of public education have come to accept
the ideals upon which American public education is established. Education for all, to suit all, to preserve country under God.
II. "During almost half a century of Public Schools Week dynamics in Masonry. educators, administrators, supervisors, and teachers
have had the benefits of direct and impressive learnings about Masonry
and California Public Education."
These public schools personnel groups have learned that Masonry
in California is an informed, loyal. effective Friend of public education.
School people know that Masonry constitutes a dedicated, organized.
unselfish, devoted, and working agency for the protection, advancement,
and strengthening of the public schools and the California program of
public education.
School leaders have learned that California Freemasonry wants to be
informed, intelligent, and ever-ready as an agency for the interpretation
and strengthening of public schools. Never have public schools found
Masonry operative as a body desiring to "run-the-schools" or to specify
a program of teaching for use in our public schools. In this regard
Masonry is without ,doubt one of the greatest of the organizations expressing in belief, in practical works, and by Faith. a firm bulwark of
strength ready and waiting call to maintain and service public schools.
School people have learned, not that by power of Masonry--or by
the wealth of Masonry. or by the militant action of Masonry; but that by
sympathetic understanding. by faith in public education, by confidence in
public school leadership and teachers, we are a body of God-fearing men
of families. of community interest, of loyalty to country and of dedi-

cation to free public schools who stand ready. We are Friends. We
are Ready.
III. "What school students have learned by participation in Public
Schools Week activities during forty years."
This is the greatest good that has come out of our devoted efforts
during these forty years.
Public school pupils have learned that there is a great body of men
who have faith in youth. Public school students have been taught by our
efforts with the schools during these forty years that every thinking
man of us cares, and cares sincerely, that public school pupils have the
very best opportunity that can be provided.
School pupils have learned that their good efforts are recognized,
applauded, and appreciated by our great group of men in California.
Public school pupils have learned that their learning efforts and
accomplishments will open doors to our hearts, our friendship, our support, our readiness to aid them in any and all of those ways in which
good citizens, Brotherly men care for a needy young member of our
society.
Through our efforts in support of the enrichment and extension of
public education, public school pupils have learned.-

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
OF THE MASONIC CLUB HOUSE, LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M., of California:
Your Board of Directors takes pleasure in presenting its report for
the fiscal year ending June 30, 1959.
In reports for preceding years we have explained that our building
was one of the first constructed on or near the campus-in fact this is
its thirtieth year. During that time, repalirs have been necessary to
maintain the building in perfect and modern condition.
This year we had two major items of repair:
1-The Los Angeles Department of Building and· Safety served us
with a demand that our building be earthquake proofed.
2-Extensive re-roofing was done.
The first item is explained in further detail in our budget listed
below.
The second item developed after the preparation and submission of
our budget. However, both items will be taken care of out of our
reserves.
During the year the Grand Master recommended Brother Bates
Mason as a member of our Board to succeed Brother John M. Askin,
resigned. Brother Mason is a Past Master of West Los Angeles Lodge
No. 373, and brings to our Board a working knowledge of the Club's
operations. His son, while a student at UCLA, was a member of our
Club and an officer of the Student Council.
Our Club membership remains fairly constant-between 150 and
200. We could, however, accommodate twice that figure with no increase
in expense. This situation has caused your Board some concern. Five
years ago, on the occasion of our twenty-fifth anniiversary, we had a
dinner and evening of entertainment attended by the Masters of the
Los Angeles County Lodges to let them see the Club and its facilities.
It was hoped that they would go back to their Lodges and pass on what
they had seen in order to stimulate membership.
Our Club sends a brochure of its facilities to the new enrollees at
UCLA. Grand Lodge has also recognized the need for publicity, for
the California Freemason has carried articles on both club-houses. Also,
several Grand Masters, in their communications to the subordinate

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Reference is made to previous reports of this Committee for information on this First Masonic Han in Los Angeles.
The State of California now holds title to the property and it is
officiany a part of the Pueblo de Los Angeles State Historical Monument.
A barricade has been erected at the sidewalk and the work of restoration has commenced. This building is only a small part of the entire
restoration program for the monument and it will take two to three years
to complete.
The other members of this Committee express appreciation to Matthew M. Codon, Past Master of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42, a member
of the Committee from its inception, who has maintained contact with
the public officials assigned to the project. Brother Codon is working
with Orvel B. Johnson, Direct Construction Supervisor for the State,
and doing research to make the restoration as completely authentic as
possible.
The Committe has in its files a letter from Mr. Johnson relating to
various aspects of the authentic restoration. It is too lengthy to quote
in fun, but the following excerpt will be of interest:
"When the restoration work actually commences we will begin
a search for the cornerstone of this building. In this respect, we would
appreciate the cooperation of your Lodge (if the cornerstone is located)
in opening the cornerstone and retrieving the contents thereof."
Mr. Johnson is a member of the Craft.
Until the restoration of the building is completed and we commence
the furnishing of the Lodge room on the second floor as it was 100
years ago, the Committee does not anticipate any expense. We recommend the continuation of a Special Committee, and the authority, previously granted, for the Grand Master to make nominal expenditures, if
necessary.
