GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Freemasonry in those early California days. We are still a young California, and in a sense. perhaps, living in a raw, exciting kind of existence.
Certainly. at the increasingly rapid pace of change in our state, in much
less than a century from now our successors will look back upon our
days as days of pioneering excitement also.
But again there is my question-are we relatively as influential as
we have been or should be?
Recently a friend of mine, a brother of my Lodge, loaned me a
book which had been sent to him by one of his relatives, a Mason in a
small community in Texas. The book, cloth-bound and over three
hundred pages in length, is titled "A Century of Light." It is the detailed
history of Brahan Lodge No. 226 of La Vernia, Texas. In 1858, the
Grand Lodge of Texas granted dispensations to thirteen lodges to work.
One of them was Brahan Lodge. I recently read this entire book, even
though I have never sat in Brahan Lodge. have never been in La Vernia,
Texas. and know absolutely nobody who is a member of that Lodge. I
found the book fascinating. because here was the story of a small community and of a small Lodge ( Brahan Lodge had 107 members at the
time the book was published this year). Here was a Lodge that seemed
to me to be an indispensable part of the community which it served. In
1871, after a number of years of money-raising effort, this Lodge completed its first Lodge hall. And let me quote from their history here-"Brahan Lodge has always given attention to the educational needs of
the community. Knowledge that the lower floor of the Lodge hall would
be used for a school was responsible for some of the contributions and
for much of the free work on it. When the building was erected it was
meant for the lower floor to be used as a school and a place of public
worship. It has been used for some purpose of the school almost every
year since it was completed." Here is real community service and influence for good and betterment. Throughout this book one is impressed
with how Brahan Lodge has been inextricably bound up in the affairs
of La Vernia in Wilson County, Texas, actually beginning before the
organization of the county. The author, in compiling this documentary
account of the growth and development of a moral and progressive force
in La Vernia, has shown conclusively how Freemasonry has contributed
in one community to that community's society.
Brahan Lodge is but an example of hundreds and hundreds of
essentially similar Lodges in our country. Their history is fascinating
too, and their position of influence and importance in their respective
communities has had profound effect also.
We can always take pride in the accomplishments of our predecessors, but this is of no real value unless we are able to apply the lesson
of their experience to the problems of today and the future. The true
worth of all history is in the fact of its explanation of how we got to

where we are--and the wise practitioner is the one who can use these
explanations to aid in plotting the course for the future. Generally.
history demonstrates that goals are attained by struggle and that when
one goal has been attained there is still a further goal that must be
reached. Satisfaction is never present.
A story is told of a famous artist who painted a great picture. It was
the finest work he had ever done, but one day he was found weeping
beside his masterpiece.
"What is the trouble?" he was asked. "aren't you satisfied with your
picture?"
"Yes," he replied, "that's just what the trouble is: I am satisfied."
He knew that being satisfied, he would never do better work; his
ambition would wane; he would begin to slip, and the future would no
longer be a period of increasing greatness as an artist. It meant that the
stimulus for improvement had gone and the joy of doing work would
be no more. The climb up the hill. the effort to do, the struggle to accomplish. is what brings to us our greatest and most enduring satisfaction, without which life is worth little.
So it is with Freemasonry. The greatest and most worthwhile
satisfaction is for those who concern themselves with how best to strive
for the goal. It would be most presumptuous on my part if I were to
say. "here is an answer; here is a way." Rather it is the collective
thought and the collective work of all of us. and especially of you who
are the leaders in your respective lodges. which. when applied with the
basic tools of Masonry, can bring us steadily along the road, no matter
how rough and r)lgged it may be.
I can suggest, though. an area for our thoughtful consideration. Integrity is the very core of Freemasonry. An example of integrity. worthy
of all ~mit~tion, provides one of the most essential lessons in Masonry.
Integrity is moral soundness, honesty, uprightness. In a broad sense,
too, it is steadfastness to the right course no matter what influence there
may be to vary the course. Our quality, our value, our reputation, are all
the result of our integrity in this broad sense. This is an area which
today. and other days too, might stand some reappraisal. Are our
Masonic teachings. based on integrity and moral truths. applied as rigidly and as fully as they have always been? Or is there an occasional
tendency to rationalize just a little bit here and there? Have we slacked
off? Have we rationalized by saying," we should be broadminded about
that?" Is there as occasional tendency to permit other, softer sets of
values to have "just a little" share in influencing our decisions and
actions? It is not my intention by raislnig these questions to imply any
softening or slacking off. But these are pertinent questions, and I hope
they are provocative also. They are intended as such and if, because of
such questions and because of similar ones which will undoubtedly occur

172

174

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

to you, there is some reappraisal of our integrity then it is good that
the questions have been raised. We must never be satisfied with the
way we are.
Just two years ago this Grand Lodge confirmed the edict of Grand
Master L. Harold Anderson which effectively banned certain activities
engaged in by affiliated organizations which were clearly commercial
in their purpose and thus tended to depreciate the integrity of Masonry
in California. This was an historic and courageous decision. I am
confident it was the result of self-analysis, of reappraisal. of determination that what had been happening was wrong and not in keeping with
our purposes, our dignity, or our integrity. Softer sets of values were
cast aside. This was altogether proper and I use it here as an example
of what I have been talkin9 about-reappraisal of integrity. The wise
man is the one who can apply with clear-headed directness the facts of
moral truth to the situations presented in an ever-changing world.
The Oregon state capitol building is one of the newer such structures in America and certainly one of the most beautiful. Flanking the
main entrance are two inscribed panels. On one of them is this
meaningful statement:
"The mind of man knows no employment more worthy
of its powers than the quest for righteousness in
human affairs; no goal of its labors that is superior
to the discovery of the good in the guidance of life."
Now let us interpolate this slightly with the change of about three
words and read it thusly:
"The mind of Freemasonry knows no employment
more worthy of its powers than the furtherance of
righteousness in human affairs; no goal of its labors
this is superior to the application of good in the
guidance of life."
No thinking Mason will quarrel with the rightness of that statement, but will a thinking Mason today conclude that we are employing
our powers to the fullest for the attainment of this righteous but never
completely reachable goal? I think not. Rather the thinking Mason will
quickly say, "we can always strive to do better; we should strive to do
better; we must strive to do better."
Approximately ten years ago Tehama Lodge No. 3 in Sacramento
celebrated its centennial. The feature of that observance was a graphic
and dramatic portrayal of the influence of that lodge spread over a
century in the community which it serves. Some of you have been

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

175

privileged to see this portrayal. for it has been produced several times
since the first presentation. It is worth telling about again.
On a simply set stage were two standing panels, each about four
feet wide and eight feet tall. On one was mounted a large electric
clock, in motion. On the other panel hung a one-gallon glass jug. inverted, and filled with blue ink. A special stopper permitted this blue
ink to drop from the bottle at the rate of a small drop each second.
Directly below the jug there was a large glass vessel which held perhaps
fifteen gallons of clear water. Between the two panels stood a brother
of Tehama Lodge who. as narrator, described the beginning years of
the Lodge and told of the deeds of some of the more prominent of its
members. As he spoke, the sweep hand of the clock moved steadily
around, and from the inverted jug there dropped each second a drop
of blue ink. As the narrator continued to recount the deeds of the
members of Tehama Lodge. the vessel of clear water began to turn
blue; first scarcely noticeably. but gradually and steadily becoming
bluer and bluer.
The illustration was simple, but altogether complete and clear. With
the passage of time, and the steady occurrence of deeds of influence for
good. the quality of living in Sacramento became better and better, ever
better. So it has been, and is, in every community where Freemasonry
influences the deeds of its members.
But what if we reversed this illustration? What if we considered the
darkening of the color of the vessel of clear water to have been caused
by deeds of which we were not proud: deeds which took place because
we did not hold as closely to the integrity of Masonry as we could have
--could we then say that the waters became darker and darker until no
light would shine through? Yes, the illustration could be reversed, but it
will never be reversed as long as we are willing to be self-critical. to
reappraise ourselves, to sincerely and wholeheartedly apply Masonic
teaching to our daily lives. to ever strive for betterment.
We have in Masonry incalculably valuable tools with which to
build for continual betterment. They are the great moral truths which
are inculcated within our Lodge. They are ageless and changeless. They
are fundamental truths not subject to experimental challenge. Applied
diligently in all our activities they can be a most powerful force in the
guidance of life for the betterment of all.
Today in this world are two powerful forces opposing each otherour way of life and the totalitarian system. Ours is based on the dignity
of man. The other is not. Masonry is compatible with only one---our
way of life. because Masonry too, is based on the dignity of man. Perhaps at no period in our country's history has there been a greater need
for our system of government, and of society. to work well. We must
demonstrate to the world that American democracy is the best system.
But to do this we must be certain that in every community in our land,

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON DE MOLAY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on De Malay is pleased to submit the following report for your approval. At the present time, well over one hundred constituent lodges are actively sponsoring De Malay Chapters in the
State of California. A partial list of those lodges sponsoring chapters
in Southern and Western California is attached to this report. The
details of De Malay sponsorship in Central California had not been
received at the time this report was prepared.
Your Committee has noted a very marked improvement in the effectiveness of the De Malay movement in California during the past year.
De Malay leaders unhesitatingly credit the active interest and sponsorship of Masonic Lodges for this gratifying situation. There has
been a re-emphasis of the fundamental principles of De Malay which
are so Masonic in character.
There have been no reports during the past year of any actions
by De Malay Chapters which were contrary to the policies of the
Grand Lodge. Instead, there has been a complete and unequivocal
acceptance of those principles. Prior to the adoption by this Grand
Lodge of the present policy permitting lodges to sponsor De Malay
Chapters, compliance with our policies was oftentimes grudgingly given.
Support of the Order of De Malay gained ~mpetus during the past
year when the Grand Lodges of Pennsylvania and Wisconsin gave
their constituent lodges unlimited authority to sponsor De Malay Chapters. The list of Grand Jurisdictions encouraging and sponsoring the
De Malay movement has indeed become impressive.
Your Committee has accepted every invitation to meet with Masonic
and De Malay groups. We wish to emphasize particularly the observation that there is a growing interest in information concerning the
De Malay movement. We have received a great deal of cooperation
from various qualified De Malay personnel to whom inquiries were
referred. Of particular note were visitations to the California State
DeMolay Association Convention in San Jose, the Southern California

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

181

De Malay Association Convention in Long Beach, official De Malay
Activities at the California State and Los Angeles County Fairs, and
various regional meetings throughout the State. Every Master Mason
should be pleased with the manner in which these affairs were conducted. They truly reflected credit not only on De Malay, but on our
Order as well.
The Annual De Malay Week observance held by the San Diego
County Masonic Officers Association has grown to be one of the most
outstanding and best-attended functions of the Masonic Year in that
area. The many benefits derived from this annual event prompt this
Committee to recommend to future Grand Masters that they declare
a De Malay Week throughout this Grand Jurisdiction. Constituent
lodges could be requested to have a program during that week centered
around the local De Malay Chapter, or a speaker could be obtained
who could give an informative talk on De Malay.
It is our sincere recommendation that this Committee be continued,
and that the sum of $750 be appropriated to cover its necessary expenses.
This Committee wishes to express its appreciation to our Most Worshipful Grand Master Phil N. Myers for the privilege of serving this
Grand Lodge. His wisdom and encouragement have been a source of
strength and inspiration to us.
fo closing, we would like to leave this thought with you. "The
hopes of the world and our fraternity are in the youth of today. Your
help is urgently needed to assure the realization of those hopes."
Fraternally submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE

As of June 30, 1959, there were 34,0H regular subscribes at $1.00
per year. The expense of sending renewal notices and in obtaining
new subscriptions is very large as will be seen on the financial report
herewith. This would be eliminated if the magazine were sent to the
entire membership. The unit printing cost for the last issue was $.0765
per copy. This would be reduced if 240,000 copies were printed. The
cost for members would probably not exceed 35c each per year if the
present format was retained.
In order to pass on to individual subscribers some of the saving
on renewal costs, the Grand Master set the subscription price for two
years at $1.75; three years at $2.50; four years at $3.25; and five years
at $4.00.
This is our financial report for the year ending June 30, 1959.
It does not tie in exactly with the report from last year because the
Finance Committee has now set up a reserve for unexpired subscriptions and we have changed our statement to conform with this arrangement.

184

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This marks the end of the sixth year that the principal duty of your
Committee has been the publication of California Freemason. It has
also continued its traditional function and has reviewed the proceedings of our sister jurisdictions throughout the world. Short summaries
of many of these reviews are printed .in the quarterly California Freemason.
There has been a gradual evolution of format from volume l, number 1. The present 48 page, 6 by 9 inch lithographed magazine has
been well received and it is intended to continue with this style for the
next year.
Our editorial policy has continued to feature popular articles relating to Freemasonry and material intended to keep the Craft informed
as to the activities of Grand Lodge. We do not have sufficient space
to attempt to carry the news of all the subordinate lodges but we do
print stories of local activities which have more than a local interest.
The Committee was, of course, disappointed that, at the Communication last year, Grand Lodge did not see fit to send the magaZiine to
the entire membership. The labors of the Editor and Committee have
been undertaken to show Grand Lodge that an interesting and informative quarterly can be produced. It should reach the hands of every
member. We are losing the opportunity of spreading Masonic information and inspiration, an opportunity that other organizations, both
fraternal and civic, do not overlook.
Many lodges are aware of this opportunity and send the magazines
to their members under the arrangement that if a lodge adopts a
resolution so to do, each member will be mailed the quarterly and, in
January of each year, Grand Lodge bills the lodge at the rate of 60c
for the number of members shown on its last annual return. Changes
of memberships during the year do not affect this charge.
The lodges now operating under this group plans are 5, 10, 12, 25,

As items of interest and in spreading ideas it is in keeping to mention several of what we consider our most outstanding celebrations.
These may be considered as patterns of what we have tried to accomplish and are presented here for their ingenuity and originality. There
were many others of course, some with even more impressive attendance but these each contained something unusual which could be well
imitated throughout the jurisdiction:
The city-wide celebration at Merced, culminated on September 23,
sponsored by both Yosemite Lodge No. 99 and Merced Lodge No.
749. Chairmen for the two lodges were Bros. George Wolf and Sam
Daniels. Almost every segment of the community was brought in, including the public schools. Their meeting drew 500 persons. What is
more important the people of Merced were well aware of Constitution
Observance through support from the press, civic organizations, radio
stations, the public schools, the local library, contributions of booklets
containing the Constitution from an insurance company, special notices
to members, etc. This is not unusual for Merced, for each year they
have entered into this Observance with boundless interest, energy and
enthusiasm.
The city-wide celebration at Napa, inspired by Yount No. 12 and
Silverado No. 782, drew about 300 persons and was sponsored by 21
civic and religious groups-far and away the most successful celebration of its kind held in Napa. They heartily recommend that "this type
of group sponsorship be adopted throughout the State."
The celebration of Lakeshore Lodge No. 551, !in Oakland, which
featured a "speech drama depicting possible consequences of public
fear and apathy; accent on necessary unity under our Constitution.''
The cast was composed of officers and members of the Lodge. A smorgasbord preceded the program and wives of deceased Past Masters
were guests of the Lodge. About 140 were present and to encourage
attendance they arranged with Job's Daughters that they would baby-sit
in another room, "proV'iding clay, cut-outs and colors for all youngsters.''
The unique celebration of San Diego County, sponsored by the San
Diego County Officer's Association and attracting 1000 persons: they
listened to a short talk by Bro. Robert James, County Clerk, after a
concert by the Shrine Band of Al Bahr Temple, the entrance of massed
American Flags and a choir presentation by members of Job's Daughters. District Court of the United States was then opened by Judge
Jacob Weinberger, and citizenship was conferred on a class of 75 aliens.
Certainly this celebration was a credit to Masonry in more way than
one.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This year, because of the lateness of Labor Day, our Grand Master
decreed that the Constitution Observance period shall extend through
October. A number of Lodges took advantage of this latitude and
are holding their Observance celebrations next month. To date,
enough Lodges and Districts have reported on their celebrations that
we can deal here with live facts and immediate events. As of today
50.7% of the Lodges have reported and while this is but a bare majority of all of the Lodges it represents more reports that we received
in total for each of the last two years after all were in that were coming
in.
At the outset, your committee is pleased to report that this year's
Constitution Observance is more outstanding jn many ways than in
any of the last three years. In this respect we can report progress
although with more facts at hand than previously and consequently
less guesswork, we have mathematically retrograded. We are deeply
gratified at the response accorded our efforts throughout the jurisdiction. It has been our purpose to provide leadership and guidance

188

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

La Mesa Lodge No. 407 should be commended for holding two
Observances-their own which attracted 88 persons and also their participation in the San Diego Observance just referred to. From their
Lodge program they apparently had a lot of fun doing it.
Altadena Lodge No. 678, had a most outstanding celebration which
attracted over 200 persons, on Saturday, Sept. 19th. They first held
a pot-luck picnic at Farnsworth Park, followed by community singing
with an accordian accompaniment. "The crowd then moved to an outdoor amphitheater in the park where a patriotic program was presented
appropriate to the occasion" in the form of a series of tableaux composed of members of Altadena Lodge, De Molay, Job's Daughters
and O.E.S. members. A narrator read from a script as each picture
of the tableau was depicted in full costume, scenery, props, and lighting. The title of the pictures bring to the imagination a cross-section
of our American heritage:
"Boston Tea Party: Spirit of '76: Designing the First Flag: Signers
of the Constitution: Pilgrims: Immigrants: Abraham Lincoln: Judge:
Family Picnic: Iwo Jima: Red Cross-Shrine Crippled Children Charity:
Family Going to Church: Miss Liberty: Alaska."
At the conclusion a short address was given by the U. S. Congressman from their District. From the word of WM Joe L. Schwimm,
of Altadena Lodge, describing this project in his report, it is easy
to deduce that Altadena Lodge is justly proud of their effort and of
its success, as well they might be.
A number of Observances are yet to come in October. This year
again the San Francisco Lodges are joining together in sponsoring an
Observance celebration here in this room on Wednesday evening, Sept.
30, at 8:30 P.M. We understand that they have planned an interesting and entertaining program which includes the United States Marine
Corps Band. We urge you to attend.
Most of the Lodges of Contra Costa County are joining to present
an American Heritage Day program entitled, "The Naked Communist,"
on Sunday, October 25, at 3:30 P.M., at the Richmond Civic Auditorium. Entertainment will be furnished by the combined choral groups
of the Richmond High Schools and Contra Costa Junior Colleges. The
speaker is W. Cleon Skousen, Chief of Police of Salt Lake City and
a national authority on Communism. Aside from his police duties he
is a member of the Utah Bar, a public speaker and author, and is on
the faculty of Brigham Young University. This program should be of
especial interest to Masons as it will provide authoritative information
on this most acute, timely subject which today is on the minds and lips
of everyone.
We wish that we could describe with glowing phrases through the
balance of this report a tremendously successful 1959 Observance but
since we are here to accept and digest the facts we must take, along
with the sweet, some of the bitter, too.

Perhaps if our recent distinguished visitor, His Excellency Nikita
Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the U.S.S.R.,
sometimes otherwise referred to in less polite language, has his way
and all the nations change and subscribe to his system-as he freely
predicts we will-there will be no bitter, as he claims, since all will be
sweetness. But we fear that His Excellency has spoken to us with
the tongues of men and of angels but without Charity and, except for
his appearance, that he greatly resembles the maidens known as the
Lorelei, who with their beautiful songs and graceful forms tempted
Ulysses and his men onto the rock which diversion detained them from
reaching home for twenty years on their return from the Trojan War:
a successful war by the way, as apparently was His Excellency's tour
of America but with frightening and tragic aftermaths, for Ulysses.
As in prior years this committee still is concerned at some evidence
of apathy, lack of interest and even passive resistance to this annual
Grand Lodge patriotic event. These are evident in Lodges scattered
over the jurisdiction and there is some evidence that the situation is
worse than it has been in the past. Because of the damage they do to
themselves as well as to the Fraternity, and possible violations of our
Law we feel that mention here is warranted as being important to the
wellbeing of the Craft.
As you know, Grand Lodge has for years sponsored among the
Lodges but three annual projects: Public Schools Week, Endowment
Month, and Constitution Observance Month. Each of these arise out
of a Proclamation, or Edict by the Grand Master. All of us are obligated to obey these edicts and Worshipful Masters twice so, and while
it is true that we do not specify the degree of enthusiasm with which
they shall be obeyt!d, "it must follow as the night the day" that obedience in this sense certainly means wholehearted, sincere, sympathetic
co-operation and not half-hearted, apathetic, or mere lip-service gestures. If we do not like the Laws or Ordinances we have enacted under
which we work, and can persuade others to our way of thinking, then
we can invoke the mechanics available to us and charge or altogether
revoke the Law or Ordinances which we do not like. But, this committee takes the viewpoint that it is incumbent on each one of us to carry
out the provisions of the Law, both in letter and spirit, to the utmost
of our individual capability. In the application of the pure principles
of Freemasonry, there ~s no alternative course, no mental reservation,
no half-hearted way or no half-measure co-operation. It must be all.
It must be total. What we refer to here are Lodges who persist in holding their Observance celebrations, if they can be called "celebrations,"
behind tiled, closed doors when the last four Grand Masters' Proclamations required that these programs were to be "open to the public
and to which the public was to be welcomed": or, where some Lodges
have not held and do not, we believe, propose to hold a celebration
at all in spite of the Edict by the Grand Master that such celebrations

189

191

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

are to be held. For three years. at least, this situation has existed although how it escapes the eyes and instructive tongues of some few of
the Inspectors is beyound our comprehension --especially when those
same Inspectors are so quick to discern the word "but" injected into the
ritual in place of an "and." Or, where two or more Lodges join together,
as was reported just last week, and only the Worshipful Master doesn't
show up at all but two of his minor officers do: or, where no one at
all shows up from a participating Lodge. If time permitted, we could
go on. It's in the record and in our Oles but this is sufficient to illustrate
what we mean by "apathy" and "passive resistance." It is our sincere
feeling that this minority group of Lodges which we here ref er to,
and to some few of the Inspectors too, are not wilfully disregarding or
disobeying but rather that what appears to be violations of our Law is
but the result of ignorance due to lack of education in such matters, or
of unawareness or a lack of understanding. With proper attention and
careful. dedicated effort on the part of all of us perhaps we can within a
short time turn darkness to light and ignorance to understanding.
Let us hope so for the good of Masonry in general.

In the opinion of the committee a meeting attracting an audience
of 11 7 persons will command greater respect from speakers, radio
and the press, fellow townspeople and officers of community organizations other than Masons, than will an audience of 49 persons.
On the contrary, it may also be deduced from these tables that
we are not on the right track in scheduling combined celebrations as
against each Lodge holding its own affair. While combined programs
attract more people, they lessen the burden on each participating Lodge
with a resultant decrease in interest and decreased support per Lodge.
In this connection, considerable thought must be ,given before combining the celebrations and especially where Lodges are far apart from
each other. Our records and observations prove that more harm than
good is done to Masonry and the warm, fraternal spirit that should
exist between Lodges when Lodges combine to sponsor a public event
such as this, or perhaps any event, and where they are miles apart
as the further from the scene of the event the fewer persons will attend
from the distant points. As a guide it might be said that Lodges should
not combine if they are more than 8-10 miles apart if they expect to
attract either the general public or even the Masons and their families
living a distance ttway. If the Lodges would carefully study and make
use of the suggestions to be found in our Constitution Observance
Guide booklet, there is no reason wny any Lodge, even in the smallest,
most remote town or village of our State. should not put on a very
satisfactory celebration of their own, and, in fact, without resorting
to bringing in a so-called "big name" speaker but using their own local
talent and their native ingenuity. If any Master of a Lodge doubts this
statement let him write or contact the chairman of the Constitution
Observance Committee. Our files contain a number of interesting reports
of what.our brethren have done to make up an excellent program where
there is the will to do it. We have the proof. Ask for it.
For the past three years we have required reports on each Observance celebration from the Masters of the respective Lodges. These reports are in our files and are open to inspection. In addition, this year
we required reports from each of our 14 committeemen. They are also
in our files. We divided the jurisdiction into committee areas, assigning
a committeeman to each area. At a committee meeting in the North
and another in the South, this was unanimously agreed upon and
further, that each committeeman would endeavor to personally meet

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

with each Officer's Association in his area insofar as he was able to do
so. Although we requested $450 in funds at the last Communication to
finance travel to the more distant points, the funds were not forthcoming.
Even so, many miles were covered by various committee members, one
of whom had to commute to the mainland from Catalina Island on
numerous occasions all requiring overnight lodging and subsistence. All
this was done out of the pocket of each individual. with not one cent
paid out of Grand Lodge funds. And, it was done out of love for the
Fraternity and the work in which we are engaged with no feeling of
resentment on the part of any committeeman, if not the chairman. In my
humble opinion, if this Grand Lodge wishes or ordains a program of
any kind, it should be prepared to pay the just and necessary expenses
of supporting such a program and not depend for too long a time on the
private resources of its members.
During the past 6 month we requested time to appear before approximately 60% of the District meetings. Of those requested, about 60%
graciously ·arranged their programs so as to allow time for a discussion
of their Constitution Observance problems. The remainder of those
asked, or about 40%, either did not reply to our solicitations and
follow-ups at all or were unable to give us the time requested, or in some
cases refused to give time at all for a variety of reasons. In all cases the
requests were made of the Inspectors. We have many fine, conscientious,
capable Inspectors but it is apparent that some cannot afford to give all
the time that is demanded of them and consequently must pick and
choose their program, leaving out that which to them is of lesser importance. We believe that the time is not far distant when we will have to
re-apportion the work-load more equitably to the end that no part of
the program will have to suffer nor that anyone shall be over-worked.
Usually personal contact work like this does not suddenly blossom
forth in unexpected beauty and this has not been an exception but we
think the tree appears healthy. the buds are forming and the radiance
of its beauty perhaps is but another season away. A study of the 1959
Master's reports has convinced us that this personal contact work obtains results. For the most part, where advice and counsel were personally given, the celebrations have improved over previous years. As
a result, we unanimously feel that this is the most likely way that success
of the project will be achieved, if the program is to continue, and we
recommend to the next committee that this same method be followed.
For this purpose we have requested of the Finance Committee that the
sum of $450 above last year's appropriation be given to finance this
phase of the program, should this committee be continued through 1960.
A number of Master's reports object to the Observance program for
a number of reasons. Adding these to the list of Lodges whose support
is but apathetic and half-hearted at best, and the number of Lodges who
hold no Observance at all, and in spite of these constituting a minority,

this committee feels that the time has come when the Lodges of the
jurisdiction should express themselves as to whether they desire this
Observance program to continue or not. We therefore offer the following resolution:
"RESOLVED. that the annual Constitution Month Observance
shall be and hereby is continued."
In the event these observances are continued, then it is recommended
that at the next Communication a new Ordinance be adopted that will
provide the terms and conditions under which the Observance shall be
held.
In the further event that the Observance be continued, it is highly
recommended that the name of the Observance be: "American Heritage
Day." This theme carries the same connotations as heretofore but tends
to broaden out in its very implication the manner in which we may
memorialize the United States Constitution. It stimulates ingenuity and
originality at the local level, both of which are particularly needed in
the smaller communities and, we might add, in the larger communities
too.
Should this committee be continued, we respectfully request that the
sum of $1200 be allocated for our use during the coming year.
It has been a rare privilege and an interesting personal experience
to have been able to serve on this committee for which I express the
appreciation of myself and all of the hard-working members who have
so loyally and conscientiously served with me. For this privilege we
tender our gratitude to the Grand Master and to this Grand Lodge.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF
THE COMMITTEE OF MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
On behalf of all the members of the History Committee, I wish to
extend to you, Most Worshipful. our sincere thanks and deep appreciation for the privilege of serving you and the Grand Lodge.
As in former years, it is intended that this. Report should not only
contain an account of the committee's activity during the past year, but
also place into the record certain historical data important to this
jurisdiction and not covered elsewhere.
From time to time we have reported on the disorderly appearance
of some of the historically important burial sites, containing the remains
of illustrious brethren. We are most happy to report that as of this
communication matters are somewhat better, but lest we mislead you,
there is still room for considerable improvement. If we can assume that
no new, blighted graveyards are in the making and if we continue to face
up to our responsibilities, then shortly the last resting places of departed
brethren will be kept permanently green with budding Acacia and bright
with summer's flowering roses.
Grand Master Louis C. Drapeau, in his message to this Grand
Lodge on Monday, October 13, 1952, commented about the laying of
wreaths at the places of rest of all of our Past Grand Masters. About
Past Grand Master William H. Howard's grave, he had this to say:
"We were unable to find the exact place of rest of Past Grand Master
Howard in the old cemetery at Virginia City, Nevada. Vandals have
destroyed or carried away his headstone. But we laid a wreath for
him at a monument erected in memory of another celebrated California
and Nevada Mason, Brother (Edward Faris) Storey."
While this committee appreciates Grand Master Drapeau's generosity in sharing the renowned Edward F. Storey with our sister jurisdiction o~ Nevada. we feel the record should show that Bro. Storey was an
ardent Mason here in California, having been instrumental in founding
Texas Lodge No. 46, at San Juan Bautista and Visalia Lodge No. 128,
Visalia, both Lodges of which he was the first Master, he did nothing
to promote Masonry over in Nevada, probably because he was not
there long enough before he was killed in the Piute War. Storey arrived in Nevada in late 1859 and was killed on June 7, 1860. The first
Masonic Lodge in Virginia City, Virginia No. 3, did not come into
existence until 1862, and then through the efforts of our beloved Past
Grand Master William H. Howard, who had arrived in Virginia City
the year previous. A mistake was made by placing the wreath in memory
of Howard at the Storey marker. The wreath was not placed on
Howard's grave which Bro. Drapeau correctly described as being lost,
but it was placed in the wrong cemetery! The Storey Memorial marker

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

195

is located in what locally is called the "new" cemetery, although it was
started about 1870. Some careful, patient research work conducted this
past year up in Virginia City and at the University of Nevada, and
with the most gracious help of several distinguished Nevada brethren,
revealed that Past Grand Master William H. Howard was buried
in Flowery Hill Cemetery which is about 3 miles east and slightly south
of the present Virginia City. We also have good reason to believe that
Storey is buried in this "new" cemetery and, of course, not at all under
the memorial shaft erected to his memory in 1933 in the present cemetery.
Flowery Hill Cemetery first was the "Boot Hill" cemetery of
Virginia City, burials having started there in 1859-60. In the hurry and
bustle of the mining camp no other ground was set aside for burials and
Flowery Hill soon began to hold the remains of respected and esteemed
citizens. We are indebted to the original files of the "Territorial Enterprize," of September 14 and 19, 1866, and the courtesy of the librarian
of the University of Nevada Library, for Howard's death notice and
obituary which give his burial place as Flowery Hill Cemetery. Further
research convinced us that the old, abandoned cemetery was Flowery
Hill Cemetery, despite some contrary opinions notwithstanding. Up to
this time, despite much searching, investigating, and some exploratory
digging, the exact gravesite of Past Grand Master Howard, in Flowery
Hill Cemetery, has not yet been located and may well never be, but
y9ur committee intends to continue the search. The total absence of any
headstones on any graves is a severe handicap. and to show how vandals
work there was last year about 4 broken headstones scattered among
the sagebrush and graves, and just a month ago, upon re-visiting the
place, not one of t~ese 4 could be found. So now there are none.
Last year, in our Report, your committee proposed that this Grand
Lodge enact legislation permitting the establishment of what we called
a chain of "Registered Historic Masonic Landmarks." The project, as
recommended, would require no financial contributions by Grand Lodge
and was thoroughly described in an appendix to the Report, which was
published in full on pages 204-6 of the 1958 Proceedings. Through inadvertance, we neglected to put the matter before you as a Resolution.
which was the intent. It therefore is still before us in the form of unfinished business. For the record, we now move that this proposal be
placed before this Grand Lodge for approval and I now so move, Most
Worshipful.
Last summer and during the fall months, Bro. 0. J. Wohlgemuth a
member of the committee took over 300 colored photos of about 30 of
our oldest and most historical Masonic Halls throughout northern California. These pictures, supplemented by pictures and photos of several
pioneers and other subjects, loaned to us of a private collection, made
up the lecture entitled, "SOME CAME BY LAND AND SOME
CAME BY SEA," which Bros.
Kenneth Downs, M.A. Epperson and
u

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

members of the History Committee have been showing throughout the
jurisdiction. When we fill several engagement s within the next three
weeks, we will have shown this illustrated lecture before nearly 40
Masonic Districts, comprising about 200 Lodges. We estimate about
5000 brethren have seen the program to date. About 30 lectures in all
will have been given. Despite using 6 lecturers, there were weeks in the
Spring when we could not possibly have squeezed in another date. The
lecture, as developed is not only historically accurate, but is filled with
human interest stories. It requires a full evening to give, running about
1 hour and 45 minutes. Because of the response, we feel it is still necessary to require that wherever possible Lodges join together by Masonic
Districts in requesting dates for a showing. In requesting a presentation in your area, please indicate the day of the week you would like
to have it and give us about 3 choices of dates. In remote areas it is
necessary to schedule it for a Friday or Saturday evening. Address your
request to the History Committee chairman, care of the Grand Lodge
office. Lodges are asked to bear travel and sustenance expense of the
lecturer. He will bring all the equipment he needs to give the program.
"SOME CAME BY LAND AND SOME CAME BY SEA,"
being a "first" in this field by the History Committee, has given rise to a
project which we propose to commence in the fall. It is the production
of several 30 minute short subjects, any one of which we will send
out to a Lodge along with program notes and manuscript. All a Lodge
need do to present the program is to show the pictures and read the
manuscript. Some demand for this sort of presentation has arisen out of
the present program. When we are ready, appropriate announcement
will go forward to the Lodges. The subjects will be historical and of
the same human interest kind as in our first project. The funds we are
requesting in large part is to finance this new project. This year we
contemplate the production of three of these special short subjects. If
they prove popular we will produce more of them in the future.
Your History Committee has endeavored to find where Peter
Lassen visited a Lodge. We have assumed that he visited Western Star
No. 2, but the early tiler's registers of that Lodge are missing. However,
we are indebted to Theodore Meriam, Grand Orator, for having called
our attention to the tiler's register of Chico Lodge No. 111 which shows
that Peter Lassen and John Bidwell visited that Lodge on October 17,
1857. Bro. Meriam states that Lassen visited Chico Lodge on other
occasions, but he is quite certain that this date was the last visit.

We respectfully request the sum of $750 be appropriate d to our
use for the ensuing year.

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON RESEARC H
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your research committee is grateful to the Grand Master for encouraging and supporting the work of Masonic education in all its
phases. Our appreciation also goes to the Grand Secretary for his help,
especially with mailing lists and distribution of material.
All Grand Lodges endorse Masonic education with varying degrees of emphasis. California is a leader in the field, not following any
sterotyped program but building an original self-contained system
which it is belived is best fitted to the needs of our jurisdiction. The research committee is the instrument for carrying out the Grand Lodge
program of Masonic education.
CONSTITUENT LoDGES
is to supply blanket coverage so that

every constituent Lodge will partiicipate. Each incoming Worshipful
Master is requested to name a research committee in his Lodge. His
secretary reports the name and address of the chairman to the Grand
Secretary who compiles a research mailing list. The list is used for
periodical mailings of educational helps gathered by the Grand Lodge
committee and issued under the title of "Research Notes." The Lodge
committee thus has available suitable material to be read to the Lodge
or used as the basis for remarks. Lodge chairmen who have the time
and inclination to work up their own material are encouraged to do so.
The success or failure of Lodge committees in bringing educational papers and talks to the attention of the Lodge is controlled to a
great extent by the attitude of the Worshipful Master, since this is not
a mandatory observance imposed on the constituent Lodges by Grand
Lodge but only made available for their benefit.
Your committee is pleased to report that most Worshipful Masters
are receptive to the plan outlined and arrange for educational reports to
be given at some time during the year. The procedure favored by your
committee is to have the Master call on the research committee of his
Lodge for a five to ten minute committee report at each stated meeting.

205 Masonic Education. The educational program of Grand Lodge

shall be carried out through the system of committees herein provided,
each consisting of three members or more, appointed by each incoming
Grand Master for the ensuing Masonic year, as follows:
(a) Committee on Research for Norther n California.
( b) Committee on Research for Southern California.
Each of these committees shall have the duty in its respective area
to plan and supervise Masonic education generally, to promote the naming of a research committee by the Master of each Lodge, to maintain a
mailing list of research committee chairmen in the ofRce of the Grand
Secretary. to encourage the research Lodges in rendering the greatest
possible assistance to constituent Lodges and to promote regional
seminars and other educational meetings through out the jurisdiction.
with special attention to population centers not in the vicinity of a
research Lodge.

This committee shall have the duty to supply Masonic information
and educational helps for the use of the research committees in the
constituent Lodges and to circulate printed material to them under the
title of "Resear ch Notes" in Februar y, April and June of each year, over
the mailing list maintained in the ofRce of the Grand Secretary.

This committee shall have the duty to plan and present a research
seminar during each annual communication for the instruction and benefit of prospective Masters, in matters other than ritual, and also for the
benefit of members of Grand Lodge interested in Masonic education.
This ordinance shall not be construed as replacing or limiting the
functions and integrity of the research Lodges.

REPO RT OF COMM ITTEE ON
DISPO SITIO N OF GRAN D MAST ERS' PORT RAITS
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
After careful consideration of various alternatives for the display of
the portraits of Past Grand Master s in the new Memorial Temple and
after discussions with members of the Grand Lodge and with other Past
Grand Masters , this committee recommends the following:
1. That photogr aphs of and biographical data on all Past Grand
Master s be suitably displayed in the main entranc e foyer, with a
duplicate set of photos and histories to be prepare d for the archives.
2. That existing portrait s of Grand Masters. with the exception of the
one of the first Grand Master, be returne d to the various home
Lodges with the underst anding that these Lodges will hang the
portrait s in their own rooms or present them to the families.
3. That the portrait of the first Grand Master continue to hang in the

201

Grand Master 's ofRce in the Memorial Temple where it is now
located.
4. That the policy be adopted of ceasing to commission the painting
of the portrait s of future Grand Masters.
An explanation of the reasons behind these recommendations follows:
Lack of Available Space in the Memorial Temple for Hanging Large
~ortraits. The .Committee feels that the Temple has no place which
is Sllltable for hangmg large portraits of past and future Grand Masters.
The Committee considered, for example. the possibility of utilizing the
marble walls in the entranc e foyer, upstairs and down; the second Boor
wall outside the auditorium; the committee rooms; and the corridors in
the back of the auditorium leading to the committee rooms.
The Committee feels that the style of architecture in the Temple and
the co.nstruction of the walls do not lend themselves to the type of
portrait s we have, and proper lighting facilities for display purposes are

Future Display of the Portraits. The Committee recommends that

with the fine men who have led the fraternity. The Committee recom-

mends, incidentally, that a duplicate set of the photographs and accompanying information should be prepared for the archives.
As an example of the type of display it prefers, the Committee presents the attached sketch from the Royal Showcase Company of San
Francisco. The sketch pictures a stand holding 10 panels, each to have
two pictures on the front and two on the back, or a total of 40. Starting
with three stands to accommodate the present need, we could later expand by the addition of other stands as the need arises. The panels will

copy. The approximate over-all size of the panels (although design
of the entire stand and panels cannot be fixed until decisions with regard
to the Committee's recommendations are made) will be approximately
10 x 16 or 12 x 15, according to whether the historical information is
placed at the bottom or at the side of the photographs.
The frame and beveled molding panels probably should be of metal
with a special double baked-on silver finish to the sample submitted.
Cost of each frame and accompanying panels is estimated at $350.
The Committee wishes to point out that its proposal is flexible and
subject to ready modification, e.g.: Each stand could be designed to
hold more panels, and thus the number of stands could be reduced: or
the panels themselves could be mounted on the metal separating the
doors to the terrace or on the pillars instead of being swung from stands;
if additional space is needed for biographical data, the number of panels
could be doubled. and the copy could face the photograph, with two
photographs thus appearing on one side of a panel and two writeups
on the back.
The Committee understands from the Grand Secretary that photographs already are available for most of the Past Grand Masters. It
assumes that the necessary biographical data will be furnished by the
Masonic History Committee and that the final design and location of the
stands and/or panels will be approved by the Memorial Temple
Trustees.
Existing Portraits To Be Returned. The Committee recommends that
each of the existing portraits, with the exception of the one picturing the
first Grand Master, be returned with appropriate ceremonies to the
Lodge of the former Grand Master. The portrait thereafter should be
hung in the home Lodge of the former Grand Master or, if the Lodge
and his family so desire, returned to the Master's family---and, again,
with appropriate ceremonies.
Portrait of the First Grand Master. Feeling that the portrait of
Brother Stevenson is especially inspiring, the Committee recommends
that this particiular portrait remain in the position of honor now given
it in the Grand Master's office in the Memorial Temple. In addition to
having the historical value that comes with its marking the beginning of

the Grand Lodge in California, this particular portrait appears to be one
of the better ones.
No Future Portraits. Since it is not recommending further display
of Grand Masters' portraits, the Committee suggests that the Grand
Lodge cease commissioning the painting of portraits for future Grand
Masters. It makes this proposal. not only because of its feeling about the
limited opportunity for display of the portraits. but also because of the
difficulty of securing consistently high quality at a reasonable cost.
Respectfully submitted,
EDWARD H. REDFORD
CHESTER R. MACPHEE

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
During the past year, your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries has
undertaken a complete review of all information accumulated during the
past three years. This Committee first came into existence late in 1956.
Since that time every effort has been made to establish a complete list of
cemeteries owned by California Lodges together with their history and
their present physical condition.
From the very 8rst your Committee has found that the information
received in many cases is either vague, subject to interpretation or contradictory. It, therefore, seemed important that these items be cleared.
We believe that we have accomplished this during the past year or at
least have materially reduced the number so as to now give to Grand
Lodge a detailed report which reflects the true picture of California
Masonic Cemeteries.
Again we wish to point out that our cemeteries fall into several well
defined categories. To understand the problems involved it must be made
clear that we not only have many cemeteries owned and operated by our
Lodges but we also have joint ownership of cemeteries with other bodies.
usually the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. We have another group
which formerly were Masonic cemeteries but now are maintained by
public funds. We have Lodges which own plots within private or
public cemeteries: we have at least three Masonic cemeteries where the
actual ownership has not been established, although present information
sems to indicate that they may belong to this Grand Lodge. due to their
having been established by Lodges now extinct: and finally we have
innumerable single graves which are marked by a Masonic emblem.

204

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Attached to this report, but not necessarily a part therof. is a complete list of the cemeteries grouped as has just been indicated, showing
present and past ownership, history whenever available, and present
condition of the cemetery.
Also attached to this report but not necessarily a part thereof, is a
photograph album wherein we have attached pictures of our cemeteries
whenever available.
Our report also gives a complete numerical list of Lodges reporting
that they do not now nor have they ever owned a Masonic cemetery or
part thereof. This report therefore now shows:
23 Masonic cemeteries owned by Masonic Lodges.
8 cemeteries jointly owned.
27 former Masonic cemeteries. now operated by public funds.
23 Lodges owning plots within private or public cemeteries.
Total 81 resting places for Brother Masons.
At the last annual Communication of Grand Lodge, legislation was
passed which required all Lodges owning cemeteries (in whole or in
part), or a plot within a cemetery, to make an annual report to Grand
Lodge. As this report is written only fourteen Lodges have filed such a
report. A continued study of Masonic cemeteries has brought forth
certain weaknesses in our legislation. This lead the Committee last
year to submit certain recommendations to Grand Lodge for its consideration. Some of these recommendations were approved. However,
the Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommended, and
Grand Lodge approved, that five of the proposals be returned to the
Cemetery Committee for "more specific proposal as to policy and
legislation."
We therefore submit as a part of this report, the recommendations
referred to above. We now believe that they will meet the requirements
as set forth by your action in 1958. They again are the recommendations
of your Cemetery Committee and we offer them for your consideration.
This Committee is deeply indebted to the Inspectors. Masters and
Secretaries for their patient cooperation. Without their help this report
would not be possible. We also are indebted to the Grand Secretaries
office and staff. Their courteous, friendly and efficient assistance has
made it a pleasure to work with them. We appreciate their assistance.
Respectfully submitted,

No. I

SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CEMETERIES

Masonic cemeteries have existed in California since 1850. This
Committee has been unable to find any serious breach of Masonic law or
of commercialism in our entire history. All of our cemeteries have been
conducted in a dignified, quiet and wholly Masonic manner.
In 1891, Grand Master Conklin ruled, and it is still our Masonic
Law (Code No. 409a) that "Providing a suitable place for burial of its
dead, and maintenance thereof. are legitimate expenses of a Lodge."
Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries reads Section 333 B-3 as
meaning that no Mason shall use or be a party to the use of the word
Masonic unless it shall be a cemetery or burial association conducted
wholly by Masons and only for the use and benefit of Masons or
Masonry.
It is the opinion of this Committee that very few of our cemeteries
come within the scope of this interpretation. There are some Masonic
cemeteries which limit the sale of lots to Masons only. Many restrict the
sale of lots to Masons and their families. Still others permit the sale of
lots to the general public. This last group includes all of those cemeteries
which are jointly owned with the Independent Order of Odd Fellows.
In raising the question of possible commercialism it is not the intent
of this Committee to set aside customs which have long been practiced
by the Craft. Some of these customs have existed within our cemeteries
since the beginning of Masonry in California. It is because these have
been permitted to go unnoticed all of these years that we now feel that
our records should either recognize them. if in error, then necessary
corrections should be made.
During recent years, Grand Lodge has focused attention on commercialism and through its Committee has attempted to define and limit
such activity. There can be little doubt that originally and perhaps
basically all Masonic cemeteries are to some degree commercial. We
now feel that the time has arrived for us to determine the scope of our
cemeteries.
Your Committee on Cemeteries therefore recommends: that a new
subsection be added to California Masonic Code No. 333 to be known
as section No. 333Q to clarify any possible misinterpretation as to the
operation and maintenance of Masonic cemeteries. such subsection to
read as follows: .
Masonic cemeteries have operated in California since 1852 without
the need of special legislation and have so conducted their affairs as to
reflect credit upon our Fraternity. They therefore shall be permitted to
continue their operations as in the past. They may sell lots within their
cemetery (or plots) to Masons, their wives, widows and family, and to
orphans. when in keeping with Masonic principles and practices. New

206

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

Masonic cemeteries shall be operated as non-profit units, however. lots
may be sold so as to provide for perpetual care and all lots sold should
provide for the continued well groomed appearanc e of the cemete_ry.
Nothing in this section is intended to in any way ·reflect upon the wording
of section 333 except as it may apply to Masonic cemeteries. Any violation by a Lodge, Cemetery Committee or other Masonic group or individual as to the terms of section No. 333, except as above provided.
shall be subject to Masonic penalties as provided by our laws.

415a-Th e proper care and maintenance of all cemetery property,
owned in whole or in part. including all lots or plots, are the responsibility of the Lodge or Lodges holding title thereto. and it shall be mandatory
upon them to so maintain the cemetery. lot or plot, as to reflect credit
upon the Fraternity . This responsibility shall rest fully upon a Lodge
owning a cemetery, or in joint ownership with another Lodge. or joint
ownership with some non-Maso nic group, or a lot or plot within a public
or private cemetery.
415b-lt shall be the responsibility of a Lodge or Lodges to care for
all graves within their jurisdiction which carry Masonic emblems or other
Masonic identification on their headstones.

SPECIAL CoMMIITE E ON CEMETERI ES

Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries has carefully studied the
California Masonic Code. Within its index we find twenty-five sections
which deal with our funeral service; fourteen of these same sections are
listed under burials, plus six additional sections. This makes a total of
thirty-one sections in our code which outline our proper course of action
following the death of a brother. When we investigat e cemeteries in
the code, we find but three sections to which to refer.
.
Sections 409A in 1891 provides that "a suitable place for a burial
of its dead and the maintenan ce thereof are legitimate expenses of a
Lodge." Section 333h passed in 1954 and 1955 provid~s t~at "a Lo~ge
owning cemetery property may relieve itself of trust obhgatton s ~o ~am­
tain the property if such burdens are assumed by a cemetery district to
which the property is transferre d." Section 332A passed in 19.36. pr~­
vides that "a privately owned cemetery with the word Masonic m its
name or advertisin g itself as Masonic it subject to proceedin gs to cease
and desist."
It is the opinion of your Committee that there exists a definite obligation to our deceased brothers and that it is long past time to give thought
to some definite legislation which will continuall y remind us of this
obligation. We attend funerals and we deliver a beautiful service but
it seems that once a brother is lowered into his grave that we forget our
responsibilities to him. We forget the pride of the Craft in a well cared
for grave.
Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries therefore recommends:
That section now known as Code No. 409a be deleted:
That a new section be added to our California Masonic Code to be
known as Section No. 415.
That the cross references of Section 409 include a reference to this
new Section "Masonic Cemeterie s No. 415."
That Section No. 415 read as follows:
Providing a suitable place for the burial of its dead, and maintenan ce
thereof. are legitimate expenses of a Lodge. Conklin. G.M .. 1891 '. pp~l.
214; RD No. 605. The care of our dead is clearly a Masonic obligation
as is our care of the living.

SPECIAL CoMMITIE E ON CEMETERI ES

Approved by Grand Lodge in 1958-No legislation prepared.
Your Committe e on Masonic Cemeteries has carefully studied the
rulings made in 1954 and 1955 by Most Worshipf ul Past Grand Masters
Harwell and Clausen in which they decided that a Lodge may relieve
itself of its trust obligations to maintain a cemetery property if such
burdens are assumed by a cemetery district. Investigat ion by your
Committe e has brought to light some seventeen Masonic cemeteries
which have received "relief of its trust obligation s" by the formation of
cemetery districts.
Your Committee is not altogether sure that this ruling should be followed in all cases regardless of circumstances. For example, we agree
that in the case of Humboldt Lodge No. 79, that such action was wise
and in the best interest of Masonry a!Td the comunity. The cemetery
had to be moved to make room for the city's expansion. By mutual agreement the city took over the cemetery as an historical landmark. On the
other hand should a Lodge be relieved of its obligation merely because
lack of interest and poor manageme nt has forced them into a position
wherein the Lodge must use some of its own funds to rehabilitat e the
cemetery or are they to be permitted to slide out from under by forming
a cemetery district which will assume their responsibilities.
Your Committe e questions the use of public funds as a means of relieving us of our obligation. We wonder at the reaction of a brother or
his family in the purchase of a plot in a ·Masonic cemtery, when they
suddenly find that the cemetery has become, not a Masonic plot, but one
supported and managed by public funds.
Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries therefore recommends: that
Section No. 333H of the Masonic Code be modified to read as follows:
A Lodge owning cemetery property may relieve itself of trust ob~ga­
tions to maintain the property ( 1 ) if such burdens are assumed by a
cemtery district and ( 2) if such cemetery district will maintain the
cemetery as an historical landmark. The Lodge, of course, should not

208

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

engage in any political campaign in connection with any such transfer.
No Lodge is relieved of any of its obligations by permitting its
property to be transferred to a cemetery district, except as provided
above. They shall be responsible for the Masonic graves that existed at
the time of transfer and shall be held responsible for their care, maintenance and general upkeep. This section of the cemetery must be maintained as a Masonic section as that was the agreement at the time the
grave was sold.

RECOMENDA TION No. IV
SPEc.1AL COMMITTEE ON CEMETERIES

Your Committe on Masonic Cemeteries has found that Masonic
plots within private cemeteries have been and are being kept in excellent
condition. As long as a private cemetery displays the proper respect in
the use of our name, we realize that there is little to be done.
The mere fact that a private cemetery has a Masonic section (usually
not exclusively sold to Masons) may in itself indicate that our name is
being used in fostering the sale of their lots. This custom, however, is
one of long standing and no breach of our laws has come to the attention of this Committee.
With this generally accepted practice of Masonic plots within private
cemeteries, your Committee believes that proper legislation should be
provided prior to the time that conflict with our standards might develop.
Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries therefore recommends: that the
following sub-section be added to Code No. 302 to be known as 302 B.
302 B A privately owned cemetery that maintains a plot which has
been designated as a "Masonic•• section within said private cemetery,
(such section may be indicated by the use of our emblem or other
Masonic representati on) shall be subject to all of our rules and regulations, and shall be subject to Masonic action whenever infringements
develop.
RECOMENDA TION No. V
SPECIAL COMMITTEE OP CEMETERIES

Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries has information on nine
cemeteries where a Masonic lodge has ownership jointly with the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. One of this group has a cemetery
operated jointly by the community, the Masonic lodge, the Independen t
Order of Odd Fellows and the Catholic Church through a board of
directors.
Two of the a}n:)ve now indicate that they are within a cemetery dfs.trict. Of the remaining seven cemeteries, one is neglected, two report that
their condition is very poor, two indicate that they are well cared for
and two have given the committee no report as ~e condition of. their
cemetery. It is the opinion of your committee that joint ownership of

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

209

a cemetery is not conductive to good maintenance. With the passage of
time one or both organization s are apt to lose interest and live in hope
that the other will pick up the full responsibility. Two organization s may
enact legislation and, though well intended. may stir up misundersta ndings and may even lead to hard feelings.
This committee has been unable to find anything in our code which
permits of joint-membership of a cemetery. or any other property, with
a non-Masoni c group. Neither is there any indication that such action
is prohibited. In early California Masonic history such joint ownership
seemed to be an accepted practice.
Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries therefore recommends: Add
section J to code No. 405.
405 J No lodge may use its funds to purchase in joint ownership with
a non-Masoni c body. any real property to be used as a cemetery or for
any other joint purpose. It is not intended that this legislation exclude
the lodges' right to purchase as sole owner any section of property within a cemetery to be used as a Masonic plot. Any such section or plot
must be the exclusive responsibility of the lodge.
405 K All lodges now operating cemeteries under joint ownership
should prepare to secure a clear title to that portion of the cemetery
used by them and prepare to secure the relationship of joint ownership
either through mutual agreement or by purchase. Our obligation to our
dead cannot be a divided responsibility. Care should be exercised in a
transaction of this type to prevent any injury to the lodge. It is therefore
important that each such lodge be given ample time to work out its own
solution.
The Committee submitted with the above report carefully prepared
descriptive material, which listed and described all phases of Masonic
cemetery programs which had come to their attention. This material
has been flied in the Grand Secretary's office as part of the records applying to the Committee on Cemeteries, where it is available for reference
and guidance.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMIT TEE ON SCHOLAR SHIPS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The special committee appointed by the Grand Master to perform
certain duties in connection with the program of awarding scholarships
for advanced study in higher education has had several meetings in
1959 to date. The committee has studied ·the various submissions of
applicants during the past few years and has found them wanting in
many respects and leaving much to be desired. The committee feels that
the fraternity has not received from the scholarship program any of

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the results originally hoped for. In addition, the program as now set up
has not had the cooperation of the universities having graduate schools
in education. Under these circumstances the program has been dormant
during the past year with no entries submitted and no awards made.
The committee has some definite ideas as to a scholarship program
and within the next few months should be able to formulate them. It
would seem, however, that the authority of the committee was to administer the program, judge the entries and recommend to the Grand
Master the granting of awards. The committee feels that it should
be given authority to make concrete suggestions as to whether the program should be continued and if so, in what form. Under these
circumstances the committee requests that the appropriation made last
year for the purpose of awarding scholarships be continued in the
forthcoming budget and that some committee continue to work upon
the problem. Since one of the functions of the new committee would
be to make recommendations concerning the continuance of the program
and its future administration, it is suggested that the size of the committee be augmented so as to consider all possible viewpoints.
Respectfully submitted,
SAMUEL I. JACOBS
GEORGE D. GAVIN
WARD M. NICHOLS
Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

At the 109th Annual Communication in October 1958, a majority
report was presented rejecting completely any modification of the
ritual as it would be affected by the use of visual aids. A minority
report protesting the limited study made of the topic assigned and
recommending restudy by a new committee was adopted. The
present committee is the result of this action.
B. Purpose: The responsibility of this committee has been defined in
two ways: ( 1) the recommendation of the minority report that this
committee "present to Grand Lodge at its 1959 Communication
recommendations relative to the type of aids to be used, if any, and
the manner in which they shall be used" and ( 2) the charge of the
Grand Master to the new committee that "the question of visual
aids be thoroughly explored and a report presented to the forthcoming Communication which will dispose of the question once and
for all."
C. Personnel: Something of the background of this committee may be
helpful to the members of Grand Lodge in evaluating this report.
All. of course, are Past Masters of California lodges. Two are former
inspectors and thus are well acquainted with the problems of ritual,
instruction, and law. Two have served Grand Lodge as appointive
officers. One is connected with the motion picture industry and
hence well understands the potential of visual aids. One is a public
school educator thoroughly conversant with the use of audio-visual
tools as learning aids. All are dedicated to the fraternity and thus
to the ideal of making Masons, not merely adding members.

210

REPORT OF
THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON VISUAL AIDS
I. INTRODUCTION:
The five members of the Special Committee on Visual Aids are
unanimous in their opinion that service on this committee has been a
unique and rewarding experience. We can only trust that the hours of
study and deliberation, dealing by the nature of our assignment with
basic issues of Masonic law, ritual, and education, and the recommenc;iations resulting therefrom, will prove of value to the welfare and harmony
of our esteemed Grand Lodge. It is in this spirit, plus the conviction that
better answers are possible than can evolve from either indifference on
the one hand or arbitrary prohibitions on the other, that this committee
is pleased to submit the following report.
II. THE CoMMIITEE:
A. Reason for: Brethren who have followed Grand Lodge proceedings
closely will recall that at the 108th Annual Communication in September 1957, resolutions were presented which in effect protested
decisions by the Ritual Committee banning use of ship models and
pictures and favored more extensive use of visual aids in the three
degrees. The action taken was appointment of a special committee
"in order that a full evaluation may be made of the entire subjttt."

211

III. PROCEDURE:
A. Meetings: A ·criticism was made of the original committee that it
met only once, and at that time all members were not present. This
committee has met flve times in three to four hour sessions. In addition, many individual conferences have been held including one
in Berkeley by the Chairman with the Grand Lecturer and three
proponents of the original resolutions.
B. Questionnaires: A study as complete at this committee was expected
to make must be based on facts. Therefore, utilizing questionnaire
techniques carefully planned, we have contacted every lodge of this
Grand Jurisdiction, as well as the forty-eight other Grand Lodges
within the continental United States, to ascertain both practice and
opinion as they relate to the use of visual aids. The nature of the
inquiry is reflected in the findings of this report.
C. Solicitation of individual opinion: Through a printed fovitation in
the 1959 summer issue of THE CALIFORNIA FREEMASON,
as well as directly through conversations by individual committee
members, we have received many points of view freely volunteered.
These replies have even included sample visual aids.
