B. Masonic practice:
1. Most other Grand Jurisdictions in the United States are less
restrictive in their use of visual aids than is California.
2. A clear majority of the California lodges replying to our questionnaire believe that present degree practices are adequate and should
be retained without modification except as the Ritual Committee
approves.
3. The area of confllict in California centers in definition and
semantics. What is esoteric and therefore secret? Honest differencies of opinion ex·ist. Frankly, this committee sees no reason
for banning a representation of a sailing ship any more than we
would ban use of an evergreen sprig in the public funeral service.
C. Masonic education:
1. We presently make extensive use of visual aids in all of our degrees e. g. the Bible, the square, the compass, the pillars, the
working tools. Hence extending the use of visual aids would not be
a violation of principle.
2. Visual aids are an important factor in the learning process. This
has been so well established by modern research as to need no
documentation here. The question for us is not, do visual aids
have value, but rather how can they be used within the limits
inherent in our work.
3. The educational methods used should be based not alone on the
desired impressions for the candidate and the convenience of the
officers, bot certainly as much in terms of significant values for the
audience (members and visitors on the side line).
.

2i4

C. Individual responses. Opinions of California members vary as
completely and widely as other Grand Lodge practices. The following quotatiions illustrate the differences which exist.
1. "I personally feel that we have gone steadily backward in the
effectiveness of our degree work, as one after another, all physical
props to assist the memory of the candidate and the pleasure of
the side lines has been prohibited by the Grand Lecturer or other
agency."
2. "We feel that carefully selected slides add to the effectiveness of
the lectures no matter how well given they are. We do not, however, feel that we need any more rules or diets to accomplish this,
but that each lodge be allowed some latitude in providing these
as their capabilities permit."
3. "The entire membership of the Ritual Committee joins me in the
belief that to tamper with the time-honored and time-tested method
of imparting the secrets of Freemasonry to the candidate is to
commit a disservice to Masonry and incalculable harm to our
Institution."

v. CONCLUSIONS:
For purposes of convenience only, we shall group certain facts, clear
to us as a result of our study, under three major categories.
A. Masonic law:
1. The twenty-third landmark is "the secrecy of the institution."
2. A 1908 California Grand Lodge rul:ing reads in part, "It is no
excuse or justification for any that men are eager to break these
laws, or that men have broken them before, or that in other degrees
or orders of American Masonry cipher rituals may be in common
use. Our duty and obligation as Ancient Craft Masons compel
our obedience to these ancient regulations.''
3. In 1938 the Grand Lodge supported the Grand Lecturer's ruling
that, "Any slide, map, chart or picture of any nature, showing in
part or in whole, the secret work of the three degrees of Masonry,
is contrary to the laws of the fraternity and in violation of the

VI. RECOMMENDATIONS:
A. This committee sees no reason for change in the presentation and
lectures of the three degrees as now constituted. Although California's position is conservative, when compared with the law and
practice of other Grand Jurisdictions as they relate to the use of
visual aids in the several degrees, we believe the uniformly high
quality of California work is a tribute to present procedures.
B. Handwork of Masonic craftsmen ought to be viewed with appreciation and recognition within the limits imposed by the landmarks, our
law, and due propriety. We can see a real place in a lodge building
for appropriate physical representations, whether they be a ship
model or painting, murals in lodge halls of carefully selected symbols, or display cases of Masonic relics~ These should not be a part
of any ritual, but would add richness and beauty to the degree environment. Our Memorial Temple is an excellent example of the
potential along these lines.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

C. Masonic education programs built around visual expressions of the
three degrees are possible and would have value in promoting ~th
interest and understanding. These should not be a part of our ntual
but would be designed to supplement the degree experiences even as
the seminars conducted by the Research Lodges.
D. If recommendation C •is accepted, a new committee should be appointed consisting in part of representation from the present Vi~ual
Aids Committee, the Ritual Committee, and the Research Committee
with the limited assignment of developing an appropriate visual
education program for each degree with supporting written or audio
commentary consistent with California standards and objectives.
Representation from the three committees named should assure continuity of information gained this year, strict compliance with ritual
and law, and authentic commentary to make the pictures meaningful.
This materials when approved by Grand Lodge should be available
through the Grand Secretary's Office to assure uniformity throughout the jurisdiction. Their use should be optional by lodges but when
used should be subject to conditions outlined by the committee.
E. The $300 tentatively approved for the work of this committee for
the coming year should be allocated to the new committee if and
when appointed.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Board of Library Commissioners begs leave to submit the
following report:
We have canvassed the situation with regard to the Masonic
memorabilia and the substantial number of books now owned by Grand
Lodge, the space provided for a library and museum in the Masonic
Memorial Temple, the practices of a number of other Grand Lodges
regarding maintenance of libraries and the use made of them, the
problem of suitable furniture and shelving for a library, and cases
for museum items and, so far as we have been able to do so, the needs
of the brethren for library service. We present the following recommendations with, in some cases our reasons for each:
1. The Grand Lodge of California should have a library and museum
and these should be established eventually in the space provided for
them in the Masonic Memorial Temple.
A) In 1957 Grand Lodge adopted a resolution containing the following declaration:
"It is the earnest desire of this Grand Lodge that a vigorous program
for the furtherance of a Grand Lodge Library be carried forward, by
such measures as may be deemed expediant and practical."
B) Space for a library and museum has been specifically mentioned
in various Grand Lodge publications and in soliciting funds for the
building of the temple. We can do no less than keep faith with our
brethren by providing that which has been promised them.
C)The ability of a library to assist brethren to advance in Masonry,
and to spread 1\fasonic light among their fellows, is unquestionable.
Likewise the availability of Masonic relics, old records, jewels, mementoes, aprons, diplomas and other memorabilia helps to preserve the
history of our institution and is of solid value to the student.
In his report in 1956 Grand Master Stewart said:
"It goes without saying that the need for library facilities has
become more apparent with the advent of our active research program.
A library is practically a necessity if we expect to reach the heights to
which our present research program can carry us if properly supplemented with library facilities."
Grand Master Stewart also quoted Brother Everett Houser, chairman of the Research Committee, to the effect that his committee had
been "besieged with requests for books and research material."
Although not presently in position to comply, your Board of Library
Commissioners has also been requested to supply books for Masonic
study.
D) California Masons are finding it necessary to apply to Grand
Lodge libraries in other jurisdictions for books they require in their
work.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

E) Where Grand Lodges maintain active libraries - such is New
York, Iowa and Oregon. to mention only three - Masons make active
use of them. New York alone loaned more than 20,000 books last year:
the Iowa library. started in 1845 with an appropri ation of only $5, is
even more active.
F) The dignity of this Masonic jurisdiction, its extensive membership and the advancem ent of its brethren all require that Californ ia
establish a library and museum for the use of its members. the promotion of Masonic study and the interest of those who may visit our
magni8c ent temple.
2. Grand Lodge should signify to the lodges and brethren its willingness to accept and preserve gifts of books having Masonic interest and
Masonic records and mementoes.
There are many brethren in this jurisdiction who have Masonic
libraries and it is believed that if assured these would be properly cared
for, would arrange for their transfer to the Grand Lodge library. Until
it is possible to occupy the alloted space, the books should be kept, as
at present, in the "Confere nce Room" of the Temple. where they may
have some limited availability for student use, and the mementoes and
records should be stored in the Library- Museum room.
3. When the library goes into regular operation, all books which
are not rarities. or portions of sets. and which can be replaced without
exhorbitant expense. should be made available to Masons all over the
state.
There are several methods by which this can be accomplished.
Your Board of Library Commissioners does not envision a library
which would be a mere reference room for Masons living within a
convenie nt distance but an active, working service to brethren seeking
light no matter how remote their Lodges may be.
4. The library should be put into active operation only when, and
to whatever extent. Grand Lodge may direct but we believe that the
sooner library service is made available to Lodges and brethren in
remote places, even if on a limited basis, the greater will be the benefit.
5. When it becomes appropriate to remove the volumes currently
shelved in the Conference Room to the permanent location. the furniture.
shelving and cases in that space should be of a quality and nature compatible with the dignity and beauty of the Masonic Memorial Temple.
6. We recommend the continuation of the Board of Library Commissioners for the gradual development of a working library and museum
in line with the requirements of Grand Lodge and the demands of the
constituent Lodges and the brethren.

catalogu ing of the books now on hand; to Wor. Bro. Eugene Hopp and

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Grievances reports as follows:
The committee has considered 66 trial records of which 38 will be
covered by this omnibus report and the others will be the subjects of
special reports by committee members, covering petitions for restoration, appeals. reversals, and other records which require special consideration.
We again urge those having to do with trials or discipline to read
carefully the Masonic Code and trial manuals.
Copies of charges should be sent in promptly to the Grand Secretary, and it seems advisable to notify the Grand Secretary of the start
of any proceedings for so-called automatic expulsion.
In one record this year it appeared that the Master, after declaring
the expulsion of a member, asked and received the approval of the lodge
by ballot. This was not only unnecessary, but improper, but it did not
prejudice the accused and the expulsion is affirmed in this report.
Restoration of a member suspended by a lodge. and not by action of
Grand Lodge, may be made by the lodge itself and needs no approval
of Grand Lodge. 'In Trial Record No. 1562 there was such a restoration
of a suspended member by the lodge, and inasmuch as the record was
ref erred to us we approve the same.
When an accused Mason is in jail or prison, or otherwise plainly
unable to attend his trial in the lodge. he should be informed of his right
to be represented by counsel and that such counsel need not be an
attorney at law.
There seems to be much unnecessary delay in bringing matters to
trial after charges are filed in some lodges, and also delay in retrying
cases which are reversed by Grand Lodge and remanded to a lodge
for retrial. Although all trials are unpleasant they are necessary to dis-

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1389
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In addition to the usual matters before the Committee on Grievances
there has been referred to us a resolution presented by the Master and
Wardens and two Past Masters of Silver Gate Lodge No. 296, asking
that the restoration to all the rights and privileges of Masonry of a
former member of that lodge, granted at the 1958 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, be rescinded.
Since said member was restored by Grand Lodge last year, he has
been elected to membership in another lodge in San Diego.
We feel that the action requested by this resolution would be
contrary to Masonic law. Our laws provide for the methods and procedure by which a Mason's status as such and his membership in a
lodge may be takep away from him, and are exclusive. To take away his
membership by rescinding a restoration granted to him by Grand Lodge
at a former communication without notice to him or any opportunity to
be heard violates the spirit of our law.
We, therefore, move that the resolution be rejected.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1570
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A member of Patterson Lodge No. 488 entered a plea of guilty
to Grand Theft in 1957. He was placed on probation for eight years
and required to make restitution in full. He was not required to serve
any time in jail.
Masonic Charges were preferred against him by the Junior Warden
of Patterson Lodge No. 488 .. To these charges the accused made no
plea either of "guilty" or "not guilty." The Master of the Lodge then
attempted to hold a trial under the provisions of Section 692.1 et seq. of
the California Masonic Code. The record discloses, however, that the
Master failed to comply with the procedure specified in said Sections.
He failed to make a written report as required. He also failed to inake
a finding of guilty and stated that because the accused had entered a
plea of guilty in the Superior Court of Stanislaus County, he could not
make a finding of "not guilty," stating further that the accused had
already · been punished sufficiently and ruled that the accused was to
continue in good standing as a member of the lodge.
In 1958 Grand Lodge reversed the action of the 1Master and the
matter was remanded for a proper trial by Patterson Lodge.
The matter is now again before the Grievance Committee for review.
The record submitted again discloses a complete lack of compliance
with Sections 692.1 to Section 693 C.M.C. The Master did submit a
written report in which he attempts to show that the accused was guilty
of no wrongdoing and closes with_ a suggestion that a short suspension,
with a promise of immediate restoration, should be imposed on the
accused.
·
The second trial, just as the first, fails to comply with the provisions
of the C.M.C.
Your committee, therefore, offers the following resolution:
RESOLVED, That the action of the Master be reversed and Trial
Record 1570 be remanded to Patterson Lodge No. 488 for further and
proper proceedings, and that the Grand Master appoint a Trial Master
from some other lodge to conduct said trial.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1599
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A member of Palms Lodge No. 512 was accused in four specifica~
tions of:
1. Wilful negligence and failure to make arrangements for funeral
services for his mother, and allowing her body to reach an advanced
degree of decomposition.
'2. Failure to attend his mother's funeral.
3. Conviction of being drunk and serving of a jail sentence on
July 20, 1958.
4. Drunk arrest and fine on two occasions, October 23, 1957, and
September 14, 1958.
The action of the Master suspending the member was based on
amended specifications. The record shows that neither the original
charges nor the amended charges were ever served on the accused.
Although Sction 707 C.M.C. clearly provides that where service is
not made, or cannot be made, there must be an ex parte trial; the
Master proceeded as though the charges had been served on the accused
and he had failed to plead "Not Guilty" as provided in Section 692.4

C.M.C.
Because of this and other fatal errors in procedure, the case must be
reversed. InasJl1:uch as all the specifications have their origin in pro~
longed and excessive drinking, the committee would suggest that the
charge might be in one specification of habitual public intoxication
bringing discredit on the fraternity and setting forth the several episodes
as overt acts evidencing the same.
Your committee respectfully presents the following resolution:
RESOLVED, ~hat the action of the Master in trial record No. 1599
finding the accused guilty and ordering his suspension be reversed and
the matter remanded to the lodge for trial in accord with the Calif9mia
Masonic Code.
Adopted.

PROCEEDING S OP THE

Based on this letter, on July 6, 1959, the Master attempted to revert
to C.M.C. 732 and announced the accused automatical ly expelled and
again erroneously alleged that certified copies of the final judgment
of conviction of a felony had been Bled with the lodge. A copy of the
minutes of this meeting declaring "automatic expulsion" was then
sent to the accused.
The procedure herein, in all phases has been fatally defective. The
duty us upon the trial lodge to comply with the procedures set down
by this Grand Lodge, and not hope to perfect irregular procedure by
liberal interpretatio n of rules framed to safeguard against injustices.
Untrue statements relating to filing of certified copies of the judgment
cannot conceal or cure the lack of jurisdiction existant due to the absen~e
of said certified copies.
Further, the trial lodge lost jurisdiction to pronounce "automatic
expulsion" under C.M.C. 732 for the reason that the withdrawal of the
demand for trial was not received until after the sixty-day period had
lapsed. Accordingly. the lodge should have proceeded with trial under
C.M.C. 688 and 689 as required by the decision of the Grand Lodge
in 1958 and reported at C.M.C. 733b.
The lodge must start proceedings again in this case.
Wherefore, we offer the following resolution:
RESOLVE D. That the purported expulsion of a member by Arcata
Lodge No. 106 is reversed and set aside and the lodge is directed to
proceed against him as provided in the Masonic Code.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1633
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A member of Canoga Lodge No. 6H was charged in his lodge with
two specifications of lewd conduct with children, of which he had been
convicted in the Superior Court of Los Angeles County by .which he had
been placed on probation without imprisonment. Strangely the commissioners voted 4 to 3 in favor of a finding of guilt on each specification
but differed on the vote on unmasonic conduct. Lewd acts with minors
is surely unmasonic conduct. Were the procedure in this case correct we
would ask Grand Lodge to supply the finding of unmasonic conduct.
However. in this case nine commissioners were elected to try the
matter. Only seven appeared at the trial and acted. This is permissible
but Masonic law requires that a decision can only be reached by a
majority vote of the number of commissioners elected, (Section 721 j.
Masonic Code). Where the majority number cannot agree there is a
mistrial, or what in civil courts is called "a hung jury." and the case
must be retried. In this case the votes of five commissioners was
necessary to render any judgment. The vote on each specification being
fonr to three, the Master should have declared a mistrial and called a
meeting to elect a new commission.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

231

We there offer the following resolution: ·
Resolved that the purported suspension of a member by Canoga
Lodge No. 611 be reversed and the matter remanded to the lodge with
instruction to elect a new commission to try him on the charges.
Adopted.

REPORT OF THE COMMI TTEE ON NECROL OGY
To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge of California:
One of the great benefits of Masonry is the friendships it engenders .
We all know that it "causes true friendship to exist among those who
might otherwise have remained at a perpetual distance." There are the
friendships of our own lodges; those we make in our Districts and
Officers' Association, and also those made at the Communications of
Grand Lodge and in its many activities. All of us have enriched lives
through the Lodge associations and we have found strength and peace
in the warmth of its fellowship. We are indeed a "Society of friends and
brothers" and we are all deeply thankful for its blessings.
Among those who come annually to Grand Lodge Communications
there is an eagerness to meet friends we may not have seen during the
year. The warmth of handclaps, the kindly smiles of our friends and
brethren make Grand Lodge Week a session of heartwarm ing joy and
refreshment. However, there is always a measure of sadness in our
rejoicing. Some familiar faces are missing; voices we loved to hear are
stilled forever. The Scythe of Time has cut the brittle thread of life and
the souls of many of our brothers have been launched into eternity and
gathered into the land where their fathers had gone before them. Death
is an inevitable experience for all mankind.
Thomas Gray wrote:
"The boast of heraldry, the pomp of power,
And all that beauty, all that love e'er gave,
Await alike the inevitable hour.
The paths of glory lead but to the grave.
As we might very well expect, a large number of our brothers have
crossed to the land from whose bourne no traveller returns. Your Committee has to report the passing of three hundred seventy-tw o of our
members. Among these are some whom we expected to be with us for
years to come, as well as many who for long years have served faithfully and in the fulness of time have gone to their reward. Included in the
three hundred seventy-tw o are some who have served in Grand Lodge

234

and whose names are well known: Harold A. Meyer, a member of the
Charter Committee: Milton Sapiro of the Jurisprudence Committee and
former Grand Orator; Harry F. White, former member of the Endowment Board and long-time member of the Board of Control; Boy C.
Bryan, many years Chairman of the Necrology Committee; John W.
Shenk. member of Jurisprudence Committee; Ralph M. Holden, Inspector of the I 06th District of Grievance Committee; James R. Eubanks
of the Decoto Home.
The losses this year are distributed among two hundred sixty-eight
lodges. Three lodges - South San Francisco #212, Los Banos #312.
and Parnassus #388. each lost five Pastmasters; two lodges - Howard
#37 and Sunnyside #577, each lost fou.r. ten lodges lost three; sixtyeight lodges lost two, while one hundred eighty-seven lodges report
one lost each. The list this year is the longest in recent years, perhaps
for all time.
By special permission the eulogy for one of our most beloved brethren
will now be presented by Brother John W. Baker. a Pastmaster from
the same lodge as our brother.
RoY CASWELL BRYAN

The Most Worshipful Master has graciously permitted me. on behalf of Cahuenga Lodge No. 513, to bring to the attention of this Grand
Lodge the passing of a brother illustrious in Masonry, Brother Roy C.
Bryan.
Brother Roy C. Bryan was born in Texas in 1886. He died in Los
Angeles, California. in June of 1959. He was 73 years old.
Brother Bryan became an Entered Apprentice Mason on October 8.
1923. He became a Fellowcraft on November 12 of 1923. And he became
a Master Mason only a few days later on November 24 of 1923. He
became Master of Cahuenga Lodge No. 513 in 1932. And after service
as Master, for in excess of 7 years he was an Inspector of the district.
In 1951 there was adopted by the Grand Lodge a ritual to be used by
the officers of Grand Lodge. This ritual was written by Roy Bryan.
along with two other fine Masons. And even today at this present
convention of the Grand Lodge that ritual is being used.
But the stature of Roy Bryan in the minds and hearts of his friends
is measured in terms of his strength of morality. his warmth of friendliness. and his simplicity, integrity, and sageness of counselling.
Roy Bryan is the man who for so many years stood before this
Grand Lodge, at the place that I am now standing, and, as head of the
Necrology Committee, told you of the passing of so many of the
brothers. And now Roy Bryan's turn has come.
To his friends . a poet's words may be paraphrased to express their
feelings in his passing: He so lived that when his turn came to join
that innumerable caravan which journeys to that mysterious realm from
whose bourne no traveller returns he went not like a quarry slave at

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

235

night scourged to his dungeon; but sustained and soothed by an unfaltering trust. He approached his God: he approached his grave; like
one who wraps the drapery of his couch about him and lies down to
pleasant dreams.
To Masons, a poet may be paraphrased to express their thinking
on Roy's passing: That when he fell in whirlwind. he went down, as
does a lordly cedar green with boughs goes down, with a great shout
upon the hills. and leaves a lonesome place against the sky.
Our friend Roy Bryan is gone.
HAROLD ADOLPH MEYER

On October 14. 1958, Harold A. Meyer died of a cerebral hemorrhage at Children's Hospital, San Francisco. at the age of fifty-three
years.
Harold Meyer was a native San Franciscan. having been born in
this city and spent most of his life here. He graduated from LickWilmerding High School and the University of San Francisco. He
made work with boys his life work. From 1927 to 1930 he headed the
Mission Branch of San Francisco Boys' Club. In 1930 he went into
private business but in two years returned to the work he loved. He
served with the San Francisco Recreation Department as Director and
Assistant Superintendent. During World War II he served with the
Infantry and in 1947 returned to the San Francisco Boy's Club as its
Executive Director. in which position he continued until the date of
his death.
Harold Meyer was Secretary of the 1952 Grand Jury and also served
as Chairman of the Mayor's Advisory Committee on Juvenile Problems;
as National Chairman of the American Red Cross Water Safety Committee; as a member of the Juvenile Problems Committee. and as a member of the Citizen's Advisory Committee to the Attorney Genera l on
Crime Prevention. Only three weeks before his death he hi:ld been named
by the Juvenile Court Judge to the Juvenile Probation Commission.
Harold Meyer was raised in Mount Davidson Lodge #481 on
March 25, 1940. Afterward serving it as Master. He was also <1 member
of Royal Arch Masonry; California Commandery # 1 Knights Templar,
and of Islam Temple of the Shrine. In Grand Lodge he served for many
years on the Charters Committee having been first appointed in October.
1946, and had been reappointed thereon for the present year.
He was a member of many clubs in San Francisco, including the
Rotary Club.
He is survived by his wife Leonore Larson Meyer to whom our
sincere sympathy goes out.
His chief interest was the welfare of boys and youth. There are no
great economic rewards in this field but there were rich dividends in the
knowledge of boys guided into fine citizenship. In his passing at a com-

MILTON DISRAELI SAPIRO

On December 22. 1958. San Francisco lost a "just and honorable
judge" and the youth of San Francisco a devoted friend when death
came to Judge Milton D . Sapiro. While addressing a group. of Boy
Scouts at a Christmas party on December 13th. he was stncken by
cerebral hemorrhage from which he never recovered. He was 65 years
of age.
Milton Sapiro was born in Oakland, December 28. 1892. He grad~­
ated from the University of California in 1914 and studied law at U. C. s
Boalt Hall School of Law. In May. 1917. he joined the Army and was
in heavy fighting in France during which he was wounded. He was
awarded the "Purple Heart." After the war he returned to San Francisco and engaged in private practice of law until 1944 when he ~as
appointed to the Municipal Bench. He was elevated to the Supenor
Court Bench in 1947 and served until his death. For five years he served
as Juvenile Court Judge and was instrumental in bring in~ about many
changes in the City's Juvenile Department. He was a friend of youth
at all times. spending much time with Boy Scouts and other youth
organizations. The Mayor of San Francisco said "_Ma.?y of the yo~ng
people will be better citizens because of Judge Sap1ro. San Francisco
mourned his passing.
Masonically, Milton Sapiro had been a member of Fidelity Lodge

# 120 since 1921 and was a Past Master of his lodge. In Grand Lodge
he served on the Jurisprudence Committee and had been transferred to
the Grievance Committee prior to his death. He was Grand Orator in
1954-55. appointed by Grand Master Henry Clausen. A member of
Scottish Rite he had been awarded his 33rd degree.
Milton Sapiro was a member of many civic, service, and legal
organizations. The American Legion had been greatly hel~ed by. his
services and he served on the Jewish Welfare Board. He 1s survived
by his wife Edna , and two sons, Warren and Allen. to whom goes our
sympathy.
He was truly a servant of men. and Masonry has gained lustre
through his life. This Grand Lodge has been enriched by his services
and many of us miss the warmth of his kindly smile. In the many
tributes paid to him the people of San Francisco have indeed risen up
to "call him blessed."

239

On January 19. 1959. this Grand Lodge lost one of its truly beloved
members when death came to James R. Eubanks .
Brother Eubanks had been a Mason for over forty years, having
been raised in San Mateo Lodge No. 226 on M arch 21, 1918. He was
a Past Master of his lodge and was a well known member of this Grand
Lodge.
Nearly forty years of Jim's life had been devoted to the service of
elderly people; for twenty-four years. he was superintendent of San
Mateo County Old Peoples' home. On April 3rd. 1941 , he assumed
the duties of superintendent of our Home at Decoto and continued in
that office until his retirement on July 28. 1956. During his superintendency. m;rny advances were made in the care of our elderly brethren at the Home. These have contributed greatly to the physical wellbeing as well as to the morale of the members of the family. Many have
had the sunset years of life made happier and more peaceful by this
kindly man. who understandingly sought their welfare. To those of us
who visited the home. Jim was always a helpful. courteous host, whom
we lea rned to love.
During his time at Decoto. he was honored by his fellowworkers
in Ma sonic Homes by being elected to serve a term as President of the
Masonic Homes Executive Association of the United States. A colleague
said of him , "he was a man of great kindliness and was like a father
to the rest of us."
To his wife. children and grandchildren. we extend our sincerest
sympathy.
We commend him to his Heavenly Father, believing that He who
said "inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my
brethren, ye have done it unto me." has received him into the Kingdom
of the Blessed.
RALPH NEWTON HOLDEN

Ralph N. Holden. a resident of Mount Shasta, passed away on
April 21 . 1959, in his sixtieth year.
Brother Holden was raised in Sisson LodHe #310 in Mount Shasta
City on August 19. I 942 and has been a working member of his lodge
during the intervening years. H e served the lodg e as its Master in 1953
and contin ued to be a support to his brethren. On July 16. 1956 he was
appointed Inspector of District 106. comprising four lodges in Siskiyou
County. Our present Grand Master is a member of a lodge in this district. Brother Holden served in the hardworking Corps of Inspectors
until summoned to the Celestial Lodge above. He was a true and faithful Mason and a loyal member of society.

JO HN

w. SHENK

C alifornia lost one of its finest legal minds when A ssociate Justice
John W . Shenk o f the California Supreme Court, died at P alo Alto
H ospital on August 3, 1959. He had been stricken by a heart ailment
two days before. H e was eighty-four years of a ge and he and his wife.
who survives him. ha d celebra ted their golden wedding anniversary two
years ago.
Justice Shenk was born in Vermont, studied law at the University of
Michiga n. came to California and was admitted to the California Bar
in Los Angeles in 1903. He served as Deputy City Attorney then as
City Attorney for Los Angeles a nd later served for eleven years as a
Superior Court Judge in Los Angeles County. He was appointed to the
Supreme Court in 1942 by Governor Friend Richardson. He served with
great distinction in that Court up to the time of his death. A s a member
of the Court which ruled the "ham 'n egg" pension scheme of the
initiative ballot in 1948, he became the ta rget of a recall move. The
move failed as civic leaders. jurists and lawyers all over the State
ra llied indignantly to Judge Shenk's defense. H e was the recipient of
many honors incl uding honorary degrees from the University of
Michigan and the University of Southern California.
Justice Shenk was a Past Master of South Pasadena Lodge # 367.
In October, 1943 Grand M as ter Claude M orrison appointed him to the
Jurisprudence Committee and he continued to serve on that Committee
until his death.
His citation from the University of Michigan said in part " ... Schola rly in his opinions. erudite and humane in his review of cases. especially
in the area of Sociological Jurisprudence. He has brought honor to the
contribution of Michigan to bench and ba r." M asonry is proud to have
had John W. Shenk as one of its members and of the contribution he
has made to California. He lived long and served nobly.
THOMAS BENTLEY COPELAND

This Grand Lodge lost another of its faithful members w hen death
ca me to Thomas B. Copeland on August 15, 1959. He was 68 years
o f age.
F or many years he served as Local Superintendent for the Pacific
Gas and Electric Company in the R ed Bluff area. For several years he
has been in the San Francisco offices of that company.
H e was made a Mason in 1920 in Northern Light Lodrie # 190 at
Redding. He later served that lodge as Master. He was appointed
Inspector in 1951 and served for some yea rs in that capacity. In 1950-5 1
he served this Grand Lodge as Senior Grand Deacon. He served on a
special Committee whic h devised the form o f credential which we are
a ll wearin g. In 1951 he was Chairman of a special committee on balloting and devised the ba llots with which we a re a ll furnished and helped

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

241

to end the confusion which often con founded the Grand Lodge when
a ballot became necessary.
In season and out of season Thomas Copeland was a true and trusted
Mason and we a re proud to have known him as a friend and brother.
What shall we more say of the remainder of the three hundred
seventy-two who are no longer with us? Time prevents our reading
their names. A complete list is attached and made a part of this report.
lt contains the names of brethren we have known and loved. Men who
have helped us and spoken kindly, encouraging words on many
occasions. They served their Communities, their Lodges, and their
fellow men, many of them without the inspiration of much public
notice. We honor them for their contributions and will close our report
by paraphrasing a famous passage of scripture
"These all, having labored abundantly, did not finish the
tasks, Since God had provided that their labors, apart
from ours, would not be complete. Wherefore, brethren
seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses,
let us lay aside every weight and the sloth w hich does so
easily beset us, and let us run with perseverance the race
that is set before us ."
We honor them by accepting the tasks they have left behind and
giving to them the full measure of our ability and strength.

MORNING SESSION-THURSDAY, OCTOBER 1, 1959
At 10:00 a.m. Grand Lodge was called on, the Grand Master presiding. The invocation was delivered by the Grand Chaplain. The
minutes of the morning session of Wednesday, September 30th, were
read and approved.

The special order of business covering ''Public School
Fund" was the first item considered. See report of Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Several items reported on by the Committee on
Grievances are listed under Wednesday business for conveniences of reference.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON FINANCE
To T he Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
In accordance with the requirement of our Reg ulations, an audit
for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1959 has been made by the firm of
Skinner and Hammond. Certified Public Accountants. of all accounts
of Grand Lodge, the Masonic H omes, and the Memorial Temple. Your
Committee has examined these audit reports and it is our opinion that
they correctly present the financial condition of Grand Lodge, the
Homes. and the Temple Corporation.
The audit shows total revenue for the support of Grand Lodge of
$383,386. 17, and expenses and appropriations of $340,496.12. lea ving
a balance of unexpended revenue of $42,890.05, which has been transferred to Capital Account.
It s hould be noted, however. that a substantial portion of th is surplus income is represented by the unexpended budget appropriation for
Employees Retirement Pension Plan, which must be re-appropriate d
in the current fiscal year, as will be explained further in our report.
GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT
We have examined the Grand Treasurer's Report which was referred to this Committee and find all financial items to be in accord
with the audit. We recommend approval.
GRAND SECRETARY'S REPORT
That portion of the Grand Secretary's Report was re ferred to this
Committee in which he recommended that certain Lodges under Dispensation be not required to pay the Per Capita. We recommend
approval.

Master's Message in w hich he reported approval by him of expenditures in excess of budgeted items for the last fiscal year totaling $5,-

CORRESPONDENCE COMMITTEE-"CAL!FORNIA FREEMASON ..

The audit report shows that the operations of our official publication, "California Freemason," in the last fiscal year resulted in an
excess of income over expenses of $3,457.55, which was credited to
Capital Account.
We recommend that Grand Lodge approve the appropriation of
the above amount to be paid into "California Freemason Reserve" which
was established by Grand Lodge at the last annual Communication on
the recommendation of this Committee. This reserve is listed in the
balance sheet of the auditors' report and was created for the purpose
of setting up a reserve against subscriptions to the magazine paid in
advance. Your Committee is of the opinion that we should continue
to build this reserve until it at least equals the amount of advance subscriptions for which we are liable.
MASONIC HOMES

In the last annual report of the Finance Committee reference was
made to the building program at Decato under which an extensive enlargement is being made to the hospital facilities.
The Trustees of the Homes estimate a decrease in income of $60.000.00 per year, beginning this fiscal year, from capital investments
which will be liquidated to cover building costs.
In addition to this loss of income, operating expenses at the Homes
have increased in excess of $50,000.00 annually, largely due to a substantially higher wage scale.
In addition, the Homes are now paying the annual Endowment
Board expense: they are praying Grand Lodge annually for their proportionate share of utilities and maintenance expense in the Memorial
Temple; they are underwriting the expense of the delegates' visit to
Decoto during Grand Lodge Week. All these are items of expense not
borne by the Homes up until two years ago and total in excess of
$30,000.00.
As the result of our conversations with the Trustees. an examination of their report and the financial audit, we find that it will be necessary to increase the per capita for the Homes from 50c to $1.00 to
support their operating budget for the current fiscal year.
We, therefore. offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the sum of $1.00 per capita be levied for the

RETIREMENT PENSION PLAN

A previously noted, no disbursement was made during the last fiscal year of the appropriations for Retirement Pension Plan for direct
employees of Grand Lodge and those of its agencies, such as the University Clubhouses and Employment Bureaus. The Homes Board
adopted the amendment to the Plan necessary to include the above employees but we have been waiting for a communication from the I nternal Revenue Service that the P lan as amended would qualify under
the Internal Revenue Code.
Such a communication has now been received and we are ready to
proceed with the program to place the above mentiond employees
under the Retirement Pension Plan.
We are advised by the firm of Actuarial Consultants retained by
Grand Lodge that the approximate sum of $41,000.00 will be required
for direct employees of Grand Lodge to cover all costs from January
1, 1956, the established effective date. to the end of the current fiscal
year.
There has been previously set aside, or appropriated but not expended, approximately $31,000.00 for this purpose. We .recommend
that Grand Lodge approval now be given to the appropria tion from
Capital Account of $31.000.00 to be transferred to the current Administrative and Office Expense budget and paid out as required. We a.re
budgeting $10,000.00 which. together with the above appropriation,
will bring the total to the estimated amount needed.
Relative to employees of Grand Lodge agencies. applications have
been filed to bring certain of these employees under the Pension Plan .
Our Actuaries advise us that approximately $11,300.00 will be required
to cover these costs from January 1, 1959, the effective date, to the
end of the current fiscal year. There has been previously appropriated
for this purpose but not expended approximately $11,300.00. Your
Committee now recommends that Grand Lodge approval be given to
appropriation from Capital Account of $11.300.00 to be transferred to
the current Administrative and Office Expense budget and paid out
as required for employees of these Grand Lodge agencies.
For the future we anticipate that Pension Plan costs for both groups
of employees will be ascertained on an annual fiscal year basis and
the financial requirements of the program be currently met by a budget
appropriation each year.

MEMORIAL TEMPLE-CAMPAIGN FOR VOLUNTARY CONTRIBUTIONS

When the plans to secure voluntary contributions to the Building
Fund of the Memorial Temple were first presented to and approved
by Grand Lodge, the Temple Building Committee made a pledge that
every dollar contributed would go into the construction of the Temple.
Grand Lodge backed up this pledge by agreeing to underwrite all
costs of the campaign. Yau will be interested in knowing that, as of
the end of the last fiscal year, Grand Lodge has paid out of income
for this purpose over a period of six years the total sum of $185,584.92.
Incidentally. while on this point, you will be interested in knowing that, in addition to the above sum, Grand Lodge has appropriated
out of Capital Funds in the same period the total sum of $444,217.87
toward the construction cost of the Temple.
Yau are familiar with the "Open Book" now in preparation in
which will be listed the names of all voluntary contributors. Your
Committee is in agreement with the Trustees of the Temple that the
cost ~f this b~o~ is a proper charge against campaign expense and
have included 1t m the budgeted appropriation of $22,000.00 for Campaign Expense in the current year. We hope to be able to substantially
reduce this appropriation next year.

Memorial Temple, the low total per capita was $1.00 in 1946, with
the high jn 1952 and 1953 of $2.90. The average for the period was
$1.75.
For the last fiscal year the total per capita was $2.75. This is made
up of $1.00 for the Memorial Temple, 50c for the Homes, and $1.25
for the expenses of Grand Lodge. Deducting the $1.00 for the Memorial Temple, we find that the remainder of $1.75 is only 20c above the
30 year average of $1.55 for ordinary expenses, or approximately 13%.
Another striking comparison can be made with the year 1933. In
that year the total per capita was $1.75, all for regular expenses of
the Homes and Grand Lodge. Today, 26 years later, in spite of the
40 cent dollar and much higher administrative and operating expense,
the per capita for such purposes is the same-$1.75. This has been
possible, of course, because the number of members for whom the
per capita is paid has increased in that 26-year period from 140,000 to
235,000.
The increased revenue from membership growth fortunately has
matched the increase in cost of operation, with something over for
buildmg the reserves of Grand Lodge.
However, in the new fiscal year the Homes, for the reasons given,
will require, and you have voted an increase in the per capita from 50c
to $1.00 to support their operating budget.
In endeavoring to hold down your per capita tax to the lowest possible figure, your Committee gave considerable thought and study to
the present and future position of the Reserves of Grand Lodge and
the necessity, we feel, of not only maintalning them, but gradually
adding to them. We point out that these reserves are invested and
earning income, without which your per capita would be proportionately higher. It is simply good business to maintain this Grand Lodge
on a sound financial base.
Our reserves have been built largely from surplus income and can
be kept intact and increased only if we spend less than we take in. We
assume that this is an aim which meets with your approval.
As noted, the budget will allow for a small surplus to add to
Grand Lodge reserves, but only if all concerned stay within budgeted
appropriations, and no emergency needs arise.
The obvious is sometimes overlooked. The most likely prospect of
a future reduction in per capita tax is in the elimination of the $1.00
per member paid to the Memorial Temple Corporation. It bears repeating that the earlier the debt on the Temple is liquidated, the earlier
can the Lodges be relieved of this levy. That day can be brought closer
with a renewed determination that every Lodge in this jurisdiction shall
achieve the Merit Roll.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution:

PER CAPITA
Your Committee has made an analysis of annual per capita for the
last 30 years covering the period 1929-1959. You will be interested
in some comments on the figures disclosed.
For the period covered, and referring only to that portion of
the annual per capita paid for the support of the ordinary activities
of Grand Lodge and the Homes, the low was 85c in 1946 and 1947,
with the high in 1949 and 1950 of $1.95. The average for the 30 years
was $1.55.
It should be noted that the 85c low in 1946-47 included nothing
for the Homes, but was entirely for support of Grand Lodge. The
Homes had been able to build surplus during the preceding war years
due ·to the restricted supply of building and other materials available
for purchase.

REVOLVING LOAN FUND
THE COMMITTEE ON FINANCE:
There has been referred to the .Pinance Committee the resolution
which would add a new Section No. 288 to our Code under which a
per capita of indeterminate amount would be levied on the Lodges to
create a "Revolving Fund for Loans to Lodges for Building Purposes."
Your Committee believes that it would be unwise for Grand Lodge
to incorporate such a plan into our Regulations.
Recognizing the good motive behind the proposal. we are of the
opinion, nevertheless, that it is outside the scope of Grand Lodge to go
into the loan business. It should be noted that in cases of real emergency
and, at times, distress, Grand Lodge has not been unsympathetic to the
needs of constituent Lodges, and in a number of cases has voted financial
assistance.
The resolution proposes that the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge
Financing administer the Loan Fund which it seeks to establish. This
Committee is of considerable assistance to Lodges in working out
financial plans for new Masonic Halls.
If the knowledge and experience jointly held by this Committee
and the members of a Lodge with whom it .counsels cannot arrange
from the resources of the Lodge itself a sound financial building program,
we doubt the wisdom of asking all Lodges of this jurisdiction to tax
themselves to underwrite such a building project.
For the above reasons the Finance Committee opposes the adoption
of this resolution and recommends a "No" vote.
The Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General Purposes,
on Lodge Financing. and on Local Temple Association Finances reported their concurrence.
Defeated by majority vote.

REPORT OF COMMITTE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In the spring of this year the Chairman of this Committee, while on
a tour around the world, visited several Grand Lodges.
In Tokyo he was graciously received by the Grand Master of the
Grand Lodge of Japan, Most Worshipful Sadaichi Horiuchi, Right
Worshipful George Togasaki, Deputy Grand Master, Right Worshipful
Carl T. Nakamura, Senior Grand Warden, Very Worshipful Nohea
0. A. Peck. Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful George B. Margulis,
Grand Secretary, Worshipful George H. Booth, Junior Grand Lecturer.
Worshipful Norman Cohen, Master of Square & Compus Lodge No. 3
and Worshipful Francisco A. B. Yule, Master of Far East Lodge No. 1
of Y okahama. The Grand Master is an outstanding lawyer and a

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

263

dedicated ~ason: This Grand Lodge has been recognized by more than
seventy Jurisdictions. Its financial condition is excellent and it has a
major interest in the exceedingly valuable property on which the Grand
Lodge Temple rests. Its future is bright. The only cloud which casts
its shadow is the fact that the Grand Lodge of the Philippines, some
1500 miles distant, as a price of recognition, retains jurisdiction over
four Lodges in Japan and deprives the new Grand Lodge of Japan of
needed revenue and fraternal cooperation. This invades the jurisdiction
of~ local Grand Lodge and may be characterized as Colonial Masonry,
which should have no place in our modern concept of Masonic freedom.
M~st -yv~rshipful George Fitch, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of China, invited our Chairman to visit him at Taipei, Taiwan, but illness
precluded acceptance; however, the Grand Master with the assistance of
Brother Alfred S. Lee, Past Grand Secretary, caused a luncheon meeting
to be held in Hong Kong at which prominent Masons of China paid
respects to our Chairman.
The Chairman was entertained by members of the Grand Lodge of
Egypt in Cairo in Lodge Ani No. 384. Similar courtesies were accorded him in a previous visit in 1956.
In company with Hon. Newcomb Condee, Chairman of our Committee on Correspondence, our Chairman attended the Quarterly
Communication of the United Grand Lodge of England in June. The
Assistant Grand Master, General Adair, and Very Worshipful J. W.
Stubbs, Grand Secretary, were attentive and gracious. Both were personally present as our guests at our last Annual Communication and
were still singing the praises of their fraternal treatment while here.
The United Grand Lodge of Germany, as such, has disappeared
and a new Grand Lodge has been created bearing the name United
Grand Lodges, Brotherhood of Freemasons in Germany, which represents a consolidation of the old United Grand Lodge and certain other
Grand Lodges called Land Grand Lodges and Grosse Landeslodge, the
latter being the surviving Christian (Swedish Rite) Grand Lodge. It is
~ncertain whether the Swedish system will be used. In light of this, it
is necessary that our recognition of the United Grand Lodge of Germany be cancelled. Because of this transition, problems have arisen
which have not yet responded to solution. The new Grand Lodge also
recognizes the Grand Lodge of France, which fact confers no blessings.
The petition for recognition of the new United Grand Lodges, Brotherh~d of Freemasons in Germany, is before us but we suggest that no
action be taken thereon at this time and that such be laid over for
further investigation and study.
The situation in Guatemala is still baffling. In 1923 we recognized
the Grand Lodge of Guatemala ( 1923 Proc. 700). During the year 1954
a political revolution occurred in Guatemala, which resulted in a new
government under a military Junta, which ordered dissolution of the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

264

Grand Lodge on the specious grounds that the officers thereof engaged
in pro-Communist activities, but it granted the right to form a new
Grand Lodge. The new Grand Lodge was formed under the same name,
using the same address as the old. The clash between the so-called new
Grand Lodge and the old Grand Lodge still exists. A petition for
recognition of said Grand Lodge is before us but we recommend that
same be denied and that our fraternal relations continue with the old
Grand Lodge, known as the Bianchi group.
We have given consideration to a petition for recognition by The
Lebanese Grand Lodge of Beirut, Lebanon, which we suggest be held
and study because of the confused frater0 ver for further investigation
nal and political conditions which obtain in that country and for further
reason thsit the source of the Grand Lodge is not certain.
Under consideration also is a petition for recognition from the Grand
Lodge of Pernambuco, Brazil, but the facts and information respecting
the organization and tenure of said Grand Lodge are not clear so we
suggest that said petition be held over for further investigation and
study. Another reason too is the fact that Masonry in Brazil is greatly
confused. In existence there is a federated Grand Lodge bearing the
name Grand Orient of Brazil. which is recognized by the United Grand
Lodge of England but not recognized by us. There are some seventeen
individual State Grand Lodges. some fourteen of which are recognized
by us but none by the United Grand Lodge of England. Generally
speaking, the State Grand Lodges recognize each other and some recognize. to the extent of intervisitation, the Grand Orient of Brazil.
Lastly, we have examined the petition for recognition from the Grand
Lodge of Santa Catarina located in the Capitol, Florianopolis. Santa
Catarina is one of the small states in the southern part of Brazil. which
is in the Temperate Zone, just north of the State of Rio Grande Do
Sul. The petition indicates that this Grand Lodge meets all of our tests
for recognition. It has been recognized by the Grand Lodge of Rio
Grande Do Sul, which is recognized and respected by us, and by some
nine jurisdictions of the United States. We, therefore, recommend that
this Grand Lodge be recognized by the Grand Lodge of California.
We. therefor. move adoption of this report, suggestions and recommendations.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The regular session of the 1959 California Legislature has made
changes in the Unemployment Insurance Code which may affect some
of our Masonic organizations. Effective January 1. 1960, the taxable
wage base for unemployment insurance will be raised from a maximum
of $3,000 to a maximum of $3,600. In addition, the maximum contribution rate will be increased from 2.7% to 3%. effective January 1, 1961.
The Legislature further provided that a separate fund be established,
through employer taxes ranging from .05% to .2% of taxable wages paid
beginning January 1, 1959, to provide extended benefits whenever unemployment in the State reaches 6%.
For reference purposes, there is presented a schedule of rates and
tax bases for various payroll taxes which under present laws will be
effective January 1, 1960, and thereafter.

THE COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENC E:
Certain Past Masters have presented a resolµtion to amend Section
161 (4th) to appoint as an officers' coach a qualified Past Master of a
Lodge of this jurisdiction. The present section requires that he be a
qualified Past Master of the Lodge. It is pointed out that newly constituted Lodges frequently lack such a qualified person. It is therefore
recommended that the following resolution be adopted:
RESOLVED : That Section 161 (4th) of the C. M. C. be repealed
and the following enacted in lieu thereof:
"161 (4th) To appoint _in each Lodge within his district an
Officers' Coach who shall be a qualified Past Master of a Lodge of this
Jurisdiction, and who shall serve at the pleasure of the Inspector. The
Officers' Coach shall assist in teaching the ritual to the officers of the
Lodge, and assist in preparing them to qualify for advancement."
We move adoption of the resolution and recommend a "Yes" vote.
The Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on Ritual
reported their concurrence.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

SERVICE OF SUMMONS

If the Lodge which expelled petitioner was not the Lodge of which
he was then a member, similar notice shall be given to the Lodge of
which petitioner was a member at the time of his expulsion, if the same
was a Lodge within the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge.
The notice must be read at the next stated meeting of the Lodge
after its receipt by the Secretary and the Master must state to the members present that a vote may be taken then or at the following stated
meeting on the question of approval or disapproval of the restoration. If
a motion is made and seconded either to approve or disapprove the
restoration a secret vote by written ballot shall be taken and the result
entered in the minutes, and the secretary shall promptly notify the Grand
Secretary of the result of said ballot.
The Master shall also announce that any member may express his
endorsal of or objection to the restoration by communication to the
Grand Secretary or that any member may orally state his approval or
disapproval to the Master. Prior to the opening of the next annual
communication of Grand Lodge the Master shall inform the Grand
Secretary in writing the number of endorsers and of objectors.
The Committee on Grievances reported their concurrence.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

Service of Summons. If the accused be with~n the jurisdiction of

The following points are disclosed:

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

( 1 ) Title to the real property in each instance is vested in the name
of an appropriate corporation.
( 2 ) The active management of each corporation is entrusted to a
Board of Directors who are elected upon nomination by the
Grand Master. This conforms to the practice which has been
in use by the Masonic Homes for many years.
The report further discloses that each corporation is operated subject
to the rules, regulations and discipline of Grand Lodge.
Because of these reasons, the Policy and General Purposes Committee believes that no change in the corporate set up, or method of selecting
directors is necessary or desirable. Adequate controls exist and any
change would merely complicate the present operation which is admittedly satisfactory.
The Grand Master, at all times, has in his power authority to control
and guide each Board. The Boards, in turn, have ample means to determine administrative policy subject to his limitations.
We feel. however, that it is desirable that copies of the "Articles of
Incorporation" of both Clubhouses, together with appropriate By-Laws,
be Bled with the Grand Secretary.
We also suggest that photostats of Deeds and Title Instruments
also be placed with the Grand Secretary for safekeeping.
One section of the report states, "lt is the opinion of the members of
the Committee that the relatively limited use of the Clubhouse facilities
is due to the lack of adequate publicity or communications within the
Masonic Bodies."
It would appear to us that a joint effort on the part of both Clubhouses in presenting their excellent facilities to the general membership
of Masonic Bodies through periodic bulletins would accomplish much
good.
Likewise, a close tie to campus activities through student committees
or g·r oups would be desirtble.
We believe that the Directors of each Club should develop within
their own groups adequate programs of communication along the lines
suggested.
We compliment the Committees who compiled the reports under
review and recommend that the 1958 report of the "Special Committee
on Clubhouses" be received and filed.
Adopted.

The primary feature of the proposal is embodied in its concern
for the portraits of Past Grand Masters and portraits of future Grand
Masters.
The Special Committee on the Disposition of Past Grand Masters'
Portraits has reported and the adoption of its report disposed of this
particular section of the resolution.
Most of the remaining items in the resolution are matters which
generally come under the supervision and direction of the Grand
Secretary.
We have complete confidence in his ability to supervise and direct
the preparation of drawings, scrolls and other artistic items which
Grand Lodge may direct to his care.
Further, we see no good reason why Grand Lodge should undertake
to assist constituent Lodges in any problem when its very nature is
peculiar to the particular Lodge in question.
We, therefore, urge that this resolution be rejected.
To bring the matter before Grand Lodge, I move the resolution.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee recommend a "No"
vote.
The Committees on Jurisprudence and on Finance reported their
concurrence.
Defeated by majority vote.

DUES COLLECTION EXPENSE
THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY
AND GENERAL PURPOSES:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had referred
to it, the resolution to amend Section 581 of the California Masonic Code
to provide that any member restored within two years after suspension
for non-payment of dues shall, in addition to paying the arrearages due,
be required to pay the costs expended by the Lodge on account of his
delinquency. such as telephone calls, registered letters. telegrams, et
cetera.
Your Committee can appreciate the exasperation often occasioned by
habitual delinquents, and agrees in principle with the idea that such

276

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

thoughtless brethren should not be permitted to cause the Lodge needless
expenditures. However, we feel that the proposed resolution is not in
keeping with sound business practice and that the exercise of the
authority proposed might create ill will out of all proportion to the small
monetary savings accruing to the Lodges.
We, therefore, move the resolution and recommend a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported their concurrence.
Defeated by majority vote.

COMMITTEE ON COMMERCIALI SM
At the 1958 Communication of the Grand Lodge, there was referred
to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, the report of the
Committee on Commercialism to which was appended "Regulations
Governing Organizations Subject to the Jurisdiction of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California."
At that time, your Committee did not have sufficient time to make the
detailed study that they felt was necessary to recommend action on the
regulations, and asked that the referral be continued for report at this
communication.
After a careful perusal of the five r~gulations, your Committee is of
the unanimous opinion that the regulations proposed do nothing more
than spell out in layman's language, the present existing law relative to
advertising, public support. solicitation of gifts, commercial ventures,
and gambling, as they pertain to organizations requiring Masonic affiliation or sponsorship, as well as constituent Lodges. Also included
with the regulations is a definition of the organizations to which they
apply in order to preclude possible misunderstandings.
The report of the Committee on Commercialism states that its
reasons for gathering together these regulations is for the purpose of
preventing unwilling violations of our law on the part of the various
prerequisite groups and it expresses the hope that copies of the regulations will be sent to all groups affected.
Inasmuch as these regulations involve no new law, but merely are a
serious attempt to gather together and to clarify our laws as regards the
affiliated groups, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes offers
the following resolution and recommends its adoption.
Resolved that the Regulations appended to the 1958 Report of the
Committee on Commercialism as exhibited in the 1958 Proceedings
(pages 126-127) and approved by Grand Master Leo E. Anderson, be
and are hereby approved and that appropriate distribution to the Lodges
and affected organizations be arranged.
Adopted.

COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY

The report of the History Committee at the last communication of
Grand Lodge included an extended outline providing for the creation
of Registered Historic Masonic Landmarks throughout the jurisdiction.
No action was taken at that Communication, and the proposal now has
been referred to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
Your Committee is cognizant of the fine work of the History Committee and is sympathetic with the idea of preserving worthwhile Masonic Landmarks. We feel. however, that rather than to provide for
doing so on so broad and extended a basis as the proposition provides
that if and when a worthwhile landmark is brought to the attention of
Grand Lodge, that it should and will handle the matter at that time.
Your Committee, therefore, moves the adoption of the following
resolution.
RESOLVED: That the recommendation of the History Committee
made in 1958, relative to the establishment of a program of Registered
Historic Masonic Landmarks, be not approved.
Adopted.

REQUIRING WRITTEN BALLOT
THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY
AND GENERAL PURPOSES:
To the Committee on Policy and General Purposes has been referred
the proposal to amend Section 582 of the California Masonic Code,
which concerns the method of restoring a member who has been suspended for non-payment of dues, by striking the words "a two-thirds
vote by ballot" and substituting the words "a two-thirds vote by written
ballot."
•
Section 323.5 of the Californ~a Masonic Code defines a "ballot" to
mean a secret vote by balls and cubes or slips of paper. A Master,
therefore, has his choice of voting by either the balls and cubes or the
written ballot method.
The proposed amendment would restrict the method of voting to a
written ballot and this Committee believes that the Master should have
the right to select either method of balloting.
In order to present the matter, we move the resolution and recommend a "no" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported their concurrence.
Defeated by majority vote.

RA TIO OF CUBES IN BALLOT BOX
THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY
AND GENERAL PURPOSES:
To the Committee on Policy and General Purposes has been referred
a proposal to amend Section 533 C. M. C. which describes the method

278

279

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

, of preparing the ballot box. and requires that one-third of the total
number of balls and cubes must be cubes.
This resolution proposes to change this to require that one-fifth of
the total number of balls and cubes must be cubes.
The Committee can find no advantage to such a change, but we can
find a serious disadvantage. In voting upon restorations, a two-thirds
vote ~s required to restore the member. Conversely, it requires over
thirty-three per cent to reject the member. This might be impossible to
accomplish if twenty per cent of the ballots were cubes.
In order to present the matter, we move the resolution and recommend a "no" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported their concurrence.
Defeated by majority vote.

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK SCHOLARSIDP AW ARDS
THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY ·
AND GENERAL PURPOSES:
To the Committee on Policy and General Purposes has been referred
the resolution to develop scholarship award programs.
Your Committee on Policy and 1General Purposes recognizes the
importance of maintaining our public school system as well as the desirability of providing scholarships to worthy students.
It is the opinion of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes,
however, that the amount of money which a Lodge could make available
each year would be too small to adequately provide the expenses of even
one student. Because of the limited funds available the program would
not be effective.
Furthermore, such a contribution of Lodge funds would fall in the
same category of Lodges contributing to other forms of charity.
In order to present the matter. we move the resolution and your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "no" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported their concurrence.
Defeated by majority vote.

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION-SECOND MONDAY
OF OCTOBER
THE COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has considered the proposed
resolutions relating to the establishment of a regular meeting date for
Grand Lodge and recommends the following resolution.
RESOLVED: That Section 101 C. M. C. be amended to read as
follows:
101. Annual. Each Annual Communication shall be held in the
City of San Francisco, commencing on the second Monday of October,
at ten o'clock a.m.; provided, however. that any Annual Communication
may be held at any other place in the State of California upon adoption
by this Grand Lodge at any previous Annual Communication by a flvesixths vote of a resolution so providing.
THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY
AND GENERAL PURPOSES:
To the Committee on Policy and General Purposes have been referred two Resolutipns indentifled as B-1 and B-2, each proposing to
amend Section 101, C. M. C. relating to the date for convening the
annual communication of the Grand Lodge.
Resolution B-1 would provide that each annual communication of
the Grand Lodge be held commencing on Monday of the last full week
in September.
. Resolution B-2 would provide that each annual Communication be
held commencing on the second Monday of each October.
Your Committee recognizes that any date which might be set for
the convening of Grand Lodge could be inconvenient for some who
attend. But your Committee is also aware of widespread dissatisfaction
over the present date.
This Grand Lodge held its annual communication beginning on
the second Monday in October each year from 1864 to 1955. In 1955 the
annual meeting was scheduled for Monday. October 24, in order to
obtain the facilities of the Civic Auditorium on which a prior commitment had been made to another organization for the second week in
October. Since 1955, the dates for convening Grand Lodge have been
shifted from time-to-time in order to again obtain the facilities of the

280

281

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Civic Auditorium, and to conform to special ceremonies of the Grand
Lodge.
It is interesting to note that during more than 90 years the brethren
of this jurisdiction have attended Grand Lodge in ever-increasing
numbers, completely satisfied with the date established for convening
the annual communication nearly 100 years ago.
Your Committee is of the opinion that any additional time gained
between the close of the fiscal year and the convening of Grand Lodge
would be most helpful to the experts who audit the accounts of Grand
Lodge, to the Grand Secretary's office and to the Committees charged
with the preparation of Grand Lodge budgets and financial statements.
While your Committee is sympathetic with the motives that
prompted the Resolution identified as B-1. we believe it to be in the
best interests of the craft to again convene the Grand Lodge on the
second Monday of each October.
Your Committee, therefore, respectfully recommends that Resolution
B-2, providing for convening the Grand Lodge on the second Monday
of each October, be adopted.
Defeated by majority vote.

THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY
AND GENERAL PURPOSES:
Resolution D-1 offered on behalf of the Grand Lodge Investment
Committee by Brother Paul A. PRueger, Assistant Grand Treasurer anc!
Past Master of Amity Lodge No. 370, provides for the amendment of
Section 246-l and 246-3 of our ordinances.
These sections provide an investment formula for Grand Lodge
funds. Within the limits of the formula the Investment Committee has
complete discretion. The present sections specify that at least 40% of
the funds must be invested in Group l items; to wit cash or the securities
therein specified; up to 20% may be invested in Group 2 securities and
up to 40% may be invested in Group 3 investments; to wit common
stocks and shares C1f Investment Trusts.
The proposal is to change the formula now in effect by substituting
20% for the 40% now provided for Group l and increasing the percentage allowable for Group 3 investments from 40% to 60%.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has discussed at
great length with the representatives of the Grand Lodge Investment
Committee the reason for the proposed change of percentages.
It is the view of this reporting Committee that the present general
economic outlook and the Ructuating prices of appropriate investments
justify arming the Investment Committee with this change in our ordinances.
We believe that this change is reasonably necessary to insure the
protection of Grand Lod9e assets under the rapidly changing conditions.
We know that the Investment Committee will use this additional

We move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a Yes
vote.

BINGO RESTRICTIONS
THE COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE:
There has been referred to your Committee on Jurisprudence a
resolution to amend Section 685-d to permit the playing of bingo. We,
therefore, present the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That Annotation "d" of Section 685 C. M. C. be
repealed and that there by substituted therefor a new Annotation "d"
'lo read as follows:
"685-d-The playing of bingo as a form of entertainment in Lodges
and so-called collateral Masonic organizations is permissible, provided
the following restrictions are complied with:
1. Attendance must be limited to members of the Lodge or organization and their families and guests.
2. No charge can be made, directly or indirectly, for attendance or
· ·
participation in the game.
3. Prizes awarded must be of nominal value, such as boxes of candy,
or items of similar value.
4. There can be no lottery. drawing or raffle for prizes conducted
·
incident to such game.
5.· The event cannot be advertised or publicized other than in the

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

regularly published bulletins to members of the Lodge or organization.
6. If a dinner is held preceding the playing of bingo and a charge
is made for the dinner, it must be clearly understood that no portion of
the charge is for the bingo game and that members who do not attend the
dinner are privileged to play bingo without making a payment of any
kind or description."
I move the adoption of the foregoing resolution and your Committee
on Jurisprudence recommends a "Yes" vote.
Defeated by majority vote.
THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY
AND GENERAL PURPOSES:
There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes a resolution to amend Section 685-D to permit the playing of
Bingo as a form of entertainment in Lodges and so-called collateral
Masonic organizations. with the following restrictions:
1. Attendance must be limited to members of the Lodge or organization and their families and guests.
2. No charge can be made, directly or indirectly, for attendance or
participation in the game.
3. Prizes awarded must be of nominal value, such as boxes of candy,
or items of similar value.
4. There can be no lottery, drawing or raffle for prizes conducted
incident to such game.
5. The event cannot be advertised or publicized other than in the
regularly published bulletins to members of the Lodge or organization.
Your Committee has carefully studied the resolution and the arguments in favor of its adoption and is of the opinion that no element of
gambling exists, when no charge is made for participation in the game.
We found that prior to 1955, many of our Lodges held Bingo parties
and found it to be a very popular form of entertainment and one generally enjoyed by the members. Even some church groups allow Bingo as
a form of social activity, where, if it was considered gambling, it would
not be permitted.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes fails to find any
evidence of harm to our fraternity because of Bingo being played as
entertainment in the Lodges. We do, however, feel that one point should
be emphasized, that if a dinner is held preceding the playing of Bingo
and a charge is made for the dinner, it must be clearly understood that no
portion of the charge is for the Bingo game and that members who do not
attend the dinner are privileged to play Bingo without making a payment
of any kind or description.
I move adoption of the resolution and your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.
Defeated by majority vote.
